Representing the DR requestor Mr. Brayton lives on the top floor of 2919 Pacific Avenue, east of the subject property at 2935 Pacific Avenue. Mr. Brayton's bedroom, bathroom and kitchen windows all enjoy light and air from his light well with the exception of two north-facing windows in his apartment.  These light well windows constitute all of the windows in his apartment. The light well abuts the light well of the subject building. At issue today is an elevator penthouse, which the developer proposes to build immediately to the south and west. My client is concerned that the elevator penthouse will negatively impact the light afforded to all three of the apartments in the building that have windows on the light well. My client believes that allowing the construction of the elevator penthouse would conflict with the city's General Plan, which is designed to ensure housing that represents good housing standards for all city residents, including the standards for light and air. The original plans for this project show a proposed internal elevator stopping before it reaches the roof. To my knowledge, no neighborhood opposition was filed. The subsequent plan, which is before you today, has the elevator climbing to the roof. It is being opposed because of the negative effect on the neighborhood light well. We have suggested that the developer move the elevator penthouse away from the light well. The developer has stated that at this late date it would be impractical to relocate the elevator because the elevator shaft has already been framed on the inside of the building. In response, I would submit that the date is too late to be applying for an application for an elevator penthouse. This should have been proposed at the inception of the project and discussed before the framing began. It's simply too late to be asking for this addition. Our second concern balances the utility of the elevator penthouse with the utility of the adjacent light well. I would respectfully submit that the utility of light pouring into three of the units in this building overrides the utility of having an elevator climbing to the roof of a single residence, especially where there is an alternative stair access to the roof. The developer has stated that the owner wishes to provide roof access to his elderly parents who will be living in the building. However, there are two features on the roof–a spa and a view deck–which are accessed not just by taking the stairs or the elevator to the roof, but also by then climbing additional stairs up to the spa and up to the view deck. One who can climb the additional stairs to the two roof features can certainly climb the internal stairs to the roof and not rely on an elevator to do so. Therefore, I believe the utility of the elevator to the roof is very small and the utility of light is very great. Finally, I'd like to say we have reviewed the architect's shadow plans and feel there will be a significant impact from the elevator shaft most times of the year.

I think the idea of retaining a wait-list is something we'd like to study in more depth. There are so many people involved that need housing and they tend to get stale very quickly. We would like to figure out what the best way to kind of meet the goals of the proposal from Supervisor Maxwell's legislation, but we don't feel comfortable moving forward with it as it is expressed today. We are supportive of the staff recommendation.  There are some wonderful ideas here.  Many of them we have already incorporated and would ask that you hold off on the ones that really are the subject of the study.

Sunrise Senior Living Sunrise's mission is to serve seniors. They've been in business for 25 years and they've done very well. We've wanted to be in San Francisco for some time, but the barriers to entry are pretty significant.

We have a new product a property on Van Ness that we are starting through the Planning process. We've been in the pipeline for maybe 18 months. We've done our site submittal permit process. When you do a feasibility for a project and you pay top dollar for the property, you figure the affordability and all that as far as resale. We added the 12% figured into it. Our project is only 62 units.  We're smaller.  To share that hit for an increase at this stage, really, it compromises the project. We'd like some type of grandfathering or something that would give us a little bit of leeway instead of having to make it retroactive for those who don't have a building permit because we've done everything on our side to move it through the process.

Morrison & Forester Generally we agree with the staff recommendation We do have a problem with the grandfathering element. Currently Section 315.3 would not fix the inclusionary requirements to which a project is subject until the project has received a site or building permit. The staff report recognizes that fixing the inclusionary requirements at the date of issuing a building permit would be inequitable and instead has recommended the amendment to the inclusionary housing requirements would apply to projects until they receive Planning Commission approval. An amendment should apply to projects while they're pending the Planning Commission approval. However, even if staff's proposal is incorporated into section 315.3, it would still impose a great hardship on project sponsors by eliminating any certainty that these sponsors would have when they're negotiating their land purchases. The inclusionary housing requirements have a big impact on land value on how much a project sponsor can afford to pay for a piece of land. The number and subsidy level, below market-rate units that must be included is a key piece of information the sponsor needs before purchasing the land.  Without knowing what percentage must be constructed below market-rate will affect the subsidy of the units until after entitlement. Because Planning Commission approval for larger projects is not typically received until two years after a land purchase agreement has been executed.  Supervisor Maxwell's amendment even with staff's proposed change would require project sponsors to purchase land without having a solid idea of how much they can feasibly pay for that land. A more equitable solution would be to fix the provision of the inclusionary ordinance that would apply to a project sponsor on the date of filing of the project sponsor's first application for the project. The requirements would follow the project through its entitlement because the first application typically occurs after a land deal is finalized. Also, the Zoning Administrator and the Board of Supervisors agree there needs to be an exception within the inclusionary housing ordinance to deal with certain special care facilities such as residential care facilities for seniors with dementia. Two possible solutions is that the definition of rent should not include charges related to non-housing services including food services, medical care, personal assistance in these special care facilities. Another would be that the residential inclusionary housing affordable program should not regulate these special care facilities.

McCarthy and Schwartz Ditto to the comments of Ms. Schindler. I too agree that the administrative issues are best served by having staff and the Mayor's office of Housing work those out. We support those recommendations. In addition, we support the recommendation that you defer any decision on the substantive changes in the BMR until you get the report. I would like to address the grandfather clause. First of all, the one from Supervisor Maxwell is far too late in the game. I want to make it clear that this is an amendment to 315, which means it doesn't just apply to Supervisor Maxwell's legislation.  It applies to any adjustments to the BMR in the future. We'd like to suggest as Ms. Schindler has done that the grandfather clause be on the date of the first filing. Staff has indicated you have what's called the rush to judgment and the defense of filings where people file and sit on them. We think if you move the date up to the first filing, there should be a review by staff, perhaps the Zoning Administrator, once a year to determine whether or not the project sponsor is actually diligently pursuing the project. And if in fact the Zoning Administrator makes a determination they are not, then there would be fair game for any changes in the BMR legislation. And just to ensure that there is transparency and an opportunity to appeal if there is a disagreement with the Zoning Administrator's yearly report that could be appealed to the Board of Appeals. Following are some suggestions the Zoning Administrator should take into account to ensure that people are not banking their application:  After there has been a planner assigned for the environment, that person should determine whether the project sponsor is taking advantage of having a scoping meeting, that following the scoping meeting the project sponsor has engaged a professional environmental consultant to press forward with the environmental evaluation.  He should also consider things like as or when the project sponsor has asked or responded to meetings to discuss design and other approvals; that prior to the time that either a negative declaration or EIR is published, that the project sponsor have filed all of the other needed applications and requests whether they be variances, whether they be conditional uses, whether they be 309 exceptions prior to the publication of the negative declaration and the EIR.

Pillsbury I'm a real estate and land use attorney at the Pillsbury firm here in San Francisco. I'd like to echo the remarks of the previous two speakers We have proposed an amendment that is very similar to the one that Morrison and Forester and Ms. Schindler's firm have proposed this week. We have added on language to address the concern about the rush to filing, and then the potential for the project sponsors to subsequently sit on the applications. What this carved out language basically does is looks back to the first application filing date. If you have an application on file prior to this ordinance becoming effective, then you are carved out. From there it goes on to basically say that you can't just sit on your application.  You have to continue to diligently pursue it with the Department. It is up to the Zoning Administrator to evaluate whether project sponsors are sitting on their applications. That is done through a series of criteria that the Zoning Administrator may look at to determine whether or not the project sponsor is still actively pursuing the application. That includes whether or not the sponsor has participated in a scoping meeting with MEA.  Subsequent to such a meeting, has the project sponsor engaged an environmental consultant to work with the department?  Then whether the project sponsor has filed all other applications with the department that would be necessary for a site or building permit to be issued for the project.  Then finally whether the project sponsor has hired an architect and submitted conceptual plans and has, subject to the department's resources, been able to meet with the department to go over the project design.  The Zoning Administrator would make that determination. If the project sponsor disagreed, the project sponsor would have the right to appeal that decision along the lines of any other type of Zoning Administrator appeals. We think this is a fair fix for the legislation. We think it's necessary, in any event, because the way the legislation is currently drafted, if you got your CU yesterday, it's unclear what your requirements are.

South of Market Community Action Network and South of Market (SOMA) Community We agree with the recommendations supervisor Maxwell has presented. On-site, off-site and in lieu.  Those are strong recommendations. Those are amendments that need to be made to the inclusionary housing and we stand in support. I ask you to pass this as amended and end the inclusionary housing fiasco that is before us not.

Council of Community Housing Organizations I'd like to substantially support staff's recommendation except in those areas that I disagree with staff's recommendation, which is twofold. We have proposed an amendment that we think will address one of Mr. Badiner's concerns, which is the definitional question of what is a project. There is a real world situation out there in which there's parcelization going on – sometimes three and four different parcels of two or three units have come in – although the total is nine or ten or 12 units, they come in under the 10. We have some language that we think will address that and also deal with Mr. Badiner's concern about defining what is a project in a little bit more rigorous way. First I'd like to speak to two other matters.  One is staff's recommendation that you not go forward on the off-site requirement, that you hold that for the study. I think that's a misplaced assumption that this is an economic issue. It's not an economic issue. It's basically a policy question. This City and County either supports inclusionary zoning on-site or it doesn't. The recommendation for a one-mile radius is I think a rational approach. 85, 90% of these projects are south of Market and east of Van Ness. 85, 90% of the potential off-site project sites are south of Market and east of Van Ness. No one has ever proposed doing a project in Rincon Hill and building the affordable housing in Pacific Heights. It's not going to happen. If you actually do the math, the one-mile radius I think is the reality of the situation. A majority of commissioners have repeatedly said we want the units on-site.  We don't want them off-site. That's what this legislation will guarantee. It's not an economic impact. The question is when should this apply? I'm happy to see that the big-time attorneys are arguing because at least some of them understand what the game is. That is parking and approval. Getting approval for a project at an old rate of fees and requirements and sitting on that project; and that you have no ability of hurrying that developer on. If we say they've got to pay the fees, in effect, when they pull their planning/building permit, which is what the ordinance does, they will pull their permit. We will ensure that these projects are built. They won't sit on it. I think the existing language is just fine. I would urge you to approve it.

Rubin and Junius Just a comment on the grandfather provision. Projects that have been approved and projects that are in the pipeline have already committed.  They're already invested. They have spent money; they have hired designers.  They are well down the road. The economics of the projects are fixed. To think about hitting those types of projects with new rules in simply unfair and it's something that has not been done in the past. Pipeline projects are traditionally grandfathered with these kinds of provisions and it is crucial that these rules not be changed so that they affect a large number of pipeline projects. The staff report lists I think 25 projects that have been approved and not yet pulled building permits. There are a whole bunch more that are stuck in the system and the system is slow. They're grinding it out doing the best they can. Those projects should not be penalized.

Project Sponsor 1 Hawthorn represents one of the last remaining downtown infill sites. The neighborhood is already dense. It's a built out area that is filled with low and mid-rise and high-rise neighbors and a variety of uses. The site is near transit jobs housing entertainment retail and educational institutions. We think high density is therefore a very appropriate goal for the site–both to maximize market-rate housing and to maximize the inclusionary benefits that we will provide. We have tried to address parking in a progressive way for the taller project for the 250-foot variant. We are seeking a lower parking ratio than is considered normal. We're only asking for 0.75 parking spaces per one. The ground floor has got a corner retail parcel on the corner of Howard and Hawthorne. The below grade car storage is satisfied through car elevators and stackers and it's all accommodated below grade. The upper floor of the building is what we call the side core plan because it's a relatively peculiarly shaped site. We've located the elevator core at the side then the residential units view out on all three sides. The upper floor plan has a setback on Howard Street. We are looking at a variety of permeations of the unit count between 189 and 168 total residential units. There is a setback at the 85-foot level. The roof garden is for common open space landscaping and common area for entertainment of folks living in the building.

I was surprised to see the Dwelling Unit Merger Policy on today's agenda. It was my understanding from the January hearing that we are going to take an opportunity and bring stakeholders in and talk to staff about this policy. I would like to request a continuance or a postponement until we have an opportunity to do that. Pat Buscovich I know Planning is trying to grapple with what to do with these billboards floating around the City. There is a lot misinformation about how far they are off. I sampled 15 billboards in the city. If Planning is going to do anything with these signs, it would be better to do it in conjunction with the Building Department. A lot of these signs are or have become structural hazards over the last fifty years. No name stated I represent the Southeast Development Group which is largely citizens that live in Bayview Hunters Point. Is it possible for you to come down to Bayview Hunter's Point to the Commissioners room and give your report on what the status is as far as the hiring, who is going to do it, and just a general report on what is going on down there about that building project? I am talking about the Home Depot project.

section: PUBLIC COMMENT ON AGENDA ITEMS WHERE THE PUBLIC HEARING HAS BEEN CLOSED
comment: I am here to speak on behalf of the Senior Housing at 3575 Geary. My wife and I are residents of the Richmond District. We are both seniors who are going to need senior housing very soon. I have letters that I would like to leave with the secretary. [Unclear name], Alameda County Public Works Agency. I am here to express concern about the adequacy of the inadequate response to our comments on the draft EIR for the Sunol/Niles Dam removal. The concerns are expressed in an e-mail letter dated March 13, 2006. The District expressed its desire to work with the SFPUC in the following conditions: a) to include a permit issued for the dams removal and authorization for the District to undertake it. b) to be able to quantify the value on the sediment c) that the SPUC in the District enter into some MOU to undertake certain activities including collaborative efforts with regulating agencies regarding permit issues and other resources protection activities that benefit the two entities. Today, the District is here to emphasize these points and highlight the concerns. There is no sound basis for the conclusion drawn upon the volume of sediment from the Dam. The report assessed that sediment behind the dam will be removed and transported downstream in a normal annual rainfall with no substantial studies or data. The report also assessed that the sediment handed down will take decades to reach the District facility downstream. Which one is it? Judy Berkowitz The Coalition in its March meeting unanimously passed a resolution supporting all 150 senior housing units to be built within a 50 foot building. We want to make sure that you know that we oppose the project as currently proposed and we are asking that you deny the certification of the Final Environmental Impact Report. Approve a plan that downsizes the office space, omits the conference center and increases the parking, yet retains all 150 senior housing units within a 50 foot building. Laurie Rosenthal You asked the developer to reduce to a 50 foot height with at least 120 housing units. They have not done so. And as a result they make their units too expensive to be reasonably competitive with the tax credit funding that they seek. Why do they continue to penalize seniors to maintain their office space by providing fewer and less affordable units? They reported the number of residence programs, staff, office workers or conference attendees. However, it is based only on current scattered IOA sites and not based on future development of this site. [No name] We support the senior housing, but the building should be scaled down and the conference center and offices should be taken out for in compatibility with the community. The oversized project as proposed would have a significant adverse visual affect in that it would tower over other buildings in the area and be grossly out of scale with the area. These affects are not adequately addressed in the EIR. It is insufficient and the alternative is unreasonable. Libby Benedict This project is way out of scale and character with the neighborhood. Change in the existing character of the residential neighborhood was not found to be a substantial impact in the EIR. We need to understand what CEQA requirements are merely suggestions. Greg Hylton Another deficiency in the EIR is the erroneous construction cost data provided by the project sponsor. The project sponsor has rejected the alternatives described in the EIR as too expensive and infeasible. President Sue Lee and Commissioner Dwight Alexander in the last EIR meeting asked to investigate the feasibility of the building at a 50 foot height with 150 units of senior housing. Why was that not done? Dick Millett 3575 Geary proposes a project with seniors of which one quarter of the units is for seniors with special needs. We therefore must ask for special protections. We must require increased seismic analysis and construction as being required for California hospitals. We must develop and require an updated, improved disaster plans. Current requirements are inadequate. Rich Warner The project description simply does not meet CEQA standards. It fails to adequately describe the use of the meeting room with frequency of use or number of people using the facility. The meeting room is in fact a $2.9 million, 8,200 square foot conference center capable of holding 100 conferences in excess of 100 people. The EIR does not conduct adequate analysis of traffic, parking, employment, or air quality impacts of large and frequent conferences. The Institute on Aging has refused to commit to any standards for evaluation and thus the EIR is flawed because of the lack of information from the sponsor. We ask that you require the sponsor to provide the relevant data needed to analyze this unusual aspect of the project. Rose Hilson One of the points I brought up in the last meeting was the environmental issues and wildlife. I understand the applicable laws will protect nesting sites and endangered species of animals. The proposed project will be on the previous site of the cemetery, many of the bodies remain. There are many sections in this cemetery under mitigation measures for archeological resources. I also understand from mitigation measure, hazardous waste measures will be in place for existing building materials. However, this natural recurring asbestos in the rocks is commonly known to be in the cemetery areas. Nickie MacKenzie We want the project but parking is a big issue in this area. Let us make everybody win by having employees with parking spaces and allowing the residents of Jordan Park to be able to find a place occasionally, as we now are able to do. Don Lusky I understand there have been questions raised with regard to the adequacy of the feasibility analysis that we submitted to the City. I would like to leave memorandums and letters for Commissioners and affirm our belief in the accuracy of our analysis that was submitted to the city and the supporting data. Gaby Berliner Although I am in support of the senior housing project, the size and bulk of it is totally unacceptable. This primarily residential area of single and multifamily units will be irreversibly damaged by increasing height above five stories. Traffic will be further disrupted by not providing adequate parking. I urge the Commission to require a reduction in height and provide off street parking. Bradley Wiedmayer Urged to vote against the EIR. The historic architectural resource section is completely false.

name_raw: Ann Romero, Project Manager - Mayor's Office of Housing
role_title: Project Manager - Mayor's Office of Housing
comment: I am here today on behalf of Matt Franklin, Director of the Mayor's Office of Housing who could not be here. I would like to convey to you the Mayor's Office of Housing's strong support for this project. It addresses on of the top goals identified in the 2005 consolidated plan in that it is to construct 900 new senior units in the next five years. We believe that Bridge Housing is a very strong developer and property manager and its institute on aging is an excellent service partner for the project. The City has already made an investment of nearly $2 million dollars and it would ultimately provide approximately $15 million dollars to this project in financing. David Whitaker, Project Sponsor I am a physician and CEO of the Institute on Aging - IOA as it is often called. This is a very important project for the IOA and for seniors in San Francisco and for their families. One of the greatest concerns is how to meet the needs of a rapidly growing population of older adults, especially those who are frail with chronic illness and limited financial resources. As is often the case in San Francisco, some of the most creative solutions come from nonprofit community-based organizations like the IOA. This project takes all of the IOA's comprehensive health and supportive services and combines them with affordable housing with easy access and a central location for seniors with modest means. I have no doubt that it will become a model for other senior services in our community and communities elsewhere. The Institute of Aging was founded here in San Francisco almost over 20 years ago with a mission of helping seniors maintain their health, dignity, sense of independence, ability to continue to live in their own homes and avoid institutional care in nursing homes. One of our main programs is to adopt a health center where frail seniors spend the day, get checkups, physical therapy, nutritious meals, join other senior in activities in a safe and supportive environment, and then return home to their families. Our programs are now in various rented spaces scattered along Geary Boulevard and the Inner Richmond. About six years ago, the Board of the IOA began searching for more suitable facilities when the 50 year old Coronet Theater located across from 3600 Geary became available. The Board purchased the property with the idea of constructing a building where the IOA could consolidate and improve all its services, and also provide the kind of supporti8ve housing needed by so many of our clients. The plans were finally submitted to the Planning Department in April 2003. We are in hopes that the Planning Commission will take favorable action at this meeting today. Carol Blante, President, BRIDGE Housing Corporation I am glad to be here today. Bridge has been working on this development for more than four years with the Institute on Aging. We have spent many hours in meetings and dialogues with neighbors and planning staff. We are confident that this is a model for San Francisco and that it will be a fine and exemplary facility and neighbor. We have worked diligently to respond to all the issue raised. For parking and traffic, the senior housing parking meets all required planning codes for parking and we have provided voluminous information on use of parking from other senior developments in the City to you and the staff. The IOA space is not a typical office space. Therefore, as the EIR and part of the traffic analysis, this issue was studied and concluded that the demand was for 56 parking spaces and we would provide 67. There was a suggestion for a second below grade garage. That is simply not needed and would raise the cost to a prohibitive $5 million and more. The building height is 72 feet at its highest point and it is well bellow the 80-foot height limit allowed for this site and down to 57, 59 feet on Almaden Court. The variance requested for bulk is to accommodate a better living environment, both for residents and IOA users as well as the surrounding neighbors. Last, a 50-foot alternative and many alternatives were studied for the EIR and concluded that it is not feasible to achieve both the financial and planning objectives of the development. The conference center is a meeting room that will hold no more than 100 people. The IOA has agreed to a condition to limit the use of that meeting room to outside visitors after hours during the week and on weekends. Paula Quidmeyer, Architect for the Project We are pleased to team with the Institute on Aging and Bridge Housing to design this senior center and housing. We have approached this project with the idea of creating a complex that will be the pride of the neighborhood. Bridge takes a unique approach to every building so it will fit into the neighborhood as well as the needs of the users. The existing context on Geary Boulevard is rear residential and mixed commercial on either side. The design responds to the urban context and the community process. The building has a residential appeal and avoids an institutional aesthetic. Kathy Devencinzi, Laurel Heights Neighborhood Association We support the housing but we think the project should be scaled down. Also, I think you need a variance for the parking and all the other exceptions sought by the applicant. This building would interfere with light and sun. Air would be blocked by the structure and it does not have a tendency to promote the general welfare or prosperity of the community. I also think it is discriminatory to the property owners on Almaden Court and there is no sufficient evidence of financial infeasibility to support a variance. They do not need the conference center and all the offices. These pictures that they showed are misleading. All commercial properties next to them are about three stories in height. Gladstone Liang Parking is a big problem in this area and my concern is that 67 parking spaces are totally inadequate. The second thing I want to mention is that this neighborhood would be destroyed by the massive size of this project by destructing privacy in my neighborhood. Have you ever visited Laguna Honda? It is large and massive senior housing that is nothing but a large human warehouse. It dehumanizes and depersonalizes those who work there and also impacts the neighbors equally. Senior housing should be smart enough to be personal, intimate and dignifying. I will retire in a few years and I certainly hope to utilize this senior resource that is part of my neighborhood and community. Preservation of family neighborhoods is good for everyone, especially for seniors. Laurie Rosenthal This development will tower over all the one to four-story homes and businesses for miles. Deny the 9 conditional use requests and make the developer build a neighborhood friendly project. Do you feel confident that you know the real effects of the potential use on traffic, parking, schools, children and the bus line that carries 40,000 people up and down through the area into downtown? We ask that you make the developer construct the second level of parking to avoid a parking nightmare. [Aimee Rousseau (name was not clear)] The IOA and Bridge have lied to us, the residents of Almaden Court, and to the San Francisco Police Department. The IOA and Bridge has done property damage to us and they have refused to repair the damage or provide insurance information to repair it. They failed to comply with the San Francisco Police Department's directive regarding maintaining a trash free area and removing graffiti. They have failed to provide us information in the DEIR. Paula Romanoffsky A lot of concessions were mentioned in the presentation by Bridge just now. It is a concern that this is the first time we heard of these. There is definitely a communication breakdown and to have a good neighborhood relation this really has to be addressed. Parking simply has to be addressed for environmental reasons and for pedestrian safety. One of the reasons that the Golden Gate Park has the new underground parking garage is because of the pollution and the accident risk of people circling looking for parking. Consider fully all of these comments before allowing this important solution for senior housing to be maligned by a short-sighted perspective. Sylvia Melikian I am here in support of this project unconditionally. The Bridge and IOA bent over backwards to accommodate the needs of the community. Bridge is nationally recognized as the pre-imminent developer of not-for-profit housing. Senior housing is a critical element in our community and the services that the IOA provides are really not matched by any organization in the City of San Francisco. Karl Baldauf It seems that there is a reach but not quite enough to bring together the neighborhood and the project together. There is a critical lack of parking and I am very concerned about the traffic flow in the area. I think there is one more reach that Bridge and the IOA needs to make to do a few more things and make the project work for everyone. Parking and density should be looked at again. Linda Ash I have major concerns about the project. I think the size, scope and magnitude of the project is out of scale with the neighborhood The parking and traffic are quite difficult right now. I am concerned about the additional loss of parking. I think the height, bulk and density of the building is out of scale with this single-family home neighborhood. The conference center will bring more people and cars into the neighborhood and I think we are going to have more problems. I am not against the housing project but the size, scope and the magnitude of it. Trey Macphee The need for senior housing clearly exists and the issue is not about the proposed use but the size of this project. Why does it need to be so big? The proposed project is twice as large as it should be allowed under the current code. There is no other similar sized structure anywhere near the site. Projects of this size should be in neighborhoods of like-size buildings. Why do you not see any other buildings in the pictures from the Project Sponsor? I am asking these questions because I believe that you as members of the Planning Commission with your fiduciary duty to enforce the Planning Code should ask and answer these same questions among yourselves. Exceptions to the Code or the magnitude requested by the developers of this project are essentially a request that you blatantly disregard essential components of the Planning Code that are critical to maintaining neighborhood integrity. Mike Ina I believe the senior housing is vital to San Francisco, but the development must be in concert with the community that it is being developed in. The Institute on Aging has planned to have 67 parking spots for this large development. I think it is very insufficient. Parking in the area has become very, very difficult since the Indian Consulate moved in. Every morning they have people that line up and they sit in their car all day waiting for their appointment. I would like to know if the Planning Commission monitors or who enforces the variances that are allowed so that the conference meetings would not be held during business hours where parking is going to be premium. Barbara Austin, representing Jordan Park Homeowners Association and San Francisco Heights Homeowners Association. I am bringing conditions that are very important for us. The 120 units of Bridge Housing for senior citizens should remain affordable housing if the developer sells the rights to the property. No double temporary parking of vans waiting for calls on side streets supported by Turk, Euclid, Arguello and Parker. All Bridge employees are not to drive to work and are to take public transportation to work. IOA/Bridge will institute a commuter check program for their employees. IOA/Bridge shall add two-tiered parking in each parking space that will increase parking at each parking space, or IOA/Bridge shall institute some form of parking to increase parking in the under coated parking garage. No employee or consultant shall apply for a neighborhood parking permit for limited or for limited street parking in the areas bounded by Turk, Euclid, Arguello and Parker. The project manager shall arrange for off-site parking for construction worker vehicles and provide busing to the site so worker's cars will not impact surrounding businesses and homeowners. The conference center shall not be rented out or used by other organizations and shall be used by IOA solely for its purposes Monday through Friday. No person whose primary diagnosis is substance abuse or any psychiatric disorder may be housed in the project including without limitation in the 30 supportive housing units for seniors with special needs. Libby Benedict This is a flash media presentation that we have shown once before but I do not think all the Commissioners have seen it. We admit this is not the updated design but we did not have access to that at the time this was created. We have views of the Coronet from different angles and certainly we are in the ballpark as far as the size of the building. We support senior housing but we are protesting the sheer size of this building. The project is out of scale with the adjacent residential neighborhood and sets a dangerous precedent for the Geary Corridor. The cumulative impact of large oversized buildings along Geary will ultimately promote urban canyons with walled off effects and failure to preserve or enhance pedestrian environment by maintenance scale and visual interest. Until these issues are addressed I respectfully request that the Planning Commission not grant the nine conditional use exceptions. Nicky Mackenzie A while back SPUR did an extensive survey to see what factors made people feel like they live in a friendly, welcoming neighborhood. Two factors completely obliterated that possibility. One was very high-rise buildings that are connected, and the second was a lot of traffic. About parking, I appreciated Mr. Lee's and Mr. Antonini's questions about that. The parking problem is real. Where are the parking spaces for all the family members who want to visit, love, and attend their loved ones? Richard Worner, President of Jordan Park Improvement Association There are 99 spaces in the lot. I am a CPA. I counted and certified them. The CPMC has rented 60 spaces out at 16 th and Geary, so there are 40 spaces. Section 303(C) of the conditional use code states the project sponsor must provide any off-street parking needed to satisfy the reasonably anticipated auto usage by residents/visitors to the project. In a package distributed to you by the developer, the developer states that the 8,200 square foot, $2.9 million conference center and the garage level at the project will generate a demand of 107 spaces per the time, 40 of which can not be accommodated on the site. They are going to need 40 extra spaces whenever they use the conference center. On October 2 nd of 2001, the developer's geological engineer's report stated that two basement levels of parking can be put on that site. The Mayor's Office is funding this project for over $14.2 million at 3% for 55 years. Tax credit financing may also be used. Our tax dollars are paying for this project. Please force the developer to add a second parking level and add some setbacks to make this a project we can all live with. Unclear name I am just going to limit my talk to comment on the effects the proposed new construction will have on traffic in the area. Traffic on Geary Boulevard is at maximum including Saturdays and Sundays. Stanyan Street that ends at Geary is also very heavily traveled in both directions. It is one of the few streets that continued on through Golden Gate Park to St. Mary's Hospital emergency that is on Stanyan Street. This street is a direct route also from our area to the UC Hospital. Permitting the Bridge Housing to go ahead will increase the traffic on Stanyan Street considerably to the point that it will be unsafe. The plans must be modified to conform to the area. William Goodson The developer said that there were modifications to the plan and those are basically window dressing. There is no substantive change in what they presented. Secondly, I believe it was stated that the additional cost of digging an additional parking space [level] underneath would be $5 million. I would point out that $5 million over the lifetime of this building is a negligible amount of money and totally irrelevant to what will be the budget of that building probably even within five years. I think the real issue is everybody's quality of life and stability. The Planning Code is in place so that everybody will be able to count on the stability in the City of everybody following the same rules. No where has anybody said that the seniors in this building would not be allowed to have a car. Rocky Papale As it is currently proposed, this building is unfittingly grandiose and monumental with its belligerent imposing design and scale that bullies its neighbors into submission. Like David to Goliath, we remain proud and determined to knock down the height, bulk and density of this structure philistine. This is an outlaw building seeking special treatment form the Planning Commission in the form of nine conditional use exemptions. I am here today because I believe this is about the notion that San Francisco is not divided into developers and neighborhoods. Natalie Tarnopolsky The height of the building and the density of the building, parking, and the fact that it would change the character of the neighborhood are very high concerns. I work really hard to keep my family afloat and to live in San Francisco. How do we keep young families in the City? One the main things we did after a long day is to come home and try to find parking and with the current plan underway there is no way we would find parking. Rozanne Junker If your sole purpose today is to build senior housing, then support this project. But if your purpose is also to keep families in San Francisco and maintain the integrity of neighborhoods you can not approve these nine exceptions. I also want to just take a moment to take exception to what was said by one of the earlier speakers saying that this project would become the pride of the neighborhood. I was really insulted by that. I live in this neighborhood and the pride of my neighborhood is the community and the people not the buildings, certainly not about this building. Katherine Simmonds, Member of the San Francisco Heights Neighborhood Association I am particularly cognizant of the growing need for senior friendly housing and neighborhood health care and City services for all seniors whether they are rich of poor. Planning for seniors is a difficult task but it does not mean you should construct facilities in the quickest and cheapest way possible without regard to the impacts on the quality of life for those who live here. I am sure you should agree planning for seniors should be much more than this. It is important that they be functional and create a safe and livable environment for the neighborhoods around them. I see in the City that there are indeed many examples of senior housing facilities that you have approved which seem to fit well into the character of the neighborhood. Vera Poon Many of those before me have expressed my sentiments better than I can myself. The buses for the senior citizens double park and make driving hazardous on the corner. The parents from Rosevelt Park High School double park. There is a vicious competition among the neighbors who live there for parking space on weekdays, weekends and evenings as well. Elenor Coffman I just want to reiterate what so many of the residents of Jordan Park and San Francisco Heights have said already. This is a vital project. The Commission needs to reconsider the traffic and parking needs of the community and deny the 9 conditional requests of the developers and provide a neighborhood friendly project. Ken Passameneck I think most of the points about parking and things have been covered. I would say that I think the plan to off load people off-street is a good idea but that corner of Geary and Arguello is already congested with a small bus stop with many buses and people trying to exit the garage. Unless some plan is made to move the bus stop or possibly have the entrance of the building further to the east, it is going to create a terrible traffic Professionally, I was the medical director for a community mental health facility for the City of San Francisco and I have spent my professional life working with seniors. When the IOA says they will use their conference center or meeting center for in-house activities, does it mean only for in-house activities or activities that would attract people like Community Mental Health, Catholic Charities, Jewish Family Services, etc.? Those types of conferences create a terrific amount of traffic. Another concern is the visual impact that this building would create with its bulk and density. Sarah Karlisnky, Policy Director for the San Francisco Planning Urban Research Association. SPUR have moved to strongly endorse this project. The project sponsors have worked hard to maximize the number of diverse affordable housing units - a precious resource to the neighborhood and to the community. Further, we feel that the project will fulfill the IOA's and Bridge's goal of allowing seniors to age in place while remaining integrated into a vibrant neighborhood. The second reason has to do with the public realm interface and the promotion of a pedestrian oriented environment. Mathew Weinberg . There is no question that the IOA will build on this site with their supporter's help. It is all a question of whether that site is going to be built soon or be delayed in litigation and how it will happen. Do not get fooled by economic feasibility. Get something that fits the neighborhood makes everybody happy. Tom Ross The project is too big for its site as well as the amount of parking they have allowed. Is the Planning Commission going to be content if they just put in 40 parking spaces, is that appropriate? How many of their own vehicles are going to be parking at that facility, much less the employees, much less any of the visitors that come, or the volunteers? The conditional use needs to be looked at more carefully. Patricia Vaughey I firmly believe that you should send this back to the drawing board. SPUR's speech just really disturbed me. They do not represent the neighborhood. They have been advocates for high-rise throughout the inner city for years. I am just interjecting what I have heard at this deal. This is an exceptional use for so many facilities near this corner that there should be a compromise. They don't need the convention room. I really want to make sure that if you approve this to be senior housing that you insure you have minorities in there. Jean Lynch There are many of us here today who reside in the immediate area and are in strong support of this project. We need to focus not only on our small five square blocks but how the many programs contributed by the Institute on Aging have improved the quality of life for seniors in the area. Throughout the Richmond District, there is a shortage of low-income housing and services for the frail and elderly. We look forward to this state of the art building and the continuance of the service that we already have. You also need to know that all of the supporters of this project were unable to fit into this room, but came here to be counted in support of the Institute on Aging and Bridge Housing. I also want to mention that many of the people that are in opposition of this building were many of the people that opposed senior housing that we now have on Arguello Boulevard and Euclid. Timothy Mason I am here today to speak on behalf of the project. As a resident in the area, I have seen how this project has been amended and scaled back. The graphics have been improved to reflect some of the concerns, a majority of the concerns raised by the speakers today. I look forward to the fact this development will be completed and will become a permanent part of our landscape and part of the landscape which is accepted and enjoyed. Gloria Yaros I would like to address three issues: parking, traffic and the idea that this would be the pride of our neighborhood. We can all assume we are all approaching seniorhood at the same very fast rate and it is obvious that no one is against this project. I do hope that if I have to move into a residence that it will be a building that has certain humanity to it. This looks like a prison. There are not enough spaces for people to park and I urge you to not accept this plan as it is. Greg Hylton, Co-President of the Jordan Park Improvement Association I would like to take issue with the statement earlier by representatives of Bridge that they have made many concessions on this building. They have done absolutely nothing. The façade originally was proposed and it looked like 850 Bryant Street, and the neighborhood were up in arms over that. They changed it and it is a very pleasing looking project. We have attempted many times to meet with Bridge and to get them to make the concessions on this project that would make it a livable environment for our neighborhood and they refused. We want the senior project in our neighborhood but we are simply trying to have it reduced. Cindy Kaufman, Vice-president of Adult Day Services Institute on Aging The IOA has many programs currently serving well over a thousand seniors. One of these programs is directly across the street from the proposed project. This program, as well a many of our other programs, serves people with physical and mental disabilities as well as people with mild, moderate and severe Alzheimer's disease. Our programs were created to meet a growing need in the community. We do not warehouse people. Our programs include clinical health services, day programs, case management and mental health services. This project would allow us to consolidate our programs into one location to work together more effectively to serve our aging population. Irwin Gibbs, Chairman of the Institute of Aging Building Committee I have become very aware of the need to consolidate our program and services under one roof. Owning the property will allow the IOA the financial security to continue to perform services to needy seniors and the frail elderly. The project has been before the Planning Commission for a very long time and it is critical to get approval as soon as possible so the IOA can move ahead. Bob Socholoff, Chairman of the Institute on Aging We've been hearing about the services the agency provides, affordable housing and affordable health care. This project will be replicated in cities all around the country because it will be a bench mark and a model of how to take care of our elderly citizens. I urge you to support this project. Jim Salinas, Carpenters Local 22 We work in an environment and we expect our members to be allowed to work with dignity, and as they age, we ask that they also be allowed to retire in dignity. We are here asking for your support for what we believe to be a great project that allows our senior citizens to be given the respect that they so diligently deserve. Carpenters Local 22 asks for your support for a great project that is well deserving for our seniors. Katherine Hecht I am on the Board of San Francisco Heights. When I first read about it I immediately called IOA. I talked with senior executives to invite them to our meeting to hear about their plans. All of us are very positive about senior housing. We were put off until Bridge was able to make a presentation. We were very concerned about some of the building plans. We have tried to voice these concerns anywhere venues are possible to us, inviting and trying to have friendly discussions, trying to get a mediator before coming to you. The modifications they have made are very minor. They don't address the issues. Sue Wong, Chief Financial Officer of On Lok Senior Health Services. On Lok provides total care for the elderly. We serve almost a thousand frail seniors in San Francisco. For 30 years our goal has been to keep them at home, in the community for as long as possible. Together On Loc and IOA take care of over 230 frail seniors from the Western Addition and Richmond District. This project is important because we need more affordable senior housing in San Francisco. We know that accessible affordable on-site care will help seniors as they age in place maintain their health and quality of life and enable them to stay in the community longer. Geraldine Earp I bring to you this afternoon a vote of approval and affirmation from Dr. James McCray Jr., the pastor at Jones United Methodist Church and the congregation. My dedication to this project has its foundation form the OMI Neighbors in Action and the Senior Action Network as well as my employment at the Department of Social Services, Department of Health, Education and Welfare, San Francisco Home Health Agency, Laguna Honda Hospital, and finally the Mount Zion Home Care Department. Betty Angerine 23 years ago both of my parents became physically disabled. It was hard to know what resources were available while working full time. As a nurse, you would think I had all that information at my fingertips, but I did not. They were not many day care centers for seniors at that time. I hired a daytime caregiver for two years. It made me realize caregivers face many problems: isolation, feeling overwhelmed, and hopelessness. Having this type of facility would have helped me with support for my parents and provide more services than I could have on my own. The IOA will provide a sense of independence with community access to the health facility and other services, and also to those who are caregivers. Ginny Jordan I live at 190 Coleridge and am very happy living there. Bridge Housing manages the place and I like the way they do it. It is very diverse and it represents all of the nationalities that live in San Francisco. I came here today to speak to get the housing for other people because I would like to see other people have the privilege that I have. Tim Colen - Action Housing Coalition With our 50 members we ask you to support this project without reservations. It is an appropriate use of the land at this location. It adds density in an appropriate way on a major transit corridor in San Francisco. There is a desperate shortage of housing for seniors, in particular for low-income seniors. The bad news is that it is about to start to get a whole lot worse because we are not preparing for it. We are not building housing for our seniors. A project like this could be jeopardized around an issue like parking. This is a population of very low usage of cars. Ken Donnelly, Executive Vice-President of the Institute on Aging As you know from the EIR and an independent transportation study a parking count of 56 spaces was supported. IOA and Bridge subsequently designed an underground parking garage for 67 spaces. This is a 20% increase from the recommendation made by the transport experts. IOA continues to participate in the commuter check program and has done so for many years and the vast majority of its employees take public transit to work. The parking structure will only be made available for employees and for building residents. Visitors coming to the meeting facilities would be permitted into the parking garage only after business hours on weekdays and also on weekends since no employees would be there. I want to reiterate that all clients coming to this site for health services are brought to the site by a van service. These vans are stored offsite and they will not be stored in the underground parking structure. In fact, our transportation provider currently provides van services in addition to the IOA to the City's transit system and has a very good reputation. I urge you to approve the PUD proposed and recommended by the Planning Department. [Unclear name] When I heard and found out that there was affordable housing for seniors; I was delighted. I thought this was a wonderful location for senior citizenship apartments because most of them are in the downtown. I am very hopeful that all these things are going to be built out and do not get delayed. There have been many changes in the neighborhood and I think we can not stop it because it is something we need to do to have more housing for seniors also in neighborhoods. Tom Radulovich, Executive Director for Transportation for a Livable City We are here to speak in support of this project although we have a few caveats. First of all, transit accessible affordable housing for seniors: We need much more of this in our City. This is a great project. We like the mix of uses. We like the uses of ground floor and housing above. This is going to do a lot more for Geary Boulevard in creating a continuous street and less of a street mall. We do not like the parking entrance on Geary because we think it is going to interfere with the transit line carrying 50,000 people a day. It should be on one of the other frontages. Ground floor uses: I am concerned that is all office for a block. In the future if we can add retail and lighten that block at some point, you should ask the sponsor to look at that. To require more parking in an affordable senior project would mean that we are going to have less senior housing. We need more housing for seniors and less parking. No name Thanked staff and the Commission for getting this finally to a place that might get a vote. Thanked Supervisor McGoldrick for being in our meeting the other day. He said that he will support this project if it comes to an appeal at the Board of Supervisors. He promised to persuade his fellow supervisors to be in favor of the project. Lorene Feehan [Read a letter from Mary Ann Duke expressing support and sharing a personal experience of living on social security disability and economically burdened on housing costs.] I had financially contributed to San Francisco for 32 years. Now I would like San Francisco to contribute to my needs by approving senior housing at 3575 Geary Boulevard. Nicole The intriguing balance of nature and urban architecture invites you to stroll on the sidewalk to appreciate it. There are several policies in place to protect this balance. The valleys and the planes are as important as the hills for they define their own districts and give the hills their visual meaning. Tall slender buildings at the top of hills and low buildings on the slopes and in the valleys accentuate the form of the hills The IOA and Bridge are fulfilling one of the priority policies of the City's plan by enhancing the supply of affordable housing. However, their current proposal violates five other priority policies. Sarah Nolan, San Francisco Organizing Project Last week, we gathered 80 people that supported this housing site in its entirety. We believe this site meets all the requirements and we would like it to start as soon as possible. Steve Vettel on behalf of IOA and Bridge I want to talk about the EIR analysis and a number of issues that will come up today. In particular, there was a very extensive study done on parking demands that would be created by this very unique land use. The IOA is relocating existing services into this building so I know exactly what will be happening in this building as far as employee and visitor demand for parking. This is the City's consultant study. It looked at other senior housing, particularly low-income senior housing in the City, where the parking demand is .16 space per unit. We have .2 spaces per unit so we are exceeding that demand. I did want to pass to you the parking study because it is probably not in your packet and the pages that detail this parking demand and how it was determined. The total demand is 56 spaces. 56 total for both IOA employees, visitors and the housing. We are providing 67 parking spaces. The only time there is excess demand that we would not be meeting is on the occasions on weekends and evenings when the meeting room is in use by non-IOA functions. The demand then would be a maximum of 40 spaces. There are occasions when there may be street parking because of off-site meetings in the facility. Four times a month is their estimate of how often that will occur. Normally during the day, the demand is 56 and in the evenings it is 30. We are providing 67 parking spaces. There was a suggestion to add a second floor of parking that would double the parking supply. Adding a second floor of parking would cost about $5 million dollars that is not in the budget and that would come out of additional low income senior housing. John Stewart I am here to speak fully in support of the work that Bridge does. I have more familiarity with IOA and am very much in support of their work. I do not think you would be having these kinds of conflicts if indeed the organizations had been more responsive. Debbie Baptiste I am for senior housing but I just want to go along with what the neighbors have said about the parking problem. It is just so overcrowded with the hospitals, schools and all other things that have been mentioned already. It is really quite a problem. Judy Berkowitz People are in support of the units but the bulk of the building and other things is what is not supported. The plan is inconsistent with several priority policies in regard to conformance with neighborhood character. I urge you to approve a plan that has been redesigned so that the 150 units fit within the 50-foot height limit. As to parking, I think that this is a little foggy. It seems that some of the parking plans have been quoted that is sufficient for a senior housing project but this is so much more than that. As I understand it, the parking lot is used for a lot of other things and no one knows where those cars are going to be parking when this goes in.

T-Mobile Representative T-Mobile is proposing to install six antennas and three equipment cabinets on the rooftop. All the antennas will be flush mounted to a mechanical penthouse. The antennas will be screened and painted to match the penthouse. The building was chosen as a primary candidate in this area because it provides adequate height to meet the proper objectives and the installation could be designed to be visually unobtrusive. This proposed installation would enhance T-Mobile's ability to provide its customers with consistent and reliable coverage along commercial streets. The report produced for this site concludes that under the admission guidelines of the SCC and the San Francisco Department of Health exposure levels would be less than one percent at ground level and on any of the adjacent rooftops. A community meeting was held at Newcomer High School on March 15 at 7p.m. 800 notices were sent out to residents property owners and community groups. One person attended that meeting. Don Schaefer I have done a little research on the reception and I do not think there is a need for this. They have chosen the worst spot to put it in. On health issues I've found that there is a list of diseases or conditions produced in the body and there is a correlation between radiation from antenna base stations and these diseases.

comment: The project was submitted to the Mission Bay PAC at our last meeting. We like it better than the original plan, which was an office building. President, Teamsters Local 853  Behind me are my brothers at Clear Channel and CBS Outdoor, Local 853, Labors Local 261 and 304, and The Saint Peter Local 150.  We support the proposed proposition G with the amendments before you.  In order to protect union jobs and worker's safety, the Teamsters request that the following previsions be included in the legislation: a) Assure that non-compliant structures that are completely removed cannot be replaced to prevent non-union companies/landlords from taking over union operated signs. b) Allow for corrections to signs that have minor deviations from their permits. c) The routine maintenance on signs be allowed to protect worker's safety. Jared Eigerman, Reuben and Junius - representing Clear Channel Outdoor There are nine items in the staff report.  Eight of them are fine. What we are asking for tonight are additional amendments.  You heard staff ask for policy guidance, and that is what we need. The case-by-case basis that has ruled these years is not working.  It is chaotic and t here needs to be clear rules. The only objection to the staff issues is the fee of $560 for each sign. Instead, we think the focus should be on the amendments to deal with rules and codes. I will be submitting comments in writing to go section by section. Michael Colbruno, Clear Channel Outdoor  What you are looking at tonight are very important options to protect working people. Companies do not want to be able to fix and repair signs. I think it is absolutely ludicrous to put working people up on signs that are unsafe. You have heard a couple of proposals put forth before you to allow signs to go back to their originally permitted dimensions. I think that under the current proposed legislation probably there would be 100 signs to be removed out of the City and I would like the legal non-conforming signs to stay up for people to have a job in this town. Dee Dee Workman, San Francisco Beautiful We helped craft this ordinance and it has taken four years to finally get to you. The legislation includes three important components: All sign companies must submit complete inventories. No Billboard relocation can take place until these inventories have been verified and the signs can only be relocated if the relocation meets specific criteria. In addition, the ordinance ensures that billboard companies cannot do business with the City if they own illegal signs. We do defer from Planning staff on one item in the report and that is the recommendation that the Board of Appeals hear appeals related to the penalties that are incurred when the billboard companies do not submit their complete inventories. With all do respect, we have found that the Board of Appeals have sometimes approved billboards related to appeals even if they do not conform to the Planning Code simply because they like the billboard. We recommend that an administrative law judge be appointed to hear those appeals instead. Bill Hopper, President of Clear Channel Outdoor Our industry has changed technologically over the years like most companies and industries in the Bay Area. We have standardized our signs to be more uniform with national standards. We have blueprints that we believe prove that they are allowed to be the dimensions that they are, yet the face of the application may not be consistent with it. We have provided staff with that documentation and we believe that a certain amount of grandfathering needs to take place. Worker's safety is very important. I urge you to support the amendments before you and get good policies in place to control those designs. Anthony Leonis. CBS Outdoor We do not oppose the staff report other than on the issue of fees. As spelled out, they are a bit too high. However, I want to emphasize one important point in the legislation and that is the replacement of completely removed nonconforming sign structures. This legislation does not address permit ownership. What it does address is a nonconforming sign structure and once that sign structure is removed, it cannot be replaced. It is actually codified currently in section 6.48 of the Planning Code, which provides that nonconforming signs may not be replaced, altered, reconstructed, relocated, intensified or expanded in an area or any dimension. Therefore this legislation would only be confirming the existing law. Patricia Vaughey There is no protection of the small business owner from the big corporation and small property owners are not being protected by this legislation. I am appalled at Aaron Peskin's Office, that the small people are not being protected by this legislation. Small property owners did not have enough time because I asked repeatedly from them to be heard by Supervisor Peskin and they were never heard. You should make some points that they got to be some protections for threats; figure out a way to protect those people and this does not do it. Mark Mosher, Clear Channel Outdoors We have worked with Patricia Vaughey in the past and have great respect for her.  But, I think the legislation does address the particular points she references. If you are going to relocate a sing under this legislation, you need to get written permission from the existing property owner. You need to make it clear that if a sign is taken down and is a nonconforming use, people cannot put it back up. You need to make provisions for signs to be maintained and kept up so they do not hurt people. Charge reasonable fees Debra Stein I want to just reinforce, or ensure that the language retains the definition that the general advertising sing company does not have to be this huge multinational corporation. It in fact can be a small property owner who owns the structure itself. I have to say that we feel the interests of the small property owners are being adequately protected. This legislation does not allow a hostage situation to be created where a corporation could unilaterally eliminate property owner's rights for signs unless the property owner agrees to below market rates on the renewal.  The legislation does require consent. This simply preserves an even playing field when it comes time to renegotiate the terms. Mark Pope I like the new fee structure.  It seems to be appropriate to place the fee on the number of signs primarily. What happens to historic signs that are basically antiques that just happen to still be on buildings? Is it going to be preserved? The second issue regarding historic properties is that I read somewhere in this long document that you are automatically discouraging sings on historic properties. My concern is that when signs are moved from historic properties would that eliminate the one thing that keeps it from being torn down? Patricia Vaughey I support the continuance of items 19 and 20 mainly because of the senior citizens.  Many of them were too tired to stay much longer.

Design Engineer for this project The owner wants to demolish this building They are going to move back to the same location.  At the same time they are going to provide four units.  So people who live on the upper floor can work on the ground floor and second floor – good for the community. Philip Lesser Our Association of the 2,500 block of Mission Street Business Improvement District is 100% supportive of this project. This is basically retail on the ground level, office on the second level, and then two levels of residential—creating four residences. This is an absolute perfect fit for the Mission District. Senior Vice President of Sunrise Senior Living Sunrise develops and operates its own projects. The possibility of a potential increase in the percentage of affordable units came as a total shock to us as we have two projects going through the planning process as we speak. Both project applications to the Planning Department occurred in the summer of 2004. In addition to the time it has taken us to get to this point we spent many months prior to applying negotiating our land contracts with the owners of the underlying land. To put this into perspective our memory-impaired project is only 58 units and our senior condominium project is only 62 units. 'When dealing with that small number of units being able to spread the impact of an additional 8% over the entire project is more than limiting it is impossible. Jazzy Collins – South of Market Community Action Network Our position has not changed since the last time this item was discussed before uou three weeks ago. We are still in favor of staff recommendation and also in favor of Supervisor Maxwell's amendments to the inclusionary housing. There is nothing in the amendments to indicate that it would interfere with the Housing Study. We ask that you not continue this item but send it forth to the Board of Supervisors so they can adopt and approve it. The one-mile radius is very acceptable and comprehensive to deal with. Greg Miller – with the Pillsbury Law firm in San Francisco We ask that you adopt a grandfathering clause as part of this legislation that would effectively exempt any projects that had project applications on file prior to the implementation of the ordinance that is before you. Steve Vettel – with Morrison and Forester I think most of the staff recommendation is very good and would support 95% of it with the exception of the issue of the effective date of changes to the ordinance. What we're talking about is not an exemption from the Inclusionary ordinance. We're talking about what portions of the Inclusionary Ordinance will apply to projects. The question is when do changes in the ordinance apply to projects? The reason the Inclusionary Ordinance has worked so well over the last three years—the statistics that you got a few weeks ago showed an amazing increase in the number of inclusionary units over the last few years—is because there is certainty. Everyone knows when they negotiate land prices exactly what the inclusionary requirement is going to be. They're able to negotiate land prices in reliance on that knowledge. They are able to with certainty go into a project know what the outcome is going to be and it needs to be known at the time that land deals are made. If you can't know what the inclusionary is going to be it is very difficult to negotiate land prices and you can't go back and renegotiate those prices after your entitlement. Kim Diamond – Senior Manager for Land Acquisition for Pulte Homes Any inclusionary housing requirement has a great impact on land value. Similar to construction costs and planning and permit fees the number and subsidy of the below market rate units that need to be included is a key piece of information in the negotiation of any land price. Possessing this information after the entitlement work is completed makes it impossible to accurately determine how much can be paid for a piece of property up front. I'd ask you to reconsider part 8 of this agenda item as other have discussed. The proposed change includes a grandfather clause as well. Robert McCarthy – McCarthy and Schwartz With the exception of the issue of applicability we support the staff's recommendation. We also appreciate the staff listening to the home builder community and advancing the date of applicability not from the date of entitlement which would be two three years down the road advancing it at least to the introduction of this legislation. We think this is a big step in the right direction. However we do think the real appropriate thing to do is to do it at the time of enactment of the legislation. In my experience it never gets better for the home builders it gets more expensive. We have produced a corollary to Mr. Vettle's request because many of you expressed concern about land banking permits. To avoid that we've suggested that the Zoning Administrator make a determination as to whether or not people are duly prosecuting their permits and he can make that determination by the filing of the applications. We think that is a fair resolution. It avoids the land banking issue and gives everybody a fair shot. In the transition team that the mayor put together the one point that they made about why we have a housing crisis is the single most difficult part was the uncertainty of entitlement.

Andrew Junius – Rubin and Junius for the Project Sponsor We feel this project is another great opportunity to convert an existing class B office building into residential use. The project would introduce and bring a substantial contribution to this city - The housing supply, including affordable housing would be enhanced by bringing 45 dwelling units into this location. Most significantly, the project is located right in the downtown area close to many jobs, transit and other services This is an excellent opportunity to preserve the building and ensure its continued use in the future.

000 into it all within the footprint because I respected the precedent that was set [of no one expanding beyond the existing footprint]. Deputy City Attorney Kate Stacy Wanted to talk a little about how the Commission adopts its minutes. Charter Section 4.104 requires all commissioners to vote yes or no on all matters unless that commissioner is excused by a vote of the Commission. Even where minutes are being adopted, commissioners may not be automatically excluded from that vote because they did not attend that meeting. The Commission could follow one of two routes: The Commissioners could vote on those minutes even though the commissioner was not present at that hearing because a vote on the minutes is different from a vote on a permit. It doesn't have the same adjudicative and due process implications. So a commissioner could vote on minutes for a meeting that you did not attend because you generally are aware of the accuracy of your secretary in transcribing the minutes. You may or may not get public comments on those minutes. You may or may not get commissioners comments on those minutes. Or you could review the file and the tape if you are interested in that meeting. But you can vote on the minutes without going back and reviewing the file and the tapes the way that commissioners are required to do on a permit. The other option for the Commission is to actually vote to excuse a commissioner from voting on the minutes. That would have to be a separate action taken by the Commission each time the vote is made. I just wanted to make sure the Commission was aware of that requirement and to think about how you want to vote on the minutes. Even if you weren't present at a meeting, I wanted to be sure that the individual commissioners were aware that you could vote on those minutes based on other evidence in the record.
