comment: Sunset Group We had 900 petitions that we submitted to you and I got about 283 more that I submitted this morning. Requested that the Commission do what ever is in your power to have our site removed permanently so no other renters can look at it and that Sprint can decide to apply again.

section: CONSIDERATION OF ITEMS PROPOSED FOR CONTINUANCE
comment: SPEAK I appreciate the group for gathering over 900 signatures opposing the project.  Also, for Supervisor Ma and her office supporting us.

We need to have an understanding from the Housing Element on what is the housing demand for students. It would be very helpful for you and for the public to have information from all those institutions for the next Housing Element. UCSF, USF, Academy of Arts College, New College, Culinary Institute and this one will need to file for a Master Plan and all together it might be more than 20,000 students. Ask them if they would cooperate at a future hearing to discuss student housing needs.

Regarding the discussion last week on the appropriate process to review the billboards and Mr. Badiner's memorandum explaining that the Commission has the power to recommend to the Board of Supervisors and the supervisors have the power to make amendments if they want to change the process. I have a strong position that the commission form of government works good since 1932. If you want to ensure public propose you do it at a commission hearing where everyone explains it. You would have to initiate yourself to look at this issue and calendar it for the commission to send it to the Board. I would also like to take a couple of seconds to discuss former President Bell. I want to say Shelley that you are the best of what public service is. You never forgot that it's about serving the public. You have been accessible to all stakeholders. A little animated in dialogue. You have made yourself available and prepared. You have always been gracious and heard everyone's argument. They say God answers all prayers. Sometimes the answer is no, but we respect that. I want to thank you. You served wonderfully. You were just an incredible important voice to give perspective to so many things, representing the views of renters and those who want transit first. I thank you on behalf of my colleagues for your service to the city. Patricia Vaughey The billboard legislation still does not address those people that enter contracts that the billboard belongs to them. I think this thing was piecemealed by the large corporations for a reason – to get around all of you. Small people have a right to due process as well as large people. This legislation is denying them that right. You have to start at this commission taking control and I hope today and next week you take control. Start with the billboard legislation and take on the fact these young families are being chased out of here by big business that wants high-rise condos for their personal profit. Yu don't have to listen to the department all the time. I see manipulation all over the place. I really believe that we have to be smarter and wiser and not come back to what was the Feinstein Administration where the small people were left out and we spent 20 years correcting it. I want you to take initiative. Sue Hestor On page 9 of your calendar you have Page Street on there four times and have different case numbers. Why? Staff tells me that it is instruction from you to separate the demolition from the new construction. 20 years ago the Planning Department had an E case number and a planning case number and they were different. Then they merged them and separated them with a string of letters. You can have a case that has 8 or 9 letters and they mean something. When you have case numbers like this Page Street files get lost. None of the cases are anywhere near each other. The Planning Department has had a problem with records being retrievable especially when they are split in so many places. I'm not sure you wanted them to split the numbers like this. Please tell them to do it the old way. It's always hard to see an old commissioner go. You've finally figured out the process and you don't get hoodwinked anymore. In the fourth year you asserted yourself and you told the staff what you want. I'm sorry that the three of you are going to be gone. You have grown a lot. I respect your opinion even though at times we don't agree with each other. I'm sorry you are gone and I hope you well. And for Commissioner Bell, after this I can call you up and say, let's meet in Paris. Tim Kelly I was able to catch Commissioner Bradford-Bell's statement on the Internet before coming down here. I wasn't aware this was the point, but I would like to add my voice to congratulating this whole commission and Mrs. Bell in particular for really having done a great service to the city of San Francisco. During my time on the Landmarks Board, I've had the pleasure of working with a number of different commissions. Congratulations and best wishes to all of you.

I want to take this opportunity to commend the Planning Department for their efforts. I've sat on the Task Force since '99. In my responsibility as architect historian, I do these surveys all the time – most recently Dogpatch. Until recently, San Francisco was short changed survey efforts. It's about time we get to a point where we do the surveys. They are critical in preservation efforts. The San Francisco Planning Department has completed a valuable body of research in the waterfront and Market Octavia areas and deserves commendation. As a professional in the field, I hardily endorse their quality and respectfully hope you endorse this survey. Tim Kelly I'm speaking as a historic consultant and am familiar with the process. I was the President of the Landmarks Board when the survey work began and for quite a bit of the time as it's been going on. I would like to urge your endorsement of the monumental work that the Planning Department has done. This is the first major step into rational preservation planning in the city. I hope you will agree. I hope you will endorse it.

name_raw: Kelton Finney, Project Engineer, UTS Engineers
comment: We wrote the soundness report for this building. Based on the guidelines by the Planning Department, the building is unsound if it indicates that the necessary upgrade cost exceeds 50% of the replacement costs. We analyzed the building and found structural hazards in the building. Across the board, it is under framed in almost every area – the roof, ceiling, attic, both floors and the foundation. We worked corporately with staff. We met with the planner to discuss the findings in this report. At the request of staff we removed several items from the upgrade cost. By the Planning Department's policy, the building is considered unsound. Yaku Askew, Project Architect We are proposing a new five-unit building with family size two and three bedrooms. The floor plan is the contemporary open plan lifestyle with access to light and air. The design provides a mix of private balconies. We are enhancing the housing by the diversity of sizes and types, which attracts tenants to the neighborhood. We are providing parking for each of the multiple bedroom units. We feel the project is in a friendly neighborhood and adjacent to a thriving retail center. We feel if there is a situation for a parking variance, this is a wonderful example of that. The design concept is based on the block and the surrounding neighborhood and uses a modern interpretation. We are adhering to the Residential Design Guideline principles. We are using cornices to have strong shadow lines. We provide a recessed garage and entrance on the ground floor. The windows will be recessed and the facades provide depth. There is a required stair penthouse to the roof on a slopped roof to minimize impact. We worked with the adjacent buildings and matched the light walls on both sides. We hope to incorporate sustainable design practices by using ample light. We are using energy saving tankless water heaters. We incorporated landscape plants and the required trees along Page Street. We worked closely with the Planning Department and the neighborhood. Our most recent set of revisions came from the neighbor at 1815 Page, who is here to support the project. We strongly hope that you decide to uphold the Planning Department's recommendation and not take discretionary review. Robert Weaver, DR Requestor I reside half a block away from the project. I want to address the parking variance. We are a mix of single-family dwellings and most have no parking. We park on the street. This project is a block away from the Boy's and Girl's Club. We have an enormous parking problem in this neighborhood. The last thing I want to see is something in the neighborhood that will increase the parking problem. The ordinances say one parking space per unit. But we know that if you have adults living in a flat there will be more than one car per flat. We are going to add to the parking problem. To assume that you will have one unit and hope that the person will not have a need for a car especially with the closing of the local grocery store is not realistic. You will not have shopping unless you go someplace. I ask that the parking variance request be denied. As far as the project: I understand that if I were a neighbor I'd have a grave desire to have the property demolished. The property has been in bad condition for a time. There are properties being renovated to address the character and maintain the character of the neighborhood, which is what the Planning Code is about. I don't think this project does that. I require you do something with this project so it is more in line of the look of the area. Carolyn Squeri I manage the little apartment building to the east of the project. Initially I had concerns about the project. We raised our concerns and I wanted to acknowledge that the sponsors addressed them.

I'm here on behalf of the June family. I hope this will be the simplest matter you deal with today, the removal of an unsound single-family home that is being replaced by a single-family home to house a six-member family. This is an unsound building based on the conditions of the wood and termites. It's a modest home in a modest area. I think it's appropriate. I don't have anything further to add.

Policy Director for SPUR After completing an initial review of the study, SPUR feel that the report does a reasonably good job of providing data to inform the analysis of base line conditions in the eastern neighborhoods. I agree with Ms. Durazo that it is a confusing document however and we made some recommendations on how to better organize and focus the document. SPUR also has seven sets of recommendations to help improve the study. Of the three most important, the most important of these is that the study needs to clarify the difference between impacts caused by the proposed zoning from the pre-existing social and economic problems unrelated to the zoning. Calvin Welch, Council of Community Housing Organizations I wish to thank staff and this commission for holding this public hearing and most of all for producing this document. Although I will be critical of the content of the document, I embrace the fact that for the first time in a very long time the department has attempted to take a look at the socio-economic impacts of a major re-zoning study in a critically important part of the city. There are three great problems with this study. The first is the reliance on the 2000 census data, which is inexplicable to me. More recent data is available. The 2000 census data is anomalous census for this part of the world.  It measures reality of 1999, which is at the heart of the .com boom.  So you get some very odd relationships and very odd facts that were temporary and no longer obtaining in those neighborhoods. I think you aught to take a look at more recent data. Second, this study fails to recognize the reality that the eastern neighborhoods is the principal source of sites for low and extremely low-income permanently affordable housing. There is no discussion, which leads one to believe there is no recognition of that fact, which is staggering. I would say that fully 60% of the low and very low income, and 80% of the supportive housing that has been built in the city in the last five years has been build in these neighborhoods. How can a commission contemplate re-zoning, up-zoning these neighborhoods for market-rate housing without any discussion at all of the impact it will have on the sites for affordable housing. Currently, in this year's budget, the city has allocated $126 million dollars for the development of affordable housing. I dare say that 90% of that will be spent in these eastern neighborhoods. You must analyze the nature and impacts of these zonings on affordable housing in the future if this is to be a useful study. Finally, what is the relationship of this study and the findings of this study to the EIR, to the economic development study being done, and to study that was just done by the Task Force on the Arts. All of which is critically important and has to be wielded into some sore of unified reality to inform us all. Sue Hestor Talked about the lack of analysis of what happened between 1995 and 2005 in these neighborhoods. It treats Western SOMA in a very weird way.  It just is number of units.  There is nothing saying income, sales price, who occupies these units, how that relates to the income and sale of housing prices in the neighborhoods in which they were built.  I did it on 2660 Harrison.  I can analyze the data.  Its public data.  Its Planning Department and Assessor's data. It's no big secret. But what is the impact of having 3000 units of housing being built in exactly these neighborhoods?  Is it because it's the only place they are allowed? You don't have any information on what has happened and what its impacts have been in terms of housing composition. It doesn't attempt to get you the basic information so you know what has already happened.  That is a huge deficiency. Also, you don't have any discussion of how business service determinations were used/abused in these exact same neighborhoods to allow offices for the .com boom and what has happened in terms of those sites. Almost half of the people in the Eastern Neighborhoods with earnings earn less than $25,000 per year.  That is a driving issue in these neighborhoods.  The population is a low-income population that works in hotels, food service, and transportation services.  They are a vital part of the city.  And they are human beings that deserve to not be run out of town. One of the things that you can ask of the occupants of the sites that have live/work housing on them is how many have business licenses and what are the occupations that are being done there?  It is a requirement through NSR's for live/work projects.  If you have 3,000 job sites, what is the composition of the work being done in those?  That [information] is something you get from the business reports filed with the city.  It is not public information, but you can get it or your consultants can get it.  So tell us how this area was stressed out from about 1995.  That will give you information you can use as you're looking at the plan.

Asian Neighborhood Design I think that the Housing Element should be used as a key reference point in the analysis of housing conditions, production and need rather than just sort of an evaluation of the current state of affairs of current market conditions. The Housing Element is the adopted policies of the city whether we like them or not. I think it is helpful to look at them as the benchmark or reference point in this study in terms of analysis and conditions. There is policy guidance we can look to and use. This can clearly be related to the needs analysis of the Eastern Neighborhoods.  These are things that need to be tied together through this study. The last is the process of how this is scoped.  The process the Department has for this housing nexus study is quite functional.  This scoping never had the advantage of those involved vetting from the beginning and sort of filtering things out.  I feel that it is going to take a lot of in coming fire, which is not fair, because it did not receive the thoughtful and broad scoping that it should have had in the beginning. I don't know where you intend to go from here, but perhaps assembling some thinking on re-scoping and fine-tuning from other folks outside the Department would be helpful.

Senior Action Network and Senior Housing Action Committee I've come to ask you to postpone a real hearing on this until we've had more input from leadership in our senior community and the people who live in this area for perhaps a month. Apart from that, I would suggest that there be a discussion to how we can revise the draft and incorporate it with the suggestions from Calvin Welch, Sue Hestor, and Peter Cohen.

Morrison and Forester The report says when looking at the existing employment base in the eastern neighborhoods that 86% of employees work in management, professional, sales, office and service occupations while 13% work in traditional blue-collar occupations. I was surprised by that very small number. But what that said to me was it would be useful to re-look at that assumption that the economic development strategy for the eastern neighborhoods aught to be protecting traditional blue-collar employment if that sector is not offering employment to very many people in the eastern neighborhoods. Perhaps we aught to use this analysis to look at the question of what is the appropriate economic development policy for the eastern neighborhoods?  Is the only policy objective to protect traditional blue-collar employment if that employment is not providing jobs for many people in the eastern neighborhoods and it continues to shrink regardless of land use policy?  But aught there be other economic development goals that are looked in the eastern neighborhoods – whether that is strengthening Mission Street as the viable commercial corridor that provides more jobs for people; whether that is looking at the 24 th  Street corridor; other potential economic development objectives that might be informed by the study that the Mayor's Office of Economic Development is doing. Rather than assuming and saying that we've made the policy decision that our goal is to protect PDR, let's use this data to re-examine that goal and re-examine those assumptions and figure out if there are other economic development goals that aught to be pursued as opposed to saying that policy decision is made and set in stone and this study is going to be used to justify it. Let's use this analysis to continue to examine that assumption and that issue and come up with the right policy direction. Matt Drake It would be nice if they had a map on here so you would know exactly where the lines were being drawn. Western SOMA is not in here and it should be included.  It is contiguous with Eastern SOMA and the Mission.  They have a lot of similarities.  It is referenced throughout but not included. THE FOLLOWING PEOPLE SPOKE DURING THE 7:00 P.M. HEARING ON THIS MATTER: Bob McCarthy I think what we saw earlier was be damned if you do or damned if you don't. Put into context, this is the first of many hearings. That is helpful. It gives us a chance to make comments. I hope that the next meeting is scheduled in a month. I have a couple of observations I think is important to look at. One of the major concepts of the rezoning of the Eastern Neighborhood is the neighborhood alleged to have a change of character and demographics in '99 and 2000. There is a dramatic change in'95. We need current information. What the impact is on housing positively and negatively. And that is available. The second observation I would like to make is I remember I was an observer and sometime in 2002 when there were proposals about controls that there was a survey done by the city. I'm not familiar with the city survey or the survey that was put together by the Coalition for American Justice and Jobs. There were allegations that there was a significant difference in the survey done by the Department and the Coalition. It seems to me, and I recall there was a suggestion that the Department review the other study and determine whether or not the Department study needed correction or point to the Coalition where they had mischaracterized things. I'm sure, given the limited resources it has not been done. I think that would be helpful so we can argue policy and not the facts. I hope that would happen. I think it is important you have perfect information or as close as we can get. Again, the observation I have is the PDR definition needs to be sharpened. When I read this report we have a new category called INFORMATION. I'm trying to read all the definitions and the new category and the old ones and I'm having a lot of trouble. The statistics are contradictory. I read a paragraph and by the time I get to the bottom, they don't seem to match. But then maybe I'm not good at math. Then finally, in both the Department's large presentation as well as this presentation they talk about the new technology and the new technology that will be done in the industry and job growth sector for the city, and that somehow got merged into this PDR space concept and they are not. I think the one thing I agree with the study is on the bottom of page 83 and top of page 84 where they are talking about if you want to look at the new technology there should be a separate category. One of the things that have happened in the last five years is new technology, especially during the .com boom period. This department has categorized a lot of the technology-based industry as office use. You need to spell all of that out before you figure out how much land you need for what the report calls the traditional PDR.

My husband and I live adjacent to the north of 2121-2123 Leavenworth Street. People standing behind me have come to voice their opposition to the project. This is a visible and sensitive location. It would remove affordable housing. It is out of scale and proportion with the neighborhood or two-story mid-block buildings and is in conflict with the Residential Guidelines. It's located in the crooked part of Lumbard Street The mid-block buildings are two to three stories with the corner buildings being larger. The building in question is a sound building. Mr. Cambell asserts that. It is 50 years old and was maintained by the previous owners. It had one owner until Mr. Campbell purchased it in 2002. The original owner rented two units in the building. To the dismay of the neighbors, Mr. Cambell left the building to become an eyesore to the neighborhood. He hopes to claim it as unsound and should be demolished. Despite the attempts to ruin the building, to make it appear to be derelict, it is still sound. Its removal will remove Indian fig trees. Numerous garages will prohibit trees from being planted on that side of the block. Mr. Cambell proposes the replacement of the trees with 15-gallon trees. We know how long it takes for trees to mature. This has been taken off the market for four years to allow it to decay. The building is sound and should not be destroyed. Nor should the mature trees be destroyed. Help save our neighborhood. Suzanne My husband and I own a Julia Morgan. It's a 1909 building and located adjacent to the property on Filbert Street. We purchased at the end of '02 and have been restoring it and adding a garage. There are three units in the subject building. From a flyer Mr. Campbell passed out, he acknowledges that the building is a three-unit structure that has been vacant since '03. Although he knows it is a three-unit structure, for purposes of demolition he wants you to believe it is two units. I have testimony from persons who happily rented there at affordable housing costs attesting to three units. He gutted the interiors and removed all three kitchens without a permit and left it along for three years. The building is not worthless. It is a solid building. There is a huge legacy here. If the demolition is allowed, you remove three affordable family sized units. The new units will not rent as affordable. The neighborhood will support restoring the units and putting them back on the market. John I live at 2130, across from the site. I'm a member of an organization called Leavenworth Street neighbors. We formed based on Mr. Campbell's first project in '03 and acted as a group to preserve our neighborhood history, He hired a public relation firm to get support for his project and embarked on misleading and inappropriate collecting tactics. One neighbor asked to see the plans. He said he would show her if she signed her support. She declined. I have letters that I can show you full of misleading conditions that he wrote himself. A year earlier he inspected the site and claimed it was sound, but in this letter he says it was faulty. Mr. Campbell used a PR agency to get outside support instead of negotiating with the neighbors that are affected. Dana Smith My wife and I bought into the Grenage Terrace in early '84. We were impressed with San Francisco when we arrived from Europe. This is the best investment we ever made. We love everything about this neighborhood including the neighbors. My first interface with Mr. Campbell was in April 0f '03 when he and his architect made a presentation to us in Grenage Terrace about his aspirations. It was presented to us as a single-family building and it included himself as being that family. I was concerned about the foundation. On a 30-degree slope coming to our corner of the property, they have to deal with the water. We hope this does not pass. We want the single space that the current footprint represents. The air around us is precious. The light is precious. The gardens that we found when we came to Grenage Terrace plus the other gardens on the rising terrace behind it are precious. At one point my wife called up one person in his operation and asked if we could salvage the roses and bring them to Grenage Terrace. Unfortunately he said no. That we couldn't unless we support the project. At this point I ask you if Mr. Campbell had taken a little bit of the money that he used to hire the consultants and put $150 a month into maintaining the house and the flowers and gardens were taken care of, what would it have been like today? Michelle Pruitt I'm with the school district in Russian Hill. I'm a 15 year resident of Leavenworth and I live across from the project. I'm not proud of the fact that we will compromise our neighborhood by allowing Mr. Campbell's building. People visit from all over the world to see the crooked street. We must preserve this aspect of our city. Despite the high cost of San Francisco, I stay on Russian Hill because people are proud of its character. Letting the project in will pave the path for buildings that do not honor the architecture on our street. This is a price I am unwilling to pay. Representative of Bill Campbell In '04 he wanted to add a floor to a different project – one that retained the building and expanded it south. Before the project was withdrawn, Mr. Campbell reached an agreement with the neighbors on either side – a written agreement with the two owners as well as the neighbors in the rear. We got written agreements with three of the most impacted neighbors in the area. Neighbors from up the hill opposed. Views from the lower units are blocked by the existing building. The project before you is the same height as the existing building. If the rear owners can convince you to reduce the height and scale of the building their views could be improved. These owners are not trying to preserve their view, which is not permitted; they are trying to improve them. This property will unify the block and be consistent at the street front with other buildings on the block. There is nothing unusual about occupying the full lot at this site. This building is a mess. The foundation is crumbling. This is Mr. Campbell's second time through the system trying to approve this project. He has gone on 25 neighborhood walks and talked to other neighbors. He has 59 letters of support. It is a well designed project. Jonathan – Project Architect [Using power point, he showed the existing structure and its surroundings. He pointed out how this is the biggest eye sore in the neighborhood and that it could not remotely be considered historic. He showed how it doesn't meet current residential guidelines and is inconsistent with all the architecture on the hill.] The building is 57.7 feet high from the sidewalk and was built in 1956. It extends 75 feet into the lot and has side yards filled with retaining walls and stairs – not public open space. The new design draws on the architecture of the neighborhood. It sets back 10 feet and addresses the street wall. It has gable roofs, brick base, stucco, wood, and copper trim details. The rear is one and a half foot shorter. We are adding 180 square feet to the mid-block open space. We have parking for 10 cars, which is 67% over the required minimum. We have three units that are consistent in size with the neighborhood. It's picking up the architecture in the neighborhood. In scale it is compatible. The open space is increased. We have matched all the light walls. Our features are consistent with the neighborhood and we will use high quality materials to build the building. Chris I'm President of the construction group. If the project is approved I'll be the primary contractor. I'm also an investor in 2121 Leavenworth. Mr. Campbell and I have been a developer team for years in San Francisco. We mostly do major remodels and home reconstruction in San Francisco. We have a proven record of working with neighbors as well as doing quality developments. We do it safely and professionally. [Name not given} I will begin by acknowledging we have not developed a soundness report because none is required. The cost of the building exceeds criteria for affordability. We looked at the existing foundation. At the basement level, it's subterranean. The existing concrete is failing badly. There is no drainage. The drainage issues are not being addressed by the foundation. This foundation needs to be replaced regardless of what project is approved for this site. A new foundation would improve the safety of the site. Stabilization issues involved in a new foundation for a new project are similar requirements we would require in replacing the existing foundation. We have to address the shoring and underpinning. I think everyone can agree it is not in our best interest to allow million dollar homes to slide down the hill. We share the same goal of safety. We will engage a highly respected technical engineer and undertake a monitoring program. We welcome peer review. We want transparency and want to work with neighbors. Leonard I'm part owner of the building. It's not true that I am the thug that is strong arming neighbors over the past year. I have done 30 outreach walks. I've rung 60 doorbells and met with merchants. Outside of the opposition, the general feeling I got from the people is that they like the new buildings and are eager to see it come to the neighborhood and dismayed that this much time has gone by. The building is beautifully designed near to the ground level. It will be an enhancement to the neighborhood. I urge you not to take DR on this wonderful project. Bill Campbell I along with a few friends purchased this building in August of 2002. It was the second project we started together as friends. It looks like it will be the last one to complete. We underwent a process over a year and a half in tying to et neighbor buy-in to build a single-family home I could move my extended family in. It took us a year and a half to reach an agreement that honored their key concerns. The building that they signed off on is represented by these plans. We have kept the 57 feet off of the sidewalk. That building expanded to the south and is bulkier, more massive and got a higher roof than our current design. It is true that when I came to the DR hearing, I was surprised at the level of opposition. I was almost dumbfounded. With an additional month, we had two additional meetings. I was unable to figure out a way to preserve a single-family home that would house my family and meet their demands. I gave up after a month of trying and decided I would drop back and design what many of the neighbors wanted. From the letters filed stating that the average unit was 1600 square feet on Russian Hill, we designed two buildings with three units each. The low was 1600, the middle 1900, and the upper 2,300. I went back and had meetings with the neighbors on the new plans and discovered that apparently they would not do either. It has been two years since the first suspended hearing. This has turned into a frustrating experience. Enlightening and I learned a lot, but frustrating. It is unclear to me what could be done. Six new units, reducing the bulk on the street, protecting light and air to the neighbors to the south, north and east & , and as you heard Jonathan say we are using materials that fit with the neighborhood. Milly My husband James and I lived in our house for 41 years. Our property is directly adjacent to the west of 2121 Leavenworth. He would be with me but he had a serious stroke a few months ago. The reason we were objecting to the first project was because he had a 12-foot sky light right in our face. We tried to get him to mitigate that light at least 80% but he wouldn't do it. He would sign off 50%. We have a covenant of 60 feet. I had to sign away a 14-foot flew to get agreement with him. I wish that he would tell you the truth. Penelope Clark I have not heard from the developer since April of last year. We are dismayed. We felt there should be more effort to contact the neighbors. The original agreement had side setbacks where the older buildings have property line windows. I think these should be respected and the design guidelines should setback some of the lower stories more so there is good light and air for the existing buildings. Michael Fury I agree we stick by the rules. When it wasn't an issue it was a three-story building. Not that it's an inconvenience; it's a two-story building. The building was unattractive nine years ago and it's an eye sore and a bed for rats. Neighbors are in favor of improvements but we don't want the cure to be worse than the disease. David Kimball My wife and I have lived in the neighborhood since '92. We are opposed to replacing a three-unit building with six units that's out of scale and mass with what is there today. I hope we can get back to three units. Angela Strand I live at 2130 Leavenworth. I developed the flyer and would have used a different picture if it was provided. I will try not to be emotional, but I am angry by the distortions by the team who get paid by the hour by the developer. There are a great deal of people in the neighborhood like myself who will not be directly impacted economically. We are here because we feel this building is too big. Morlena Morris I live at 2130 Leavenworth. I know my neighbors. They are lovely. We are here with no hidden agendas. We banned together because it is a proper cause and we will be affected by it. We are a military family and are delighted we can afford to move in the area. I will be affected if this is approved. I will lose all of the sunlight in my apartment. This is not an exclusive suburb. It is a beautiful area that people travel from all over the world to see. Mary Inman I own buildings on Filbert. I'm one of the persons that would benefit, but oppose it. I would financially gain from this. I oppose it because of the reasons people gave today. This is a three-unit building. There is a way this could have worked with us. The idea that it took four years is because they got angry and didn't get something the first time by building something that would capitalize from the gains. Steve Pantelik I live at 2111 Leavenworth Street The people affected by this are here. They will live in the neighborhood for the next 20 years. It means something to people here. That is why I am away from my three children to be here. This is a chance to have a positive effect on the neighbors. It's too large. Reading from a letter from a person who had supported it: I'm writing to express my wish to be taken off [the support list]. It appears the scope of the process has changed. Bill Hellendale I'm moving to the neighborhood. All I want to do is present a photo of the condition in which Mr. Campbell is keeping the property. [On the overhead, he showed a picture of the property that included the front entrance that was not in a well-kept condition.]

Representative of 340 Fremont We are on the west side of Fremont Street. This site was planed for a single tower. 379 and 399 are across on the east side of the street. The project designed before you is consistent with the [Rincon] Plan. We created excellent architecture at the ground level. We designed a human scale and a network of mid-block open spaces. At the city level, we created the slender tower. We worked with department staff for six months and made significant modifications to the architecture. The design incorporates a level of scale and detail in the lower building levels and minimizes the façade interpretations. We created a inviting landscape to open space and the tower has slenderness and adds a presence to the skyline. The project creates a quality of space and neighborhood. It provides housing downtown and a contribution to affordable housing. It will donate approximately $20 million dollars to the city and to the Rincon Neighborhood through transfer and property taxes and affordable housing in the South of Market Community Fund. We think Fremont was envisioned and studied in the plan through a process that is complete. We are proud of it and we request your final approval. Sue Hestor I didn't hear anyone mention the PG&E facility next to this site. It's the building that looks like gigantic gray corduroy. It's huge. People that live in the townhouses, except the people that have an opening to Fremont Street, are going to be at the bottom of a light well. It is going to be ugly and no direct sunlight. Where is the staff analysis? Where is the discussion from the developer's architect? Is this good policy? There are exceptions to the plan for cars and parking. I really want to hear and I want you to ask questions on what kind of a life do people have looking out on an 8 to 10 story wall that is blank and it's not unattractive, it's just beige massive.

name_raw: Michael Burke, Attorney for the project sponsor
comment: Last year the Commission had a vision for what should occur on that side of the street, that is the vision of a tall, slender tower on the corner of Harrison and Fremont Street. We are seeking from you the ability to make your vision real and we hope we met it. Rick Keating, Project Architect As a pedestrian, you don't see the tower. You are more involved with materials and things on the street. As a user, from inside the building, it's something different. The character you've driven into the planning is giving you something that is unique. They are not massive towers. They are slender. They catch the light in different ways. We created a crystalline building that has faceting and character within its spirit. These are seen from the Bay Bridge. [Through pictures, he went on to describe how the building looks next to other buildings, how it influences the light shining on and through the narrow shaft and vertical elements.] The plan provides for a wide sidewalk on Fremont that offers us an opportunity to do a double row of trees. The idea of having housing facing the street was an exciting opportunity and we took it to rethink the way houses are to step down. The way we have created the doors and patio, you have a handrail and landscaping and a stoop. This gives you a great opportunity for interaction with people living in their house that will activate the street. It captured what we love about the rhythms on the streets. Andrew Brooks I manage the Bay Crest condos and residents of the Rincon Hill Association I want to talk about quality of life issues. I've been in the area since 1991. Bay Crest was one of the first put on line in the area.. The area that it incorporates in Rincon Hill today has not received streetcar improvements, traffic improvements, electric, managerial, any civic upgrades since the late  30's. We have telephone poles on the sidewalks. We have over hanging municipal railway lines and old railroad tracks in the ground. It's a very raw urban experience when you get outside the buildings. We are doing what you wanted us to do. You wanted us to move back to the city. You wanted us to live downtown and walk and create a new urban environment. We are doing that. We are in danger of collapsing within ourselves. There is no infrastructure to support the number of people that are living there. I've heard commissioners and staff say that it is not our issue to worry about city support services. It has got to start somewhere. The city in general did not support the hill. There are no city support services available. We are under gridlock from 2 p.m. everyday to 7 p.m. And on weekends it's from 11 at night to 3 or 4 in the morning. This is not because of the Bay Bridge reconstruction; it is because of the activity in the South of Market area. My challenge to you is to work with us and get the streetscape and area improvements up and going. Sue Hestor Staff hasn't reported the debate about loading areas in this building. The garbage will be pushed out mechanically to the street for pick up because there is not a loading dock. This building will have a number of pickups and deliveries because a lot of people work at home. You have a demand for loading and you don't have enormous loading facilities. I have asked before if we could have an understanding of how pedestrians would move on the blocks. Doesn't the Planning Department think that you have to worry about how are you going to implement the pedestrian improvements? Commissioners, can you tell me how the pedestrian circulation works if you are on one side of the street and want to get on the other, especially if it's during the 10 hours a day where it is gridlocked? It's shocking to me to have five deaths in a three-block area.

comment: I'm going to be sorry to see Commissioner Hughes, Lee and Bell leave. I didn't know about Commissioner Lee until today. Commissioner Hughes, everything you say is pertinent. Director Macris talked about what was brought up at Budget and Finance. There was a request that there be a Deputy Director hired. That would subvert the public process. The Commission began hearings to select three candidates consistent with the Charter requirements and hearings went up until December 16 th and we had Director Macris come in as Acting Director. Now the Director is suggesting he hand pick a Deputy Director. At least one commissioner was not aware of this suggestion until yesterday. The community was not aware of this until this week. On the budget, this is a line item for $198,000 that includes salary and benefits. This is a policy call. Commissioners have to determine whether there should be a Deputy Director appointed or not. It is fully discretionary and should be scheduled on the agenda for a full discussion. This is like an end run in the back door. Director Macris would select somebody that would be a Deputy Director who would eventually take over the Department. This whole thing is wrong. I ask that you request that line item be held and ask that it be scheduled on the agenda. I attended a meeting on Tuesday night. The organization voted to oppose this type of a procedure. I think the commission should select three candidates, let the public respond to the three, and put it forward to the Mayor. This is the required procedure. If Dean wants to stay on however, that is something that could be decided but the process should not be subverted. This is the wrong way to go about selecting a Director of San Francisco's Planning Department. It will be a SPUR surrogate. John Bardis The Director says we have a culture in the city that has to be observed. What is a culture but the process by which we select the people who will direct our City Government? And the process includes certain people, which are not the public. And that is the process that we want to occur now and institutionalize it in the budget process and get a City Attorney's opinion to justify that it is correct. You might say you are being consistent. You had a Planning Director who was away for a year and the City functioned without a Planning Director. What's different now? I think there is a need to recognize that this budget matter was something that seems to have slipped into the budget process. This is a policy issue that this commission should have addressed in public before the public with a proper public hearing that addressed the issue. On the side, I want to thank the commission for the service you provide even when we disagree. I respect any person who is willing to volunteer and provide service as commissioners of the city and the time that is required. It is more than we in the neighborhoods have been doing. We are deeply appreciative and respect your efforts. God speed in all your efforts and I hope you come back to the trenches and help us volunteers. Hiroshi Fukuda From the neighborhood meeting last week – I am reading this on behalf of Judy, President of the Coalition [the statements are not clear and their position on whether or not they support the position or the process it was brought forward is not evident]. I personally appreciate all the hard work and services that Commissioners Sue Lee and Kevin Hughes have provided. I have been coming to commission meetings since the late'80's, the heyday of the Richmond Specials. I have to say that one of the most courageous decisions that a commission ever took was when this commission stood up and decided to send back the Better Neighborhood's Plus legislation to the Board of Supervisors. That was very commendable and it took a lot of courage. Thank you very much. D. GENERAL

I am here today not to discuss a plan or cause. I will see Commissioner Bell at her farewell party at Pier 23. Commissioner Lee we know you as the poster child of an iron fist in the golden glove. Your ability to run a meeting and allow people to express their emotions – you set a standard for people running public meetings that should be heralded and replicated. You have been accessible. You have been a great fashioner of compromise. You have in every respect adequately dispensed your duties as a commissioner and the president. For that we are thankful for your almost three decades of service to the city. We look forward to your continued role in expanding the understanding of the Chinese community, and your directorship of the Chinese Historical Society. Commissioner Hughes is known as the Grand Inquisitor. We appreciate what you brought to the commission especially from working men and women. That is an important perspective that needs to be appreciated because those are the folks who build our town and maintain it. Your fellow commissioners have such respect for you that that perspective will be in their brain when they approach a project. I want to thank you for the preparedness you bring to the process and the standard to which you held those of us who appear before you to be at least adequately prepared waiting for the question. You held us to a standard. And Commissioner Bell, I wish you well and hope your successors meet at least half the standards you have set. Thank you. John Bardis I would like to make an observation regarding what Commissioner Hughes referred to as work force housing that was constructed in the city and at one time really provided the housing for the work force. These days we can't provide anymore. How many demolitions did this commission approve of single-family dwellings over the past 4 years, which was the work-force housing of our city? Maybe they were to create new units of housing. That is a market, but not for families. When you demolished those single-family units, did not the commission/department take the initiative to see how they will be replaced? It is a serious problem as Commissioner Hughes pointed out. Commissioner Bill Lee mentioned that we have to do something about these applications that are being held up in a terrible process by which things are being delayed and the prices and costs of construction are going up. Commissioner, I invite you to look into an application that was submitted in 1999, three years before this commission was formed. It is still in effect. Why is it still in effect after seven years? If you are that concerned about how the process is, and you feel it is the bad guys or people in the neighborhoods, look into that one and find out how the departments have been wolfing up or the project sponsor. It is a mess. Hope to see you back and wish you God speed in your retirement.

section: PUBLIC COMMENT ON AGENDA ITEMS WHERE THE PUBLIC HEARING HAS BEEN CLOSED
comment: RE: Medical Cannabis Dispensaries (MCD's) We are concerned about the language in the proposed ordinance that will amend the existing ordinance governing MCD's. We are concerned about the redefinition of recreation and community buildings. We feel that some language should be in there that deals with license day care centers and licensed childcare centers. We are concerned about the notice requirement. We feel the Planning Department should provide owners within 300 feet of an MCD. The more people involved, the more it will get aired out. In the long run, it will be a great benefit to everybody. We are concerned and do ask that you add a recommendation to the proposed ordinance that would require that an MCD not be permitted in Lake Shore Plaza without a Conditional Use permit hearing before this commission. We are not asking more than what's on the books in the current ordinance that deals with West portal. West portal has a condition that says for the permit is permitted you need a Conditional Use hearing before the Planning Commission. We are concerned that the residents out in the southwest quadrant of the city are heard. Rosaura Kenyon I've been a resident in San Francisco for 40 years. For years I worked with nonprofits and the Mayor's Office of Employment and Training. I was on several Boards and Commissions. I am not able to continue that type of work. However, I am benefiting from some of the activities and some of the marches that I was on. One of those things was my freedom to be able to access any service that I wanted to access that was given to me as a citizen of not only the United States but of San Francisco City and County. Every year, we are limited to more and more services and public benefits that we have been previously given, offered and accepted. I am of the opinion that I paid my dues. I feel I should be able to access services I need. These dispensaries not only provide medicine, but they provide social services and public benefits to many of us. I went through a lot with this town and I feel that my life shouldn't be made anymore difficult because someone is not reading the posted signs that are placed on every building when an enterprise is going to be opened. I will leave you with the comment that services for us are becoming limited and you have the power to maintain these services. Lenora Brown I'm citizen of San Francisco. I'm 57 years old. I am a marijuana cannabis card user. I'm here to speak up for that service. Patrick Goggil There are approximately 11,000 registered ID cardholders for medical cannabis, and 20,000 in the city that has recommendations to medical cannabis. We estimate that approximately 25 percent of those patients are seniors or 60 years or older. 70 percent of those folks are recipients to free medicine and compassion programs. In the city, we are facing significant attrition of MCD's. There were 42 MCD's in the city and now there are 30. With the regulations and the requirements of getting a permit we estimate that will be halved. We are very concerned about the impact that this will have in the neighborhoods where the MCD's survive. I don't know whether it is the Department of Health Services or the Planning Commission that should have a study to determine what is the appropriate numbers that is needed to serve its patient base. I would like to echo the thanks and congratulations on the commissioners leaving today and acknowledge the fine term you have served. Michelle Aldrich I happen to be lucky. I live in the Marina. I'm here to urge you to vote yes on the amendments to the Dispensary law. The city has put so many blocks in front of the dispensaries, we would like a couple of holes filled. The city is a neighborhood. It's this neighborhood and that neighborhood and all neighborhoods. And people that are patients live in each of them. What you are doing with these rules/hoops that the dispensaries are going to have to jump through, are saying that we are going to come down to four or five clubs in the city. If you think the neighborhoods are going to be upset now, what are we going to see when 11,000 people try to go to four or five clubs or dispensaries? I urge you to approve these amendments. I hope that the worst fears about the dispensary provisions turn out to be wrong. And congratulations on all your service and thank you from the bottom of my heart. Michael Aldrich We have strict restrictions in place for medical cannabis – better laws than other cities in California. Some restrictions include that nay dispensary must be located outside 300 feet from schools and community centers. These regulations make it impossible for someone who is forced to relocate in San Francisco to find another place. Trying to stay a thousand feet away from a school is difficult. There have been only two successful cases of relocation. We are in the process of removing the old fashion community centers and replacing them with an expensive process that only warehouses medical marijuana sales establishments like a Walgreen's for marijuana that can survive the permit process. We will end up with a different situation than the small clubs. I urge you to adopt the amendments requested by the Planning Department. Do not make more restrictions. Do not adhere to the thousand-foot rule or you are establishing a moratorium. I think the noticing requirements should be 150 feet as the amendment proposes like any other project. There will be neighbors in every neighborhood that doesn't want marijuana near them. There will be more neighbors in the same neighborhoods that are patients of medical marijuana clubs and don't want to go across town. They would like to work with the smaller clubs with associate services. They approved the process we are discussing. David Bisho – President of West of Twin Peeks Council Our big concern is safety. Based on what we were told by the Police Department, criminal incidences occurred at every pot club in the city. There is no way to give the families with children a reason to brave it out and stay here. We don't want pot clubs or medical marijuana unless a city agency is in charge or distributing it. How can that make sense when the actions of this commission, the Planning Department, and the Mayor's Office are enabling this activity already? With respect to considering Mirkarimi's amendment, our council knows these amendments are an effort to increase the ability of allowing these businesses that no one wants to live near by changing definitions. We ask that you vote no on the amendments and give the current legislation a chance to work. In this town, once a policy is established it is hard to undo it. Veronica Gayner I'm with the Community Coalition. Last year our neighborhood was involved with a cannabis club in our neighborhood. On June 6 th there was a meeting to ask neighbor's input. As a result of that input, our neighborhood was involved with the Medical Cannabis legislation. We asked for Discretionary Review. As a result, the current legislation is what we now have. This was a compromise by neighbors and cannabis clubs. By not allowing neighborhood input you are opening yourself up to countless meetings. I suggest you let the legislation play itself out for three years and legislate accordingly. The purpose of the legislation was to prevent abuse and watering it down now seems counter effective. [Name was not given] I have a resolution from the San Francisco Coalition of San Francisco Neighborhoods. At the June meeting we proposed the following resolution: The Coalition for San Francisco Neighborhoods opposed any change of the requirements on medical cannabis dispensary and the notification requirements. Now speaking on my own: I believe that change the notification area to 150 feet presents you a standard we have for buildings or DRs or whatever is not the right thing to do in this situation. I say that because cannabis is not to be taken lightly. I support medical use of cannabis I think it is important. There are many studies to indicate that patients thrive better with it. No question. But I am concerned about the misuse. There have been stories that people who do not necessarily fit into the category of medically needing cannabis, can obtain it easily. For profit. Medical Cannabis is controversial. You should increase the notification area. Hiroshi Fukuda As a Pharmacist, the City should investigate the use of pharmacies, professional licensed pharmacies as the proper way to go. When you say club, it seems like you are going to have a good old time. This is serious business. Stephanie Tucker I'm a community activist and I'm representing 150 voters in the Western Addition. It's really important that we protect and preserve the Cannabis Clubs we have left in the city servicing sick patients. They are under attack and we are trying to resolve the situations in the neighborhoods. We need a level playing ground. That would best happen if you approve the amendments on the table before yo. David Cincotta RE: Wharf J-10 EIR Certification I want to emphasize I'm here on behalf of the Fish Company who is one of the tenants of the space. We do not reject the demolition. We are concerned in the manner and way it should be done. We all want to make sure there is no further contamination of the Bay. We know there is a contaminated site by Exxon Mobile. They said they don't want to do further testing in the area until the demolition occurs. We think that is wrong. We thing the testing should occur prior to the demolition. It would help know what could be the cause there. In the Comments and Responses document, we notice that the Port is proposing to replace concrete slabs and retaining walls that may interfere with sediment and soil. Exxon Mobile should do the testing before the structures are in place to determine whether those structures will impact the feasibility of removal of the soils. I think we all have the same concerns: We want a clean, safe Bay. On page 10 there is a correction that needs to be made. There is a sentence that says the project would not result in loss of fishes because there has not been fishing there for the last five years. There reason that is is because we have been removed from the site because of its unsafe condition. If it was up and we could use it there would be fish processing. Technically it is correct. But it should be clarified that we can't use it because it is unsafe. Finally, I spoke at the last hearing that there is mitigation measures in here to prevent the disturbance of fish migration. We want to schedule the demolition at a time when it is not disruptive to the businesses that are doing fish processing. The comments were that is a socioeconomic impact and not suitable to be considered. I think it is a valid consideration I will speak to at every possible hearing I can. [Speaker was not identified] RE: Medical Cannabis Dispensaries Amendments What is being changed is the notification. We are not saying anything about what should be done about the dispensaries. The notification requirement of 150 feet is only six stores. 300 feet is 12 houses. What is the big objection? What is bad about notification? It helps everyone get everything in order so it is on track so we don't get into more things of why people were not notified properly. There is no need for the amendments. Marilyn Amini Right off the top, you can't take action because you do not have an adequate environmental determination. This legislation is said by the department to be grandfathered under the originally passed piece of legislation General Rule Exclusion. Chapter 31 of the Code does not allow for a General Rule Exclusion unless the commission adopted criteria. This will have impact because you are redefining residential. If you look at the fourth, the last of these you see there are 42 locations. The buffer zone for recreation is being redefined and you are including criteria that serve primarily those under age 18. That is arbitrary. How will they quantify how many are 18 or over? What about the 19 and 20 year olds, et cetera. Marijuana is an important substance. There is a lot of crime associated with these dispensaries. You haven't had the Police Commission address you. The Drug and Crime Detail will be glad to give you information on the impact of the ones that currently exist. You have to request notification regarding a particular medical cannabis dispensary. That amendment is a bad amendment as well.

Architect of the Day School I'm representing the school and the San Francisco Jewish Center preschool which is present on this site. The three institutions on this site have come together to form a campus for Jewish learning on Brotherhood Way. We came before you with a Master Plan of this site. The first phase was completed. In 2001 the school moved in. The classroom and library building on the east side has been a successful project for the school. It has provided great academic space. It gave the campus a new identity and created a place for the school to grow. The success of that project lead to the school's growth. They are up to 382 students – almost full enrollment for next year. The existing gym is serving for athletics dining after school space performing arts all the special events like book fairs. They had staff moving tables in and out all day. The school has designed a new performing arts and gym building. The new proposal has the pavilion located in the northwest corner. The outdoor play space is moved to a roof top play area. We create a better courtyard in the middle of the campus for activities. We are keeping the two-story wing in the back as part of future planning. The new building is set down here and maintains the green screen on the frontage road. It creates a new exterior plaza. For the gym: You come in on the entry level. Seating and a portable stage can be moved in. There is a roof top play area with bathrooms and on the lower level we are providing a green room drama and performance space. The project serves the school and they realize it is a dream for the future and ensures the success of the students. Robert Pender I'm not trying to be a spoiled sport but the first time me and my organization heard about this was on June 6 th of this year when we got a letter from the Planning Department. I think the people that live there should receive notice more than two weeks in advance. There has already been a project planned and approved I believe at 800 Brotherhood Way which is across the street. Brother has two lanes of traffic in each direction. I think the people who live here are entitled to have a traffic survey. Are we going to be overwhelmed by the cars? This is in my opinion a poor example of planning. I'm blaming the sponsors. The churches on the odd side number of Brotherhood Way knew we were there. They know me and my organization have been there for 20-30 years. Why were we not consulted or informed about it? Why didn't they have the curtsey to inform us about this? I hope the Planning Department will continue to notify me at least notice me when something is happening in our neighborhood at least a month in advance.

Representing Lawrence Gray, the DR requestor Mr. Gray is a retired San Francisco Police Captain. He has been at that location for 30 years and raised his family.  He's been retired for 20 years. There are six buildings together that are the same height in a row. The buildings have the same rear configuration. These are the old single-family dwelling style homes. Mr. Gray raised his family there and now intends to enjoy his retirement there. One enjoyable feature of that is his backyard – the patio and garden. We are not talking about an issue of view. We are talking about an issue of side spacing and an issue that fits in the area of light and privacy. There was a one story studio/office. That studio will be expanded 10 feet from its rear when demolished and go 20 more feet higher. It will be a very short distance from my client's side yard. You will see no objectors from the southern side of the building because on the eastern side you will see that's where their patio is to take advantage of the sun and light and air. It's the folks to the north that will be impacted There was an indication they will potentially expand the side track but not completely down the line as staff indicated. It's when you are there and when you see this area in which he wishes to enjoy himself you see it's impacted gravely. It's too big a building next to a space that's enjoyable to him. I ask you for your consideration on behalf of my client to allow him to enjoy the space he has for many years and not have it impacted by a large construction. Lawrence Gray I live at 966 Corbett Street and I've lived there for 30 years. My wife and I raised my family there My two sons have now gone and grown and have families of their own. I lost my wife to cancer six years ago. I'm by myself in this house.  House of many memories. My wife and I first looked at Corbett Street 10 years earlier but could not afford it at that time. I was a young police officer at the time. 10 years later this house was available and we moved there. From the front of the house there is a beautiful view that I appreciate everyday, that looks on the east side of San Francisco – the eastern district, the Bay view. In the back of my house I have windows into my breakfast room – two sides of solid glass where the sun comes in. From the first landing and up the stairs is a large window where light pours in from behind. It is not often I have to turn lights on except at night. In the Bathroom there is a window where light pours in and there is a small bedroom, which faces the back and light comes in. The yard itself is very [beautiful].  We have a decked area where we walked out and dined in the past. My wife was a great gardner. The house is described as going up steeply. There are a series of four walls where the gardens run to the back fence. This is an area where I have my coffee in the morning or read the paper or listen to the ball games. It is an important part of the house. This wall would cut out all the light until the late afternoon hours. I guess maybe I've just become aware of how important it is to me – my house and the memories of my house. Maybe I took it for granted because now it could all be lost. Mike Connell I'm working with Lawrence Gray on the project. The initial project was submitted last June and staff recommended the building be setback five feet or the entire top floor be removed. The current staff report recommends it be pushed back three feet and we support staff. This will take out all available light. There will be a small mid-day light on the north side of the deck in the summer months. Richard (Dick) Poley I live at 972 Corbett.  That is the next house up to the north. My partner and I lived in this house for 31 years and enjoyed the afternoon sun, much as Captain Gray has. I really feel we are going to lose it due to this massive wall. It's going to block off all of the sun except for possibly slivers of it in June or July. This is a serious problem from our point of view. The amount that the extension goes back is not so much a problem as the height. These modifications that have been made are band-aid approaches. I hope that additional adjustments could be made to allow us a little more light. Carolyn E. Dutton I brought letters from three neighbors that have done similar projects, which took up more of their property than ours is going to. I grew up in this property since I was six. My parents bought the property in 1951. This property was destroyed by fire while I was out of town almost two years ago. It's taken a long time to get this going. These are a row of tract homes built at the same time. Even they are two stories above the garage, they are small. Many people who have bought these houses now have put on additions more extensive than mine. We have cut off a story. It is not going up 20 feet; it is going up 8 feet. Just one story from where the previous addition was on the back. We need the extra bedroom. We were lacking it when we lived there. We are willing to extend the light well up to his retaining wall, which is the more used part of his backyard with the deck. If we extend that light well we would like to do it on the second story. There are two stories not three in the back. If we extended it we want to do it on the upper room not the ground level room because it doesn't impact sun at all. If we indent it on the second level that would give us room for the room on the first level. My 82-year-old neighbor was here earlier but couldn't stay. He authorized me to say he is in support of the project. He is our neighbor to the south. He has been there for many years also.

Project Architect In San Francisco a 25-foot wide lot with 0 side yards has been the norm for maybe a hundred years? The original project proposal was significantly within the Code set boundaries for the property. It is somewhat confusing because the property slopes so steeply.  If we went to the 40-foot height limit that zoning allows, it would be huge and something inappropriate. We went up a floor and straight back, which gave us a triangle shaped building. There are others that built larger projects. Six were built in the recent past. These are contemporary developments you have already approved. In the case of this project, sun and light are important to us. We see the future of perhaps the southern property next to ours as being a similar development. Our intent was to get sun and light to our property even if someone built the same project in back of us. We used half of it and reserved the other half for a space that would get sun even if another building were built there. We have also tried to accommodate the neighbor to the north because we appreciate his sunlight. It's difficult to do that with his cooperation. He has refused to meet with us until Mike Smith told him that the meeting was scheduled.  Then we got a call. The first interaction was after the first proposal went to the Planning Department. We rearranged the floor plan to cut back a three-foot light well. We offered to slope the roof and the further extension of the light well and another slopped roof to get more sun to Mr. Gray's property. Basically the Planning staff's proposal I think is a good one. It does what we were going to do and I support it with the exception I would like the light well to occur on the third floor. Patrick Colling There are six projects that have done similar modifications on the block. We are close neighbors. 994 Corbett got passed through planning and it is a bigger plan. 996 Corbett has no setbacks.  There were a couple of others. We had a setback of three feet at the top.  We had a shadow study done. It sounds like they have been quite good at working with their neighbor. We support this type of project. It is a betterment of the neighborhood. The houses are small.

Representing the Project Sponsor This is about the lack of diversity in the housing stock in San Francisco. There is a hole in how the codes work together in San Francisco. The Building Code will not allow two dwelling units to exist without an occupancy interpretation between them. The Planning Code does not have provisions for two kitchens in a single dwelling unit. The Blenders bought this house in 1952. It went from one to two units. The description of the scope of work was installation of a new kitchen on the first floor. What they were trying to do was create a separate housing unit. They were trying to create a separate dwelling in their home for family members. That is what this family who are two owners removed from that owner in '52 wishes to do. The directories are consistent from '53 to '55. In 1961 only is the address 2290 used. The apartment two doors down are listed at 1
