comment: 4. The apartment down shows a separate occupant and residents. In 1988 there is no second listing. This is when the Blenders seized occupancy of the home. They deeded it to the San Francisco symphony as a charitable contribution. Through all of the records we don't see an instance of there being another occupancy of this unit. To the current there is not showing any residents at 2290. Did this ever function as an actual separate unit? Are we changing the character of the property by removing a door so the grandmothers can live down stairs? There is no evidence that the unit functioned differently than the manner this family wants to live. This is a large home for a successful family. This is a captain of industry who whishes to grow his family and companies here. He wishes to support our tax base and employment base with good paying tech jobs in San Francisco. It is incumbent upon us to provide opportunities for housing that people like this want to live in. Project Sponsor We bought this house a year ago. My mother and mother-in-law live with us and we love the fact that they do. My mother-in-law has been with me for 20 years and my mom is just moving in. We want them to have their space. Adding the upper unit will do that. I know what it means to have mother and mother-in-law living with you. Please take that into consideration.

Project Architect The property presents the unusual situation of having two street frontages and no mid block open space. There are two buildings on the lot – a three-unit building and a cottage at the rear. There are a total of 4 units.  This is one more than the allowable required by the Planning Code, which allows up to three. There is no mid-block open space. There is no parking. We propose to improve the conditions and bring it in conformance of Codes. We are removing one unit. Given the poor condition of the building we know the existing tenants do not want to remain. There is a lack of light and air, an old kitchen and stairs, and a crumbling foundation. The ground floor unit was not meant to be a unit. The building was clearly designed as a two-unit building. We feel it is consistent with the General Plan of San Francisco that calls for bringing properties [back to original intent] when possible and providing diversity of housing. This is what we are doing. At this time, units as we are proposing are rare. The only options for families are to move. The merging of the two units will help with the creation of open space.  Changing the occupancy allows us to remove the second exit at the rear.  We can remove the porch and stair and create open space between the two separate buildings. I believe it is in the city's interest to allow this project to proceed. Eric Grossman We bought the house 11 months ago. When we bought the property the tenants lived there and we presumed they would be there for a long time. They were not evicted and there is documentation there. The house is in derelict conditions. I gave you pictures of before and after of the cottage. We plan to do the same thing to the house in time. Our neighbors are supportive of this. They like what the cottage has done for the neighborhood and hopefully the main house will do that as well. The options was living here or commute from the suburbs. Devon I'm a neighbor that lives across the street. I'm here in support of them because I believe they are really doing the right thing with their house. I have seen the condition of the house previously and the result of their remodeling of the cottage. If they do that similar level of work, which I know they are going to do to the front house, I support this. They are great neighbors and I hope they stay in the neighborhood and I think they are going to make that building, that property into an attractive rental unit. It was something that just really needed to happen. I know personally my neighbors on both sides – all four of us that face their building are in support of what they are trying to do and hope they can turn it into a home where they can stay in the neighborhood and city. I hope it happens. Anna Grossman I'm pregnant and I want to raise our family here. We love the idea of being in a diverse city, especially one like San Francisco and all it has to offer – the arts and everything. We appreciate and want our children to grow up in this type of environment.

I am co-owner of 479 Arkansas Street, adjacent to 20 th Avenue. The best way for me to describe our issue and for each one of you to experience the situation would be if you owned solar panels and your neighbor puts up a structure that would block the sun - the source of energy for the panels. I paid $20,000 for the panels and they worked. You felt that since the State of California provided funding for these panels you would be protected by California Civil Code 801.5 with provisions to receive sunlight and creating an easement for a solar system. The planner says there is no such code to protect city residents. They say it's a private matter between us. I am here to see whether this Commission can find a way to get someone to be responsible, just as a City wants their documents signed by professionals. Our request is that the project does not obstruct the sunlight. They can be made of transparent materials. It's a roof deck in the most sunny part of San Francisco. I would add, in the magnitude of what we were arguing here, we failed to determine that there are issues of security as a result of the stairway. It comes close to a landing to our bathroom window. There could be someone who could jump from the landing to our property. Margaret Healy, Owner 1640 20 th Street. When he first approached me about the concern of his solar panels I told my architect to look at it. She presented a shadow analysis. It showed a minimal impact on the shadowing. They refused to accept this report and required us to prepare a full calendar year study and financial analysis of how much it would cost in terms of lost energy. I hired 2 solar experts. I made significant design changes. Ripping off the top of my roof and adding $30,000 dollars to the cost of the construction. The design changes were successful. The solar reports only showed a few dollars a year impact on the solar system. They are refusing to accept the results of the report they requested. At this point we've spent five months and $40,000 in reports, design and construction changes. I think we have done enough. I hope the Commission will see we have acted in good faith and as good neighbors.

I represent the Green Cross It is important to state why we are here today. I'm sure members of this commission are aware that the Green Cross used to be in a different neighborhood. There was a process that leads us to be here today. Mr. Reid is here today because he is one of the few or only dispensary operator who has gone above and beyond to comply with the rules. He was one of the two at the time who got a use permit, which is not what most were doing. He was trying to play by the rules. Later when neighbors complained, his permit was suspended and there were proceedings to revoke the permit. That was pre-regulations. That is what brought Mr. Reid before the Board of Permit Appeals. After hearing the evidence, they did not elect to close him down. They gave him six months and if there were serious problems that caused detriment to the neighborhood, they would have closed him down immediately. They gave him six months without prejudice to Mr. Reid to be able to move to another location. The Board intended for Mr. Reid to find another location and that is why we are here today. All of this occurred before the regulations. Now that there are regulations many of the problems, if not all that occurred in the prior neighborhood, can be avoided here today. This process, through the Commission, allows a venue for working with the neighbors so neighbors can vet their concerns and the Green Cross can respond and figure out a way to make this work as the Board intended when they created the regulations. The major issue in the prior case dealt with traffic. The Green Cross had outgrown that district. That will not occur this time around. This is not an NC-1 district. It is a mixed business district. It has a higher turn over in terms of traffic with greater availability to parking. Since the regulations have passed, one of the requirements to enter a medical cannabis property is you have to have a State identification card. I am not a patient. I could not enter the Green Cross. Even most medical marijuana patients who could have entered can't [now]. You have to be a resident of San Francisco or Oakland or the few counties that give out identification cards. The volume of traffic will be lower in this neighborhood than in the past neighborhood. Captain Goldberg of the Mission District Police Force did a study and said crime decreased. There may be misperception surrounding that. I notice there are a lot of people here from the neighborhood wearing stickers that say character counts. I urge you to look very closely at Mr. Reid's character. He has done everything he can to follow the rules. He demonstrated himself to be a responsible member of the community and neighborhoods where he is involved. The Mayor has commented to that effect. The Board of Supervisors regulated dispensaries. So did the State. They elected to regulate not pass a moratorium. Liz Moore I live on North Point half a block from the proposed site. I am one of a number of neighbors that would have filed a discretionary review that would postpone the proceedings. We want to make it clear there are exceptional circumstances specifically to this site that would satisfy discretionary review. We want to make it clear that the project is in conflict with all the applicable planning code priority policies. We want to state for the project sponsor and the record that we are not opposed to medical marijuana and have compassion for the people it helps. We feel it is an inappropriate location. I want to give you an example of the exceptional circumstances. It's in violation of the Planning Code. We identified seven property sites we feel qualify as recreational buildings. Second, with regard to traffic impacts, this is a short block that fronts on a narrow street. Any effects resulting from double parking are extreme - far more than in any other location. Third, the fact it's located in Fisherman's Wharf, which is the face we show to the world. The adjacent park creates a temptation for customers to smoke marijuana there and reduce the ability of the neighborhood to enjoy that park. Trish Heims I'm a resident that lives on North Point. I think this is an issue that affects all of us. I would like to specifically discuss the Planning Code priority that concerns protecting the character of this particular neighborhood. Green Cross had a negative impact on the former neighborhood. That's why they had to leave. Security and safety represent major concerns. The San Francisco Police reported to the Board of Appeals that the volume of police calls had increased 280 percent around the Green Cross's former location. I would like to underscore there are no substantive differences between the equipment and policies they had in place in the other location than they propose to put in place in our neighborhood. A former neighbor stated that as the Green Cross instituted their program the problems migrated around the corner. We understand Green Cross will manage the conditions. They will migrate around the corner. There is noise pollution, loud music, smoking marijuana in public, reselling marijuana, loitering and littering. The Green Cross had a negative impact on the former neighborhood and I think it will have the same impact on our neighborhood. Robert Hellwick My wife and I live in the neighborhood. One of the pleasures of living in this neighborhood involves the contact we have with the multitude of families and children that visit this area form all over the country and the world. Being the gateway to the wharf, this is a Mecca to San Francisco. Thousands of children pass by this location we are talking about today. This single factor constitutes an exceptional circumstance that warrants denying the permit. The Board of Appeals concluded that the Green Cross adversely affected the area. In this was a finding made last December and it applies more to the present location given the unique circumstances of the neighborhood. The wharf is not the appropriate location to put a cannabis operation, which is in the heart of the City's center for family activity. I would urge you to consider when you hear the comments of the local merchants, residents and concerned citizen, consider this is not compatible with the unique environment that constitutes the wharf and the residents around it. Bill Raven I'm a neighbor on North Point Street. I would like to discuss the Planning Code policy on not over burdening our streets and parking. We were told we could expect a maximum of 60 to 80 customers an hour buying marijuana. In the former neighborhood that caused massive traffic. It was so bad, the resulting quantity of the vehicles and pedestrian traffic created conditions that are potentially hazardous to pedestrians. The traffic congestion will be worse in our neighborhood and I want to show you why. It's at the intersection of three streets: Columbus, North Point and Leavenworth. They come together at the gateway to the wharf. It's a complicated intersection and it has been said that there are no public parking facilities around there. It's on a small street. Any double parking will cause traffic congestion without a question. Sally Moral I want to continue to comment about the traffic congestion problems. I walk my dog in the area daily. I can tell you how dangerous that intersection is. In addition to normal traffic, we have Muni buses, Golden Gate Transit buses, large trucks that are not allowed on Bay Street and tourists that are not sure where they are going or how to get there. That's a dangerous mix. If there is double-parking the Muni will be slowed if not stopped. There is a proposal being evaluated to remove a westbound lane on North Point. The one that goes by the proposed location, and turning it into a bicycle lane as part of the over all plan on North Point. If that is approved the congestion will get worse. Karen Raven I'm a North Point neighbor. I want to discuss the planning policy concerning protecting parks and open spaces - the park across the street from the proposed dispensary. I am concerned that people will be drawn to the park to smoke. Local children and families use the park and a great many children and families pass the park visiting attractions at the wharf and the pier. This is a special park. It marks the end of Columbus Avenue passing the Transamerica Pyramid going through Chinatown and North Beach. It marks the step to the aquatic parks and ship. A marijuana dispensary in this area does not seem compatible. Bill Gannon I'm a North Point resident and have lived here for six and a half years. I oppose this. What you are seeing are the FAQ's from your website that defines what you said recreation facilities were. A recreation building is an institution assembly of social service use. Used for public use and recreational social purposes, community club houses, neighborhood and cultural centers and meeting halls. We have found eight of them. We visited each and confirmed they were open to the public and recreation going on in their buildings. Susan McDonald I am speaking in opposition. I am a member of the Dolphin Club, which stands within the thousand-foot radius of the location. I am speaking as an individual member of the club. The Dolphin Club has been at the same location since it was founded in 1877. It is a historical institution. It is a non-profit, public access athletic organization with a diverse membership and open to the public. There are dozens of family recreation activities throughout the year from learning about our historic boats and participating in boat building. People swim in the park and build sand castles on the beach. I believe the neighborhood and the community would be negatively affected with the MCD operations at the proposed location. I am opposed to the MCD location. It does not meet the requirements. Matt Harris I live one block away from the proposed site. The association hall is a recreational cultural institution established a hundreds years ago to promote the commercial fishing fleet. This is not a proper site for this location. Paul Einstein I am concerned about the MCD application. I am the youth coordinator at North Beach Place at 567 Bay Street. We provide summer and after school programs. I consider it a safe and positive environment for kids to interact. It's 500 feet from the proposed cannabis dispensary. I am concerned with how it will affect the teens at North Beach Place. There are thousands of people that live there. 394 children that are all low income. They face many challenges and most are at risk. One of my biggest questions is will youth be approached to buy or smoke marijuana? Debbie Gannon I'm a North Point resident I oppose the MCD application. The San Francisco Maritime Historical Park defined by the federal government is a recreation institution. Set at Hyde and Jefferson Streets, the San Francisco Maritime Parks Center stands 732 feet from the proposed location and is open to the public. School groups tour the center year round. The pier offers education, music and crafts for all ages. I hope you will consider that. Gibb Ford I'm a neighbor and I oppose the MCD. The South End Rowing Club is a recreational social institution within a thousand feet. Membership is open to anybody. The club is open on Wednesday and Fridays. The club offers to the general public swimming in the bay and rowing. We have 30 watercrafts. We have handball. There are three dirt courts and five tournaments a year. There is a range of social and recreational activities, dinners, boat restoration, athletic training, saunas and events. Saul I live on Mason Street. I would like to say I oppose the application. The Seaman's Church, a cultural and religious center is located at 2454 Hyde Street. The church is located less than 860 feet from the proposed location. The church is on the first level. A recreational center is on the second level with a Hyde Street entrance. The church is open to the public 11 to 7, Monday through Saturday. There are a variety of recreational and cultural activities in the church. There is a playgroup for children. There are card games; Norwegian lesions and dinners held for the students. There are two ladies groups. They have a Christmas bizarre. There is a library with newspapers. There is Lutheran service on Sundays at 11. Allowing this club here in North Beach, in my opinion, is as inappropriate as putting it in the middle of the Galileo Football field. Trent Moore I live on the block of the proposed site. It is close to recreational and cultural buildings – to the San Francisco Art Institute. The Institute is open daily to the public from 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. There is direct and free public access to artwork. There are exhibits and films and other events that are free and open to the public. There are a couple of classes on going. One that is open to 13 to 15 year olds – that's the Young Artist program. That is in session now through August 11. Another program called the pre-college program is open to 16 to 18 year olds. The Art Institute is 800 feet away from the proposed site. There is no way you can resolve that problem. I oppose the MCD application. [No name] Read a letter written by the residents of the Telegraph Hill Neighborhood Association, in which they expressed their opposition of the MCD at the proposed location. Orlando Antonini I'm adjacent to the proposed site. I believe that at certain times of the week and summertime traffic is atrocious. People park in my driveway. You call the police and they can't respond for an hour. I don't see how you are going to respond. The cops can't remove the homeless from the park. They have to leave them alone. I'm afraid I will lose business when people can't park. Please deny this request. Michael I belong to the Senior Center and depend on it because I'm disabled. I have a lot of friends at the Senior Center. The proposed site is three blocks away from the Center. The seniors participate in daily activities seven days a week. The majority of the seniors use public transportation. The buses cannot hold any more people. They are over crowded with Galileo High School students and seniors. I think this is asking too much. I oppose the MCD application. Betty Foote I am a neighbor. I want to express the freedom to protest and to be heard. I bring to your attention the three story and what I consider an anchor building. The location is highly visible like an anchor building on two business corners. The high demand for the usage of marijuana will ensure the probability of expansion. Their records are filled with several alias, shoplifting, felony convictions and so forth. We have scratched the surface and know the Planning staff and law enforcement officers are better equipped to go to the history with the people involved. This is not a little storefront. It's first a club, a building, a corner, a neighborhood, and a city. This is important. It is precedent setting. The location, the usage, and the people involved are special circumstances. Michael In addition to the eight recreational sites we have uncovered, we have uncovered findings that we can't get our arms around. We will leave that to the Commission for further investigation. There is a lack of transparency to the ownership structure of the building. We don't know who owns what. The notion that the community is supportive of this is a lie. The café is under the same ownership of the building that is proposing to rent the MCD. I am opposed to the MCD application. Jan Mish I am the manager of the Tuscan Inn A representative of Mr. Reid told us that he really didn't want to be in that neighborhood, that it was not his first choice. It's not ours either. There will be traffic issues. School buses come to our area all the time to bring children from all over the Bay Area to visit the wharf, the number one choice to visit in our area. I am here to oppose. They need to be somewhere else, but this is not the appropriate location. Patricia, The Hotel Council of San Francisco I am here to oppose the MCD application on behalf of the members of the Hotel Council of San Francisco. We are concerned about the effect a pot club will have on the Wharf. Rodney Fong, President, Fisherman's Wharf Association We are all opposed to this happening at Fisherman's Wharf. San Francisco is voted the number one City. The Wharf is the number one destination. Linda Lau I am here on behalf of Galileo parents, teacher/student association. I am the current president of the PTSA. We have great concerns on the location of this cannabis dispensary. Earlier in the meeting I was glad to hear one of the goals of setting the new policy for MCD's is to keep youth away. I think it will be a problem for our students. Youth are impressionable. They have peer pressure and may not know how to avoid an inappropriate drug use. Urged the Commission to not approve this application at this location, in order to keep our youth safe. Denise Lima I am for the proposed opening in Fisherman's Wharf. I carry my speech in my heart. I am opposed to alcohol use because I lost four members of my family because of alcohol usage. I wish they had smoked pot. Kate Richardson I urge you to consider the location of this medical establishment in regards to millions of Americans and thousand of school children who visit the area each year. Penelope Clark, Co-Chair of Russian Hill Neighbors We voted to oppose granting a permit to Green Cross. It's an inappropriate location that could compromise the neighborhood's security and lower the quality of life. Consider the consequences of this high profile location. The wharf is a tourist attraction. The Holiday Inn is across the street from the park. Certainly, there is a possibility that those who attempt to prey on customers of this all cash business might turn their attention to the tourists and consider them easy marks. There is now national publicity about the location of this dispensary. Dispensaries should be discrete and out of the public eye. The wharf is not a discrete location. Please, do not approve this project. Robert I'm a graduate of the University of Berkeley. The Holiday Inn has criteria related to the ordinance that can guard and protect the wharf. They have meetings and seminars and 4,000 Girl Scouts of America marching through the wharf. I will follow up with a Grand Jury Investigation if this goes through. I oppose the MCD application. [Name was not clear] I am 16 years old and have lived two blocks away from the site my entire life. I am here to speak against the idea. Unlike many of the speakers my focus is not just the club's location. I will focus on something I have more qualifications for - the presence of youth and teenagers in the area. This area is full of unsupervised teenagers. Should the Planning Commission approve this, it will constitute the approval for marijuana in the middle of San Francisco's Disneyland. Tom Rubins, Merchant in the Wharf Area Our family has owned and operated a restaurant in the wharf for the past 80 years. Along with our 150 employees, we are opposed. It's insulting to read over this item number 19, which says [staff] recommends that you approve the project without discretionary review. We are opposed to this project. We feel it's inappropriate location for this site to be a cannabis house. Bill Clarkson I'm proud to be a merchant at the Cannery in San Francisco. We started out to be a restaurant for older people, but it turned into a family tourist restaurant. I didn't plane it that way. There are more and more children coming to this destination every year. I just can't see any reason that a cannabis club should be there. I definitely oppose this. Chris Martin, Chair, Benefit Planning Committee and President of the Cannery Properties, Inc. We are currently interviewing Urban Planners that will lead the effort to preserve and enhance the cultural heritage of the wharf by establishing a plan which sets forth standards and policy for land use, urban design, transportation and parking. Why does  San Francisco's number one visitor attractions have the weakest zoning in the city? Without [positive] action the wharf will lose it's character and uniqueness appeal and its cultural contribution to the city. Why do other cities do a better job preserving their historical centerpiece? We need this commission's firm and unwavering support to properly plan this community. It is time for your staff to become engaged in the planning and development of the wharf and surrounding community. I'm opposed to this MCD application. John Rubins I'm opposed to the business in question. I am concerned about the crime. We are a vulnerable community. Tom Brown I'm a property owner in the neighborhood a hundred yards away. I'm opposed. Jessica Hopkins I'm asking you to oppose this. Brian I've been a patient of the Green Cross. I have felt safe. I'm for the project. Kathy Paver I'm in charge of the Marketing Department for Pier 39 I sit on the Board of Governors for the Wharf and Community Benefit District. I will speak on behalf of all the organizations. I have the same concerns that a medical cannabis dispensary in the heart of San Francisco's number one tourist destination is a grave mistake. The wharf is a family destination and a cannabis dispensary is counter to everything we stand for. I urge you to vote against this dispensary and invite you in the future to work with us to find appropriate things for the Wharf and preserve the neighborhood for generations to come. Thomas Fell, Principal, Galileo High School We have 2,400 students. We are not a neighborhood school. Our students come from all the sectors of the city. A large amount of students travel along North Point passing near the proposed program. Four years ago Galileo was about to lose its accreditation. It has made improvements. We are a California Distinguished school. Our test scores are meeting the 800 mark. We are selected to be one of 10 schools in the state. For this to continue we need the support of the city and community to continue providing safety to our students. Many of our students have marginal backgrounds. The use of marijuana among our youth is on the rise and our students don't know how to separate the appropriate use of drugs from the inappropriate use of drugs. If you allow Green Cross to be so close to our schools it will be a problem. It is a health impact on your students in our schools. Don't let this program be so close to San Francisco's youth. Anthony, former Galileo student Fisherman's Wharf is a nice place for everyday. This is a bad influence for the teens. The teens can get access to marijuana. Anyway, I oppose it. Mrs. Chang I'm speaking on behalf of Renewed San Francisco - Revitalizing and Energizing the Waterfront of San Francisco We are concerned about the proposal. Again, it's location, location and location. I do not want to repeat all of the compelling reasons that have been expressed by the residents and merchants of the Wharf's area. Even if the proposal has met all criteria of the Planning Code, I think your job is to balance it with the interest of the residents and merchants of the area. Fred Cruise, Police Officer at Central Station The Captain is opposed to this. He's mirroring the sentiment of the community. I don't have anything to add that was not said already. Brian Denny I am a patient of the Green Cross. I have had a positive experience. They provide a safe environment. There is no smoking in the premise. I am a family man and have three children. You keep your medication away from your children. I did not have a problem finding parking. They have done everything to meet the opposition. I understand they have addressed all their issues. I think they can work well with the community. Maria Malloy I am a chemist that researched the effects of marijuana on the brain. I am here as a resident and voter of the City of San Francisco. I thought we already voted on this. I am not sure how the conservative neighbors could over ride the City's vote. Mike Aldrich I was a patient before they were forced to close. I will support this location because it's near my house. There are no MCD's in my district. I believe there should MCD's in every neighborhood. The restrictions give you a box you have to work with. It makes it impossible for an MCD to locate in any neighborhood. According to the regulations it is hard to find a landlord to rent to an MCD in the zoning and proximity requirements. This will happen with every marijuana dispensary that will come before you where the neighborhoods oppose it. Remember, that in every one of the neighborhoods there are patients like myself who needs a dispensary near by because of mobility problems. This is just a test case. If you do not allow Green Cross, which has followed all the rules to go to this location, the new regulations are a sham. Michelle Aldrich Dispensaries are not open to the public. There has been parking problems on the wharf since I've lived here. I am really insulted by my neighbors questioning my character after living in San Francisco for thirty-four years because I am a patient. Distribution was not included. Patients have to go to the streets to get their medicine. Dispensaries were set up as an attempt to deal with a grossly unjust situation. Until the federal laws are changed, the acceptance of dispensaries should be the moral way. Green Cross will be closer to my home than any other in the city. Please let them open. Richard Mullen There are a couple of misconceptions about medical marijuana and clubs. One is that somehow we will influence kids to smoke marijuana. That is not the case. That has been hoisted on us from people who've been against marijuana from the beginning. The reason to outlaw marijuana is the effect on the degenerate races. Bob Lane I'm a local cannabis patient. I want to address the concept that the Wharf is an inappropriate place. Those that are against this probably have no problem with a pharmacy. When the Board of Supervisors decided where to allow dispensaries they instituted a rule not within a thousand feet of schools. Consider the effect of this poorly thought out policy. Only a few possible locations remain. Event though the city excludes most spaces they expand the definition knowing this would be a ban on dispensaries. The Wharf is not a bad location. It's the only place that they haven't excluded. Consider the needs of the medical needy, which are the white affluent people of North Beach. Michelle Hersch I am a San Francisco resident and a caregiver. I have a card to go and buy marijuana for a friend who is very ill. I chose the Green Cross, after seeing [other] dispensaries and feel that working with them [Green Cross] is the safest. I feel I will continue to go to the Green Cross even though it's not close to my home. I travel by bike and will not take up a parking spot. Rachel I have been a patient for a year. I started going to the Green Cross in its old location. After doing the research, it was the most professionally run operation I could locate I am here because I am worried not just about the Green Cross but the future for medical marijuana places. After meeting every rule and dotting every  i' and crossing every  t' you are being asked to deny us a permit. I worry what will happen to medical cannabis patients after June of 2007. Jonathan Beaver I am a medical marijuana patient. That marijuana is highly addictive is a lie projected by policy. Prohibitionists are saying that there is a rise in cannabis users seeking help. How could it be otherwise when there has been a dramatic increase and risk for simple possession? Less than 5% of persons entering drug treatment programs for cannabis use do so voluntarily. Most first time offenders are forced to treatment. No other interest group lobbies harder to deter cannabis reform. Shona I am here to represent the cannabis dispensary in the Tenderloin. They have the most complete plans for veterans in need in the City of San Francisco. I highly recommend the permitting of this club. I have a letter from Assemblyman Mark Leno, defining the award we received. And it's my hope that the 20 to 25 permitting hearings will hopefully [provide] better education and not have so many misnomers about our community. Karen I am the Director of Government Relations for Americans for Access. Dispensaries are a compassionate response to suffering Californians; to people who need medical cannabis and cannabis based products in a secure environment. They provide the education of the safe and effective use of the products. The right to have them in San Francisco is law. Fair and equal access to all medical cannabis patients across the City is what they provide. The fact is, many critically ill medical cannabis patients call Fisherman's Wharf and North Beach their home and they need access to medicine. David Mays I am a resident of the City and a medical marijuana patient. I'm in support of the Green Cross. The Green Cross has the greatest range of strains and an educated staff to direct the patients to the strain they need. It's exceptional in comparison to the others in the City. Robert Carlton It seems to me that all the neighborhood support would make it less likely that anything falls under diversionary practices because there is so much support in their neighborhood. Again, all neighborhoods need to have a dispensary. If you put them in a couple of neighborhoods, issues like parking will be magnified. Surveillance is a good thing. Margaret I'm a resident and homeowner in the city of San Francisco in District 7. Decisions of this importance should be based on fact and not potential dangers. Merchants like and appreciated the business the patients brought. The drive to keep children away from the facilities is based on emotion, not fact. It is despicable and I wish they were closed down. Emily Souffer I've been a Green Cross patient since it's inception. I support them opening in their new location. I was at work watching this hearing and felt compelled to explain to my boss the things people are saying about Kevin are not fair. He is the nicest person I have ever met. What I was hearing was reactionary based on fear. You can't expect to have a tourist area and not have traffic. Eliminating local business will do nothing to help the community grow and thrive. During my time as a Green Cross patient I saw PG&E trucks double and triple parked. UPS and Comcast trucks double-parked. Never once did I see a Green Cross patient double-parked. The patients at the Green Cross are not looking to make life difficult; they are looking to make their own lives easier. I highly support Kevin and I hope you will as well. Miles Davis I own the T-shirt shop next to there. There is a lot of talk about tourism. What tourism? Why is Ghirardelli Square turning to condos? The Cannery is even being considered for sale. Tourism is way down. People are not spending. My business is down. Way, way down. There are a lot of empty storefronts. We've had people living in the park for years. They do everything there. It's their toilet and bed. It smells like an outhouse there. The block has been filthy and neglected for two years. The Green Cross is cleaning it up. All I know is what I've seen. [No name given] That was my father before me. I'm 23 and I grew up next door. Our shop is there and our apartment is next door. I went to high school in Pacific Heights. I've been around marijuana and never partaken in it. People say that walking by a store that doesn't have signage will make them want to smoke more. I don't think that happens. Our business pays for my education and our life. It [our business] is down. Kevin's shop would bring more business. Any traffic to my neighborhood would be great. There are cafes and restaurants. It would help all that. We are worried about the effects of marijuana. There is a bar on every corner on the wharf. There are three bars on our corner. I'm the one who is right next door to it. If there is a problem, you will be the first to hear from our family. Juan I've lived in San Francisco for 24 years. Council Representative of the Project Sponsor

We work on a lot of historic buildings and this is one of the most interesting historic structures I have dealt with.

When we entered into this with this building it was obvious that 1 Kearny was the historic building and the annex has less historic merit.

When we discovered there was a debate on whether or not it was historic, the owners of the building decide to preserve the building.

The design went through two extensive hearings at the Landmark's Board where there was a divergence of opinion.

Some say the annex should be torn down.

We changed the design in response to the comments made by the Landmark's Board.

You see a design that received unanimous support by the board.

It's an improved design based on a long dialogue with the Planning staff and the Landmark's Board on how to treat a building that is the average landmark restoration project.

Charles, Architect for the project

This is a very important building at an important location in San Francisco.

It is in the Kearney/Market Conservation District, at a very important corner in the city.

 Where one of San Francisco's grids intersects on Market Street.

It's a dramatic building especially seen from Third Street as you approach the city.

There are three parts:

 The original 1902 Savings Bank in the building, which is an early quake survivor, and the annex added in '64.

We planned to tear down the three-story build seen on left in the picture and replace it with a 10-story building.

Our design is an attempt to fill in the missing tooth to Market Street.

We are sensitive to the urban design and context as well as to the specific design itself.

One Kearny and bank annex function as one building.

There are a number of functional problems.

The annex has elevators, stairs and bathrooms.

It is difficult to divide the building into floors.

There is no air conditioning or heat in the annex.

One of our objectives is to correct the functional problems.

The building has a seismic prospect.

 Even though it was an earthquake survivor, it has a stiff element that makes it twist during an earthquake.

Our project will correct all of the functional problems by creating a new core in the new building.

 We'll take the elevators out of the annex.

 We'll make their front door their back door.

We want to put the building in architectural balance.

We are changing brick to glass.

We are using traditional materials like terra cotta in contemporary ways.

We don't have open space on the ground floor; we are proposing to put it on the roof at the top.

Commissioner Antonini There was an article in the Chronicle on Monday in the Forum Section I thought encapsulated a lot of what some of us have been saying in regards to the fact that if we don't build enough housing for the middle class it adds to urban sprawl and an environmental issue. I thought it was well presented. The conclusion was, what is the solution? For the people who can stay in San Francisco and are able to buy or rent here and feel of a like mind, they should and do show they are active politically. This is a message we here often, that people basically are not active, they don't vote and don't register. The totals from the last primary were disturbing. The key is if you feel this way or whatever your position is, it is important that you make your voice heard and be active. Commissioner Lee A couple of requests for staff A couple of years ago I asked for the numbers of registered cars and trucks in San Francisco. I would like to see if we could get the DMV number of registered cars and trucks in the city. We are not building more parking lots as a City policy. [We need to see] if there is a way we can figure out how many parking spaces we have in the city. This is an issue on Geary and Downtown. I think it would be good to have an update. The Arts Task Force report. I want to know if that was scheduled. Regarding administration: Last year we went through this hiring and I want to find out the number of people we hired, the ethnic breakdown and the number of men and women we hired. Also, on the State ballot in the fall there is a bond measure for affordable housing. I want staff to look at that and see how much money is available if it passes and how much can San Francisco get? Commissioner Olague I want to know what the status of the 199 Leland housing project is? Are we going to have a hearing? Is that something we can request? Zoning Administrator Badiner responded Commissioners, those of you who were here recall we had a hearing on senior housing and the requirements. There were three projects in this area. One of them was 199 Leland. The other two projects are in permit stages, but have not received them. This project is constructed and what was before us was pending a General Plan review of the condominium subdivision. At the conclusion of the hearing, I asked the commissioners if you wanted to see the projects and I did not focus on 199 Leland. I did not understand that the Commission had a vote or consensus that they wanted to see these. This would not normally come before you, as it is a condominium subdivision. If the Commission wants to see it you can request it. It's a recommendation we make to DPW for their ultimate approval or disapproval. It is appealable to the Board of Supervisors, as I understand it. This would not normally come before you. There is controversy. The building is built and approved and doesn't normally come before the Commission. If you request it to come before you, we can do that. Commissioner Olague There is interest on behalf of the neighbors, and Senior Action Network, and other organizations in town. It seems there is interest in having it heard here. Zoning Administrator Badiner I think the appropriate process is whether there is a consensus [on the Commission]. Commissioner Olague I'd like to request a vote. If there is a consensus we will hear it. If not, fine. I move we hear 199 Leland. [Note from Commission Secretary: The motion did not receive a second. The motion dies.] Commissioner Antonini Can I ask a question? What is the issue? Commissioner Olague There was a discussion on Senior Housing. There were issues that were raised around that particular project by Senior Action Network. Neighbors also had concerns. Because they don't have the right to request discretionary review, it would be up to us to request that we have a hearing here. It seemed there was community desire to see that that issue be brought before us. Commissioner Antonini What I'm hearing is this is appealable to the Board of Supervisors anyway. If a decision is granted in favor of this project and then there is some feeling that they want to appeal they appeal to the Board of Supervisors? Zoning Administrator Badiner That is my understanding. Commissioner Antonini We would be another step. If we heard it then the Supervisors would not? Zoning Administrator Badiner They could also hear it too if it was appealed. Your hearing it does not preclude the Supervisors hearing it. Commissioner Antonini I'm trying to figure out what we would gain other than taking longer time. If they feel strongly they will find a way to appeal to the Board of Supervisors, I guess. Commissioner Olague I guess what I will do is have conversations with people. Zoning Administrator Badiner We will take that into account. There is a serious question raised about whether it meets the laws for senior housing. That question has been raised to us and we will take that into account. I throw out another point: It may require physical modification to the building. It will require a building permit. That building permit is subject to discretionary review. Commissioner Lee One Rincon revised their plans because of seismic issues. Putting water towers on top of One Rincon, will that affect the height? Zoning Administrator Badiner In our technical terms, it is not a revision. In this case the Department approved a project, it goes to the site permit and the Building Department who reviews for safety and structure. There is always a lot of back and forth after it goes to the Planning Department. The new water towers for the building will not shake as much. Commissioner Lee The height with the three water towers will not exceed what we approved on One Rincon? Zoning Administrator Badiner That is correct. Commissioner Lee My second question: There is a proposal to do gay/lesbian senior housing on Laguna. Legally do we have a right to earmark housing strictly for sexual preferences or not? I'm trying to figure out if Mark Leno is going to sponsor something for gays and lesbians. Two years ago they wanted it strictly for gays and lesbians. Can we require this has to be senior? Can we earmark a project for senior housing for gays and lesbians? Deputy City Attorney Zoning Administrator Badiner I don't have an answer today. I think we would have to look into this further and get back to you. Director Macris Dan Sider of Department staff I have been working closely with Supervisor Dufty and Mirkarimi on this issue. We are trying to work out an arrangement so the project can proceed. We will keep the Commission informed on this circumstance. We are very intensely involved in trying to work out something that would allow this project to go forward. President Alexander I want to formally welcome our two new commissioners – Kathrin Moore and Hisashi Sugaya. They will be a great addition. They bring a wealth of knowledge and experience. I'm pleased to have them here. Commissioner Sugaya I bring greetings from the Board of Appeals. They promised me that whatever I vote for they will oppose. Representing the people next to the property It is extraordinary when a building is over a foot over the property line It's extraordinary when the city needs a variance and as a condition requires an easement.  That's extraordinary when by oversight there exists an illegal condition at the site - the stairs. This is not about views.  The views are in the front of the buildings.  You see the entire city. Why is this important to my clients? It clouds their title. If there is a question about the variance or integrity or what it means, future development or sale of the site is going to be difficult. Number one Belgrave was constructed illegally. It was built over a foot over the property line. There was a survey that found it was over the property line. The city required 1 Belgrave to obtain a variance. This is not your normal type of easement. It's an easement of convenience. It is not an easement of necessity. If you look at the drawing used by the planner, they could easily move to the other side and enter from there. This was merely for convenience sake so they didn't have to have the expense of moving the entrance, which would be easy to do. I urge you to read the conditions placed in the easement carefully. They say if you ever change the stairs or building or deck in the back you loose this convenience. We have a letter from one of the original makers of the easement.  They are not all dead.

The other issue is we found out yesterday what happened in 2001 after the first permit was rejected at the Board of Appeals because of the easement. The city says they don't interpret easements but they did then and we are talking about it now. We got a copy of the permit in 2001. The stairs were reconstructed back in 2001.  And changed and altered. A new footing was created. A new firewall without a variance. This is a non-conforming use.  It doesn't have the benefit or variance or permit that would legalize it. You shouldn't be issuing a permit for the site as long as they have the illegal situation. The stairs go along a third of the lot line. They are in violation of the Building Code. They were never legalized by the variance. They are more than two feet too narrow under the Building Code. We would like clarification on this issue because once this permit was issued and the stairs were rebuilt in 2001, it was required they become code compliant or receive outside approval, which they have not. Denise Gillman Some of the applicant's statements on the DR form are somewhat disingenuous.  The form indicates that the number of bedrooms will go from three to two.  But it appears there will be 4 bedrooms and that two of the rooms don't have code required egress and that would make them unusable as bedrooms. The existing house is at its legal maximum height. The proposed project has 6 feet 4 inches between the subject houses.  Actually, the distance between the houses will remain a plus or minus 5 feet 2 inches with the encroaching stair and landing which produces the actual separation. The applicant indicates the changes were made to satisfy the owners of 15 Belgrave.  When in fact they were made to satisfy the planning code. The applicant concludes in section B, item 2, saying the proposed addition leaves 6 feet 4 inches between the project house and its neighbor at its closest point, and 10 feet 9 inches between the houses where the neighboring house angles back. The first dimension is incorrect. Plus or minus 5 feet 2 inches will remain between dwellings and the second dimension is meaningless. The applicant discussed the easement. In a phone conversation with Elaine Tope of the Planning Department, I described there was an easement. She indicated the application included vertical addition and if they were aware of the easement it would be part of the application. She added that the department tells the parties to sue each other. It doesn't seem good planning policy to put people in that position. The same situation exists at the side yard encroachment easement. The Commission should deny or suspend the application pending the resolution of the easement issue. Nicole Gerotski Read a letter from one of the original owners of 15 Belgrave who lives in Washington now and couldn't be here today.  They believe the easement was one of convenience, not necessity and that the entry for 1 Belgrave can be relocated.  They further stated that the project should be denied.

Project Architect I'm not proposing anything within these stairs and platforms. The platforms that are in discussion are a series of landings within the stairs. It's a long uphill climb to the house.

Attorney for the Applicant So many of the issues raised are not about an easement, but manipulation. Just as there is no environmental issue, there is no issue with this easement. The easement is clear in its language and says nothing about granting rights over on the rest of the property. California law is clear that to have a restrictive easement it has to be stated expressly and it has to be in the document. Saying somebody wrote a letter about something that happened 30 years ago under apparently bitter circumstances is not legal evidence. It's a good reason for why we require things to be recorded. There is no way to know what someone will come along and say later when they say it's sour grapes, this is not what they want. Raising the issue that the staircase could be moved to the other side:  That is not a realistic proposal. The building that is found so significant, would be torn apart to do that. The 2001 issue has nothing to do with this. In that case it is indicated the city told the owner they wanted a wider staircase. The owner didn't just build on the easement, but encroached onto the Lapin's property, which is a violation of the Lapin's property rights and required to take that back. The stairs are back to where they are originally. There is no suggestion there is change to that. Nor should my clients be vilified for the actions of a previous owner who over stepped the bounds of his property.

One of the owners of 1 Belgrave Avenue I love my neighbor. I love Denise and she knows it. When we entered this building this afternoon at the same time, she gave me a hug. My father passed away last week.  She knows this.  My mother has breast cancer.  She knows this.  I had reconstructive surgery.  She knows this. I keep no secrets from Denise. I trust her with the things that are most precious to me. This project is making our home a loving environment space for all the people on Belgrave Avenue. We have never set out to do anything but make that space more approachable so we can have our family come stay with us and enjoy it; so Denise's daughter can come play with us in a playroom, which we simply don't have. It saddens me that a mere disagreement can strain a relationship. There have been significant attempts on both our parts to find a middle ground.  To find a way where everyone can be happy. We are unable to come to this and we have come to an agreement just what does the easement mean so we can settle this. If it means what the Lapins believe it means, we will honor that and not build. Our interpretation is not such. We offered to settle this legally.  They declined to go the most direct, the most efficient, the most economical route so we can all move on with our lives. So we are simply at an impasse in that regard. We love our home.  We love where we live and the city.  And we adore our neighbors and we want nothing to come between us. We ask that somebody above find a way to make peace. However it turns out, we will honor it.  We will not fight it and we will respect your decision.

Representing the Project Sponsor We are only here at the request of the Commission from several years back. To our knowledge there is no opposition to the project. The only opposition there had been was Mr. Williams who is here today on another project. I think he can confirm if requested that his concerns were addressed. We ask that you move this project on. Steve Williams I filed a discretionary review four years ago. It was a demolition that evolved to a remodel and I continued negotiating with the builder. It is in a built up area. It is a beautiful house but it is on a block of Sutter Street in an area where six-story buildings are going in and a large parking garage. Chair of the Western SOMA Citizens Planning Task Force Three pieces of legislation have passed at the Board of Supervisors last week related to Western SOMA:  A Western SOMA Special Use District was created; Neighborhood notification and Conditional Use for formula retail were approved; and a 45 day moratorium was approved. We need this time to see that special circumstances will be considered by you for a CU application.  \We ask that the Southeast Section plan with us. Last night the full Task Force unanimously asked the Board of Supervisors to introduce interim controls on market rate SRO units in South of Market and CU in all of SOMA zoning districts with the exception of the service light zoning. John Pollard I'm here on behalf of the San Francisco Garage Company. What we found in the last eight years with the Planning Department is it has been hit and miss. We had a great seven years, but the last year it has come to a halt in getting permits over the counter for wood windows or improving the façade on a stucco building, which the primary of our business is new garages. I heard there was a code amendment three years ago that says any building over 50 years old has to be approved by a historical planner.  There are only a few to approve such projects.  Those planners are at the counter a couple times a week for an hour or two. In the last two months we have not received a permit for a new garage.  We pull 50 to 60 permits a year. There is another garage company in the city that pulls 10 to 20 permits.  They are older than us and they are having problems as well with the permits. They will build three garages on the same street and the fourth doesn't get approved.  Same building.  Built in 1908 and the planner says, I don't approve it. I don't know what to do. I apologize to Mr. Macris for not going to him.  I personally don't know anyone at the Planning Department.  I have not dealt with managers at the Planning Department.  I know the clerks at the counter and a little bit about Mr. Badiner. We ask for your help.  Our clients are driving us bonkers, especially clients on multiple projects.  For years we got their plans approved in a week and now we don't have a simple permit. We ask for your help. Bradley Weedimyer 2870 Washington Street and 2304 Divisadero Across the city there are a number of buildings, important low-rise buildings that are without parking.  They are a type of residence that is different from contemporary residential buildings that have parking. I want to know the policy in place to address conversions of this type of building, which rates today as moderate-income housing.  When garages are inserted in them, they go to a luxury status.  It's a transformation. This particular building perhaps has been based on fraudulent or elderly people who lived there for decades. It's going forward apparently. What kind of differentiation within housing is there so this zoning variance can be waived because it is residential? Is there a city plan that addresses the number of conversions to vehicular residential use citywide? If we put parking in every unit in the city there will be gridlock.  Is there an annual tally or allotment included? Zoning Administrator Badiner Advised Mr. Pollard to contact Mr. Neil Hart of Department Staff Commissioner Antonini I think we should calendar some sort of a discussion in regards to this issue because it would seem to me if there has been a policy change that the Commission should be able to weigh in on the change if it is occurring because it is an important issue. Many people want to put garages in pre-existing homes. We should hear about this and find out what the things are as far as preservation. What is SLI zone?  Are there zones where you can't have market-rate housing?  I didn't know such a thing existed.  We should know about that. Zoning Administrator Badiner SLI is Service Light Industrial.  It is in south of Market.  It is one of the few districts that makes a difference where you can't have market-rate, but you can have affordable housing.  It is a unique district in that way. The matter of garages has not been brought to my attention.  We will look into this and comment more on it. I imagine at some point we will get follow up regarding the legislation and SLI's.  It will come back to us.

comment: The previous use was a bathhouse. This building has been vacant for 15 years. It's a 3-story building, 11,000 sq. ft. with a 3,500 sq. ft. basement. The height of the building is 46 feet. The taller building to the east of our project is about 69 feet and the smaller building is about 35 feet. For our project, we are proposing that we do a full restoration of the existing historical façade with the new residential and commercial entries at the street level. We are doing a full seismic retrofit of the existing building along with the addition. The two floors added at the rear of the building create a 5-story building with one level of basement. The three off-street parking spaces are actually below grade and accessed via car lift. We are proposing commercial office spaces at the ground level and nine market-rate residential condominiums on floors 2 through 5 with open space on the roof. The height of the addition we are proposing is 19 feet above the existing building. We are adding this portion with the additional 9 feet for various mechanical stairs and elevator penthouses to access the roof. The new building would have a height of 65 feet and the top of the penthouse is approximately 74 feet 6 inches. The break down of the rental units is four one-bedroom studio sized units, three two-bedroom units and two three-bedroom units at the top two floors. Our challenge in this project in maintaining the historical façade was how do we bring light and air into the residential units? We have come up with a scheme where we create this large unit court and basically create two rental towers on either side to get light and air into the rental units. There is also a smaller light wall we are cutting in at the back of the building to get light and air in to the deeper units. Also, as the light wall is steep, we are removing a portion of the existing wall and then putting in property line windows looking over that shorter building. Last November we had a meeting with two neighborhood groups – The Tenderloin Collaborative and the North of Market Planning Coalition. Last month we had a follow up meeting with the groups and we didn't get objections. We had a pre-application meeting with the Building and Fire Department because the exiting through the project was tricky to get around. We worked out those issues along with the property line window issues with the Fire and Building Departments. We believe that this project would improve the neighborhood in that it provides nine additional rental units.

I own the adjoining properties at 1672 and 1674 Great Highway. The permit applicant constructed an addition on his property and is trying to obtain approval after the fact by representing to the Planning staff that he has the same footprint. I have to state the permit applicant has acted in bad faith. In the past he's had a history of this type of behavior. He's previously been required to demolish an addition he had constructed on the rear portion of the rear structure on his property. This is not a new conduct on his behalf. In front of you, you should have affidavits submitted from the previous owner of the property, in addition to affidavits from two of the previous tenants, Christian Huff and Michael Wolf resulting in a new 200-foot addition. The crux of this issue is whether or not the permit applicant has actually expanded the size of his building. He is making representations on his building permit that he has not expanded. I take issues with that. In addition to the affidavits, I submitted two copies of appraisal reports from appraisal companies dated March 20, 2002 and September 11, 2003. They were hired by the permit applicant and said the depth of the building was 48 feet. There are aerial photographs that show the property prior to construction. The date is 2001. There is an aerial photograph showing the project in the course of construction, taken in 2004 that shows the condition of the property after the rear portion had been deconstructed or demolished and an aerial photograph, the current year of how the structure currently looks. Comparing the 3 structures it's evident that the structure has been expanded by a sizable amount. I would like to also point out that Mr. Badiner issued a letter of determination. The letter was based upon the fact that this project has not had an expanded footprint and that the new structure occupies the previous footprint of the property. Also, there are color photographs showing close-up detail of the property prior to and after construction. I think these photographs very clearly show the extent of the size increase in this project. I think all of the items together support the fact that the permit applicant has significantly expanded the footprint of this property without appropriate permits and without appropriate neighborhood notification. Action like this individual's places the Planning Commission and Department of Building Inspection under public scrutiny. I submitted motions to the committee, which I hope you will consider. The only other comment I have to make is the applicant is relying upon maps dating to the 30's to show he is not expanding the size. Douglas Jacuzzi, architect, representing project sponsor I would like to point out first, Mr. O'Flynn's comments on his photographs. One of the first things that we did in analyzing this project was to create an analysis from photographs given to us by the property owner from the time he purchased the property. In the as-built condition when he purchased the property, and when you walk yourself around the property to the setback notch where the existing rear addition extends from the higher portion of the property, you see the window at the turn and follow around to you see there is a motorcycle parked and an exterior shower. To the top of this page, from the time he purchased his property you see the rooftop of the existing extension of the extension of the building prior to any work being done. Going to the same sequence of photographs after the construction was completed we can see, moving around the side of the property back up a little to one of the key issues, the light well from the neighboring apartment building that is clouded with sheeting. This is a photograph that was submitted by Mr. O'Flynn, that we count the number of siding boards and determine the extension of the original construction. There were 13 siding boards. The photograph taken after the work took place there remains 13 siding boards to the extent of the construction. Mr. O'Flynn has taken other shots at different angles to distort that image. It is fairly clear here where the construction ends. Particularly in relation to the existing roof before construction, and from the inside existing roof seeing the extension, and again in the roof after construction, and from inside the window after construction. Ean Ever since I was a kid I wanted to live by the beach. I moved to the Great Highway and I remodeled the front house so my family could live in the unit. We have been in the unit for two and a half years and we are renting an apartment while we are waiting. I did get a permit for the work done. I did not intend to subvert the process. I submitted my permit, it was not perfect and I hired an architect to correct it. Mr. O'Flynn has a personal problem with me that stems from a bad real estate transaction. He stated that for $25,000 he would make the problem go away and continues to intimate that the financial payment would make this stop and if I did not pay he will push and push and push. This process has been going on with Mr. Jacuzzi for a year. He is trying to cloud the real issue. He submitted pictures to you that are taken from off angles to make the project seem like it expanded the footprint. If you look at the pictures with the counting of the 13 slots they are dead on. There are only 6 people in the world that are going to see this. The two people who live in the back where I live, they signed the a petition and expressed their support much the same as the person who lives in Mr. O'Flynn's rental property where he does not live and never plans to live, signed the petition. The two people in front of his unit also submitted their signed petition. All the people around this have signed the petition in favor. As far as the sand born maps, there are no dimensions on O'Flynn's pictures. If you look at the maps, the property has been in this shape since it was built in 1915.

I wanted to ask again why there is no plan or schedule to address buildings without garages. There is no distinction made about location or corridor or districts; no prototype examples we have seen of Telegraph Hill, Nob Hill, or Russian Hill about parking automobiles. Also policy without direction from Planning - if there isn't a parking policy setting review on how they are impacting the middle income housing, then there is a problem. I am very concerned about this issue.

title: Supervisor
comment: good afternoon. I think overall the message is loud and clear. I think that this is an opportunity for us to update the code that needs updating and to provide a process for enhancing the street experience where appropriate. I would like to include awnings as part of this process as well so we are catching this more thoroughly up front. Like the MCD laws where we have some corrections along the way we want to do this thoroughly.

I have the honor to represent the People's Republic of China. We are asking an addition to the Consul General's home at 85 St. Elmo Street in order to provide staff bedrooms and staff bathrooms, which are not currently possible. Because this property is so large, it calls for a PUD approval through the Conditional Use. At the Commission's request, architect Li Aison can make a detailed presentation about the design. But since it's been in your packets, this is the fifth time this item has been calendared, we thought we would go to some of the issues that have really been of concern to the neighbors. As Mr. Badiner says, this is a unique property. It is a little under 9/10 of an acre. Under the code it could be subdivided into individual lots but the People's Republic of China, who really want to meet the Consul General's needs, owns it. It really does not meet China's needs right now. This enormous property requires 5 full-time staff and right now there is only one bedroom. More importantly, security requirements make it necessary for China to host very high-level dignitaries in a quiet and secure setting. There have been continuous negotiations and discussions with neighbors since this item was first calendared with you in April. They covered a range of issues, potentially exploring whether or not it was possible to put these bedrooms inside the house by building on top or excavating the foundation or whether there's potential to put this elsewhere on the property. There was a suggestion perhaps cutting down the mature trees to the right of the house and building it up, towards the street; if it is in the rear yard how to make it further away, even from neighbors; smaller tree preservation; landscaping; construction usage; a full range of good neighbor issues. And the agreement I think produces an even better building for neighbors that can meet China's needs. It basically takes this V-shaped building and rotates it to eliminate that central courtyard and put it away from neighbors. It involves substantial set backs ranging from 18 feet to 20 feet and a 10-foot set back from the rear. A notch in the southwest corner creates a 29-foot set back from the side yard. 78 percent of the property will remain as open space. Every mature tree over 24 inches will be preserved except for one. There will be a landscape architect will be consulted to do a site-specific site plan and a variety of good neighbor construction measures have been agreed to. Including no construction on Saturday and Sunday and restricted hours of construction. With this residential addition, St. Elmo will be able to meet the People's Republic of China's needs for the Consul General. This is not to be used for commercial purposes like a boarding house or hotel or condos. Although this is an RH-1 (D), a variety of uses are allowed with a conditional use. The People's Republic of China has voluntarily agreed to a condition that as long as China owns the property, this will only be used for a single family home. In conclusion, I want to thank those neighbors that have worked so hard for so many months to create a project that would meet China's needs. They have been honest and honorable and respectful and extremely firm about protecting neighbor's interest. I want to apologize to neighbors who haven't been able to be part of this and the homeowner's association for fighting to the very last minute to make sure the neighbors' interests was protected. The People's Republic of China looks forward to being a continuing part of this neighborhood and this City and respectfully requests the Planning Commission approve the revised plans and additions for this residential addition. Susan Zurnaga, President of the Monterey Heights Association We have been working for months in this process. We feel the current compromise both in plan and conditions meets the majority of the needs of the neighborhood and we support the approval of the revised plans and conditions of the project. Joseph Mocklin I am the property owner at 125 St. Elmo Way. After months of negotiation I feel we have negotiated the best possible resolution we can have and I am in support of the new project. Mark Lynch My family lives at 135 St. Elmo Way. Our rear yard adjoins the corner of St. Elmo where the proposed addition will be built. It will be visible from our home including the rear of our balcony. We have been in discussion about this project since the Consul General first contacted the neighbors in March of 2004. We expressed our concerns about the size and location of that addition since that time on. I have continued to be concerned about the addition as well as the broader concerns of the neighborhood. In the course of our negotiations the addition has been moved away from the property line of all the neighbors and has been made more compact. In my opinion, there is no concern about the architecture. It is excellent. The Consul General has agreed to a number of conditions that will mitigate the structure of the neighborhood and I am satisfied that the revised structure before you represents the best resolution for everyone concerned. I would like to thank the Consul General for his efforts and patience in coming to this resolution and we look forward to being good neighbors for many years. Bob McCarthy I am here not to speak as a paid advocate but to speak as a member of the faculty. San Francisco and the United States really truly serves as an inspiration for the not cultural revolution, but the cultural evolution that is now going on in the People's Republic. They look to the United States as a beacon of tolerance and diversity. A place that welcomes them. A place of peace and prosperity. And they mostly see the United States through the lens of San Francisco. San Francisco has had the longest standing city relationship of any American city other that Washington, DC, through its friendship with Shanghai. I will tell you if you have had the pleasure and privilege of going to China you feel the extraordinary pleasure from everyone there. And if you get to participate in a educational or cultural exchange, you realize much of that comes from us. Today is quite a sentimental moment in San Francisco's history with both the Asian Community and San Francisco Community and the Consul General. It's a rare opportunity. I have had the opportunity of functioning as head of a Department as well as running a Commission and I can tell you in your four years here you will have lots of opportunities to improve people's lives on an individual basis, on a neighborhood basis, but this is an opportunity for you to make a worldwide impact on the consular core - all of which are watching. And today is your opportunity. So when you look back sometime 20 or 30 years from now as I look back on my experience 20 or 30 years ago, and you decide what are the things I most remember, I would hope you would think there was a day when I was asked to make a decision that was listened to by all the Consulates in San Francisco; by governments around the world; and it was my chance to confirm San Francisco's historic commitment to the Consular Core, to the people and countries they represent; and specifically to San Francisco and its Asian Community. Some day we will elect an Asian-American Mayor and I hope the predecessor of that Mayor some day when he or she wins that election, that they will say today we are all Asian-Americans. Mark Jordan I live at 25 St. Elmo Way, two houses down from the Consul General. I am a Board member of the Monterey Heights Homeowner's Association. I just wanted to let you know that I was not consulted about the apparent compromise that was agreed to with Consul representatives. The conditions of approval do not adequately address the points raised on June 1, as proposed by the General Consul. The two treaties concerning diplomatic immunity are contradictory and we have yet to receive an opinion from the City Attorney's Office that we have requested. As an example, during these last winter storms I was out in the rain at 3:00 a.m. with a representative from PG&E trying to assess the problem. Luck of the draw, he wasn't aware of Paragraph 31 of the Geneva Convention. Nor was I, and he refused to go on to the property to assess the problem. An agreement in writing about emergency access would be very helpful to us. My partner and I only received the revised plans for the residence last night at 9: 15 p.m. with the understanding they would be submitted to the Planning Commission this morning, contrary to the Commission's notice requirements. More important, many of us who have contributed thousands of dollars to the legal defense fund and many of the homeowners at Monterey Heights have not seen or approve the compromise. I don't think that we as neighbors have been given enough time to review the plans and address the proposed conditions. Kenall Patton I live two doors down from the Consul General, We have resided there for seven years. I want to take you back nearly five years. On the morning of November 24, 2001, our 11-room also unique home on St. Elmo nearly burnt to the ground because we had electrical flames and fires coming down the power lines from the Consul General's residence.
