We had electrical fire in the cable television system in the basement of our home. PG&E was not given access to the Consul General's property and when we finally sat down with PG & E and asked what the problem was they said there was a continual problem with the Consul General not maintaining the trees on their property and not providing access for safety issues to the property. I am here today to oppose the Consult General's application on one and only one ground and that is public safety. You should have in your files a copy of the letter that I sent to the Public Utilities Commission on November 27, 2001. I provided a copy of this to Mr. Tom Wang on May 3 rd . I also provided a copy to our Supervisor, Sean Elsbernd, and have discussed this with him. This was a letter written more than four and a half years ago. This was an incident that occurred more than four and a half years ago and I think it's acknowledgement of the fact we have not had excellent neighbor relations with the Consul General as a resident in our beautiful neighborhood. Our neighbors met continually throughout the middle of May and at those neighborhood meetings, neighborhood safety was of prime importance. The notice of special restriction, which the attorney's of the Association and other neighbors who contributed to the fund produced that was given to Debra Stein on June 1, read in pertinent part: In case of an emergency involving a potential immediate health and safety impact, all public agencies necessary to respond to the emergency shall be provided with immediate and unrestricted access. This is what my neighbors and I require to be in the conditions of approval of this conditional use permit. The Chinese, for whatever reason, have continually rejected this essential requirement as a condition of approval. We understand that the Chinese Government is claiming diplomatic immunity. I've been a practicing attorney fro 26 years in this City. I don't believe that they have diplomatic immunity when it comes to health and safety issues with respect to their personal residence. On behalf of the affected homeowners, and by that I mean the homeowners - those of us who live closest, I request that you include this as a condition. Tom Driscoll I live at 460 Yerba Buena across from the Consul General's property. My objection, really as with Mr. Patton's and Mr. Jordan's, relates to this health and safety issue. We are one of the last parts of the City that has remnants of the Sutro forest planted in the late 1880's. We have massive pine and cypress trees. They are mature and healthy, but with the kind of windstorms we get, branches will come down and some of them are 25 feet long, eight inches in diameter, and they will knock out power. We have had repeated outages caused not only by their trees but our trees. It's a problem that needs to be addressed. We have had power outages that have lasted as long as 48 hrs. Because of these situations access to any one of our properties is key in order to take care of these problems. So, we think that's very important. On the subject of the diplomatic immunity, nobody is suggesting that the Consul General should waive all diplomatic or consular immunity they are entitled to under their treaties. The Consul can by virtue of the treaty waive certain conditions and all we are asking is the language that Mr. Patton has suggested, that in cases of emergency access be granted to the public agencies and utilities that are necessary to protect the public health and safety. Gloria Bernstein I live at 116 St. Elmo Way. As a Monterey Heights homeowner, I as well as my neighbors seek to preserve the character of Monterey Heights and the neighborhood. It's a character composed of single-family detached homes in which all homeowners and residents are bound by the same code, guidelines, covenants, conditions and restrictions of zoning and building. It is a relief of many of the homeowners that, in fact, the residence is not avoiding issues. When we found out that the plans had been submitted to the Commission, immediately many of us contacted Tom Wang and he logged 21 phone oppositions. There were 30 letters of opposition also written. We had petitions signed by 77 neighbors against this addition. The West of Twin Peaks Central Council joined us, which is an umbrella organization representing 16 homeowner associations and 90,000 residents. All of us remain opposed to the plan as it is currently proposed and we ask you to consider the feelings of the neighborhood when you make your decision. Peter Schweikardt I'm glad to have this opportunity to share some of my concerns and some of the concerns that have been passed to me by my neighbors. But first, actually I'd just like to reflect briefly on the representation as to how the process has gone. I've heard some representations about the history of it, the involvement of the neighbors, the openness and so forth, which contrast quite sharply with what I have experienced. We did have several meetings with the Consul General starting over two years ago. And there were subsequent meetings. We always found that our concerns were not met in any way. The current size, for example, the scope of the project I believe is essentially the same or perhaps even larger than the first proposal. They have simply, I think they have wanted to tell you that they met with us this number of times, as thought this was being flexible and being open and helpful and cooperative and neighborly when in fact it was not. In addition, I also want to echo a remark that while perhaps there were meetings going on between the constant continuances, I was never asked to be part of any of them. I live at 168 St. Elmo, which is almost across the street from the Consul General's residence. So to me it was a series of continuances followed by deafening silence from the proposers of this project. And they are now representing it to you in a different way. I ask you please to consider some of this from what others of us might have experienced. We live in a neighborhood that is zoned for single-family dwellings. It's also governed by CC and R's, which have over time, I think, maintained a very pleasant residential environment. We believe that this current proposal – by the way, it's an addition. Not being a lawyer, I'm not that good at understanding some of these words, but to me an addition perhaps is something physically attached to something else. That is not the case. It is a huge apartment complex that is being added at the other side of the property, not contiguous with the existing property. We are concerned about the fact that it will become more convenient to hold more and more official consular functions if there are visitors on site. We're concerned apart from the lack of access as a security and safety measure that it would make it impossible for any agreement that might be made here to be enforced. In other words, the City would not be able to verify compliance with any agreements that have been made in connection with this proposal. David Bisho, President of the Twin Peaks Central Council We represent 16 neighborhoods of the City's western neighborhoods. I have been involved with Twin Peaks for 8 1⁄2 years and I have to say this situation is the most improper thing I have even been involved with. What they are suggesting is against the CC & R's signed by the owners of every property on St. Elmo Way. It's also against the rules for RH-1 single family. It is absolutely against the use of a single family home. No plans have been submitted to anyone including West of Twin Peaks. We don't have what we're approving here or not approving. Half the board members are in favor of it because they are afraid. Frankly, if they don't approve it they are going to be screwed and that's improper. It is just plain wrong. The rest of them are against it and are here to tell you. And the worst thing is that the Planning Department has been helping them with it. West of Twin Peaks is unanimously against it. And I just want to add that I am in the export business. And for the last 32 years, most of the people we deal with are Chinese all over the Fast East. And I have to say, generally speaking, they are the group in the world to deal with. A deal is a deal and I am very surprised with this. I hope you disapprove the project and I hope the project sponsors withdrawn their request. Jeremy Lieberman I live at 428 Yerba Buena Avenue. I share about 85 feet of back yard with St. Elmo. I agree with all the things brought up by my fellow neighbors in opposition, but I want to speak about one serious problem that hasn't been addressed yet and that is there are serious inaccuracies in the plans that are proposed. The design of the home does not show there was a large addition built in the  90's by the current owners, which, from my best estimates, is about a 1000 to 1250 sq. ft. I don't know because I'm not allowed on the property. The stated square footage of the home, the amount of rear yard open space that's currently available and being consumed in the amount of living space reported, does not reflect what I see on these plans. I have architectural drawings of the space, which have been sent to the Department of Building Inspection. They have been forwarded apparently to the City Attorney by Building Inspection and to the Planning Department. I don't know if you all have them, but it shows this space and it describes an apartment with a large bedroom, sitting room, tearoom that appears to me to extend beyond the rear set back. The plans that have been submitted that show where the rear set back line is does not show this addition on it. Four or five neighbors have filed formal complaints with DBI. It was investigated, assigned to an investigator. He was not able to get access to the property. This complaint was filed in May, so it's been 3 months they have been continuously denied access to inspect the property. There are no permits on record anywhere. This was confirmed by the Planning Department. And to our knowledge, no one has ever inspected whether this property is – this addition is safe or not. Senior officials at the Department of Building Inspection told me that they have tried to work with the City Attorney's Office to meet with counsel for the Consul and obtain access, but they have, as of yesterday, been denied any access to the property. I believe that our complaint about this structure is valid and deserves investigation. Again, I am most concerned about the safety of my property. My children play in the back yard right next to where this addition comes out to. I was dismayed to learn that when neighbors met with Mr. Macris that he told them that this complaint would have no bearing on the approval or not of this project and as he specifically quoted, he said this complaint was going nowhere. This is exactly the opposite of what Building Inspection told me, that no new permits would be granted until all complaints are investigated.

name_raw: Michael Kurtzman, Representing the Project Sponsor
comment: As Mr. Badiner mentioned, we had conversations about the height of the building, which was the issue that was brought up at the previous meeting on May 4 th . At that meeting based on the Planning Commission's concerns about the upper floor and their recommendation, as mentioned in the memo, we were asked and encouraged to seek a variance and enlarge the building footprint to recapture the building area that would be lost if we removed the top floor. So we removed the top floor. The initial design that went to the Planning Department was reviewed but because certain members of the Planning Department were out of town, we weren't able to go back and forth. That is part of the late nature of the discussion in making this decision just in the past few days. So we have agreed to move that down to 8 ft. The immediate neighbors on the right side, as well as the neighbor on the left side supported the original project. We have the neighborhood support in the immediate neighborhood. Robert Dolan I live two houses west on Clayton Street. I was originally concerned when I saw that even though the project sponsor is taking off an entire floor that the net result was only five feet. That does not make sense unless there's something that is not clear. I just wanted to say that I feel that although I was originally opposed not to the project, but to the scope, the mass, and above all the height, I now feel that they have complied with what you said or what you directed them or suggested them to do. Concerning the rear yard easement, I personally have no objection and I've talked to other neighbors who also feel that there's nothing wrong with going back. I feel that they have complied with your request and though I am going to lose that sunlight, I think the rear yard setback or the rear yard easement is worth it.

We were just informed that the project sponsor has asked for this continuance so he can work with representatives of either the neighborhood or a neighbor to try and reach further agreement. I think that was the intent of it.

I live around the corner from the project. The reason I brought this discretionary review up is the neighborhood and various neighbors have been working for three years to try to come up with a compromise for this particular lot. We feel that this option as well as the previous one that was first submitted in 2003 does not keep in context with the neighborhood. It is much higher than most of the other buildings. It is much bigger, much bulkier and has a very small yard. This particular project site, being a corner lot that is about 62 feet wide by 80-some feet long is large enough to accommodate a variety of different options that would not require a variance or any kind of special considerations. There is plenty of opportunity for designs to have been put forth that would have not required any kind of special considerations. I feel that if a typical resident of San Francisco were trying to make these types of changes and ask for these variances they probably wouldn't be granted very easily. This project sponsor has been all along the way getting a lot to support from the Planning Department, even though the neighbors have been against it for the most part. Although as mentioned there are letters in support, there are also quite a few letters in opposition to this. It's been a three-year battle. I also want to comment on the design and context of this building. I went through the Residential Design Guidelines and found 10 different issues where this building did not meet them (which I have outlined in my discretionary review). A lot of them have to do with the scale, size and context, but also about the design. I think this neighborhood in San Francisco deserves a building more in context with its neighbors and I hope you agree. Roland Salvato I live at 3924 Larkin Street. The reason I'm here is because for the last two and a half years I've been trying to figure out exactly what the logic is and justification for allowing that building to have variances. What's so special about this building that it requires a variance to allow an undersized yard, extensive height and a really bizarre design? If you look at the profile of the building, it's well over 40 feet in some places, as high as 47 feet. It is competing with the Ghirardelli Square Tower across the street. Bradford Whitaker When I first saw the drawing of this new building, I thought, you know, there are some wonderful compromises made by all parties that bothered redesigning this building. We feel that this corner elevation has a discrepancy of over a foot from the prior design and I'd like to know really where the cornerstone is, because it's relative to the total elevation of this property. I'd like to know before you make a determination on what the right elevation for this property is that you've looked into it. As far as height variance or allowable height variances, I'm totally against that. I feel there's too much magnitude here. This building would be kind of a monolithic piece. Jill Bittner I am really frankly shocked that we are still talking about this issue two and a half to three years after the fact. This is right by Ghirardelli Square, ground zero for tourists. This is something that is so flagrantly wrong. It's obvious it's too tall. It's got too big of a footprint. It is out place and out of scale with the neighborhood. Erica Whittaker I just don't understand and why we can't put a building there that will coincide with what else exists there. To me, I think we are an old neighborhood and should be considered a historic neighborhood. Our home just turned 80 years old. Our neighbors are just with us and I would like to see something that looks like it's been there for a hundred years and fits in. Joel Yodowitz, Representing the Project Sponsor What you have before you today is the redesign that expressly agreed to at a meeting with the DR requestors and some of the neighbors.. When listening to the DR requestor, I'd like to remind you that this same DR requestor who requested that the soils be tested a couple of years ago, opposed a demolition permit for this property and the purpose of the demolition permit was to remove the building to do the very soil testing the DR requestor asked for. They appealed this to the Board of Appeals, one of you was on the Board at that time, and the DR request was denied so the soils could be tested. There were countless meetings. The architect had many meetings. The project sponsor had many meetings. As mentioned, that meeting culminated in what we thought was a resolution. These same DR requestors filed a CEQA appeal on this project and therefore that June hearing got continued. When we went to the Board of Supervisors last week on their CEQA appeal, they didn't even bother to show up. We invested a lot of time and effort preparing opposition to that appeal and showing up at that appeal. The City Attorney was there. The Planning Department was there. The Supervisors were there and they didn't show up. That's is their pattern and practice. They recently appealed a subdivision map permit for Ghirardelli Square. That's a very technical type of appeal and the City's notice to parties says, this is a technical appeal. The hearing was this week, and they didn't show up. The reason I bring that up is because I think it's important to look at actions that speak louder than words. These buildings are not out of scale; they are smaller than Ghirardelli Square. There is a code compliant rear yard in this. We are not asking for a variance for the size of the rear yard. Anthony Panteleoni, Architect for the project Using power point, he gave an overall description of the project showing that surrounding neighbors are a mix of two and four story buildings made of a variety of stucco and wood siding. There is not a prominent architectural character in the neighborhood. Our building is going to be 40 feet tall, not 100 feet tall. After meeting in Supervisor Alioto-pier's office, we decided that we would end up dividing the lot into three separate lots. By doing that, we have the rear yards up against the house at 2946 Larkin Street. The rear yard requirement is 25% of the depth of the lot. That is what we provided. We are not asking for a rear yard variance. Units are typically three stories over parking, three flats over parking. 899 and 889 are essentially the same layout, but the building at the corner of Larkin Street has a penthouse unit. We are 44 feet short of the 1700 required. That is the variance we are asking for. Tom Coin, Project Sponsor I just wanted to point out that I think it's important that there's no opposition here tonight from any adjacent neighbors on either side of us. Also, across the street, the neighbors most impacted by this project, there is no one opposing us. I think most of the letters in the back of the submittal are from neighbors across the street that have been looking at a long-term eyesore. Took us three years to get this hearing. We've been stopped by various strategies but mainly this kind of abusive CEQA appeal which I know you are not responsible for. I hope you will approve the changes we have put in and approve the project. Tom Howard, Representing the North Point Neighborhood Association. My family owned property on North Beach Street across the street from the proposed site for 100 years. We are for the development of this property. It's just been an eyesore for 75 years with a gas station. And now for the last four years it's just been graffiti and we're tired of all these delays. The residents and property owners on that neighborhood are just waiting for this piece of property to be developed. Please vote no on the Discretionary Review. Tom Branch I think the scale of the building is well within keeping of the neighborhood and the most immediate neighbors feel the same so we want you to vote in favor of the project and against the DR. Josephine Mazzucco My husband and I own the adjacent building that you saw the graffiti on. Over the last three years we have seen two configurations for this building. The first was oversized and didn't fit into the neighborhood; and the second did not have space between our buildings and we would have only had a five-foot light well for our living room. This is more in keeping with the neighborhood and affords us a 15 foot breeze way that is made up of back yards. We have one concern we want to bring forward to you today that needs to be addressed, and that has to do with a letter dated May 9, 2005, from the Department of Public Health, written to Mr. Coin requiring that the project is to come up with a management plan and a health safety plan to complete the balance of their litigation if necessary. The control plan also needs to be implemented. If the health safety plan is implemented as required, we feel the project should go forward as submitted. Jane Stavropoulos I have resided at 9 1⁄2 North State Street for over 21 years. Robert Clutton and I own the site and find this configuration acceptable. We like the step down on Larkin. We like the garden across the street. We like the garages on North Point and additional parking on Larkin Street. We are in favor of the project as submitted.

representing Project Sponsor We have been working on this project for about four years with the Planning Department.  The Sponsor and I am pleased to be back here today to present the project and its evolution so that maybe we can take you into the mind of the architect and the planners as we come with a proposal that you are going to see here today. I'd like to begin first with the origins of this project and its location.  As you can see from the image on the screen where you see the label, it sits at the intersection of Market and 8 th  Streets and all the way to Mission Street is the current proposed site. For those in the audience who may not be familiar, it is on Market Street directly across from the Orpheum Building, a very well known corridor. The site is currently occupied by the original motel building or hotel building that existed on the site, a horizontal low rise building that is largely surrounded by parking lots. As you can see, there is an anomaly on the site in the fact that Stevenson does not actually traverse that parcel.  When the hotel was built, Stevenson must have been vacated and the parcel was consolidated all the way across. You will see how we respond to that unusual circumstance in the City structure. The existing building occupies most of the length of the site along 8 th. What you can see along the top of the page is how Stevenson actually dead-ends abruptly with no termination cul-de-sac or any other means of return. The site receives the sun from the South and of course east and west at certain time of the day.  And we just show you where the shadows are cast internally with the site. The diagram that is now on the screen is the shadow plan that actually cuts through the site that is truly the true limiting factor, because it really dominates above the zoning heights that are permitted on the site. It becomes really the deciding factor in the massing of the building.  The shadow ordinance requires this and, as you can see, there is a high point on Mission Street that cascades gently along the corner to 8 th  and along Market and eventually to the low corner of Market and 8 th , which becomes the lowest point of the property. But in fact, it's sort of coincidental, it sort of fits into the City texture and the fact that buildings along Market are above the height that the shadow ordinance provides and buildings along Mission, they are evolving; they are quite a bit taller. So, this takes us to the actual site plan of this project and you can see what we are doing fundamentally here, we are trying to reestablish the City grid and reestablish some of the traffic patterns in a coherent way. The axis of Stevenson is reinstated with a pedestrian promenade that takes one directly across the site. What we are actually recreating here is the two original sites with a larger site along Market and a narrower site along Mission. The dead end is extended along the site and makes a regular turn and exits along Mission far enough from the corner so it is a logical intersection at the termination of what Stevenson's is today, which is essentially a service drive. [He continued to use his power point slide presentation to describe the existing site and proposed project.]

Director of Tenderloin Housing Three years ago when we heard about the project that was planned to demolished at Trinity Plaza, it led to great concern among the tenants and groups like ours because we were going to lose 360 units of rent controlled housing. In response to that threat, I asked Supervisor Chris Daly to introduce legislation to prevent the demolition citywide. Early in December we were planning to re-circulate a special election for June 2005. The end result was that I got a call from Jack Davis, representing Angelo Sangiacomo, who said we've been fighting so long, what if we save all your rent-controlled housing? Well, keep in mind nowhere in the history of California, I don't believe anywhere in the history of America, has anyone built new housing under rent control. They might have build it under Federal, but not under rent control. Of course, State law forbids rent control in new housing. Angelo was suggesting that he would agree voluntarily with a deed restriction for rent control and that all housing would be replaced on site and none of our tenants in the building would be displaced because the minute the building was ready they would move right over. In fact in a subsequent agreement negotiated by Supervisor Daly, the builders are going to pay for the move and the tenants can take all their furniture to the new place as well. That assurance made a big difference. It looked like we could work out something that would be that rare opportunity for people who have been historic adversaries to come together. After all we've said about him [Mr. Sangiacomo], I'm willing to step forward and make peace. If we did the 15% affordable, we would end up with 275 affordable units in this project. Instead we are getting 350 rent controlled units. When you say you could work out a better deal, how come no better deal has ever come? Who could afford to build rent controlled?  Where would they get financing? The truth is if you do not have the wealth of Angelo Sangiacomo, this project wouldn't happen. There is no public money in this. Trinity is giving up 200 commercial parking spaces it already has.  Remember when you take away parking spots from revenue it is already getting, that means that you are taking millions of dollars out of the project.

we could have given up rent controlled units and gotten more affordable units. The tenants opted for more rent control rather than have more affordable units. Jim Ruben We have been working with Angelo Sangiacomo and the City to try to get this before you. I get to deal with the un-sexy parts of this project, the open issues that Craig Nikitas raised and didn't close up. I am going to try to address those in some kind of orderly fashion. The first that comes to mind and that Randy Shaw mentioned to you is the parking issue. Throughout the discussions with the City, this was collaboration between the City, the tenants and the project sponsor. We were working on a development agreement throughout the project. We had the support of the City for 250 commercial spaces, that's why the development agreement was drafted that way.  That's why all the documents originally were drafted that way.  That's why you were shown 250 commercial spaces below grade for the commercial, for the 60,000 square feet that were going to be producing. What happened is because of the long period of time it took to get before you, the C-3 parking legislation passed you and then passed the Board of Supervisors so we are now faced with that C-3 parking. Here is what we are doing though.  Currently at that site right now there are 450 spaces being used regularly. I mean they are sold out. We are going to take away those 450 spaces and replace them with 250 spaces, a reduction of 200 while at the same time the Federal Building on the same block is going to be adding 2800 employees with zero parking, we're adding 60,000 sq. ft. - actually a net of 48,000 because we're eliminating that restaurant there - but we're adding 60,000 square feet of commercial space that needs parking and won't have any. We're under parked in my view.  If you check the Planning Guidelines on residential, we're producing 1900 units with 1200 spaces. So, it seems to me to be a fair compromise to allow us to continue to proceed with the 250 spaces that we anticipated until 3 weeks ago. Similarly, there was an issue about stackers on the 12 spaces. All of our parking is below grade.  We don't have the space on the floor to floor to put stackers.  We would respectfully request that we not be required to do that. 12% affordable [in addition to the rent controlled] was the understanding of the parties – the tenants and Angelo Sangiacomo. What happened?  Again because of the long period of time a new BMR was passed.  It is not effective until the Mayor signs it, but at some point he will. We talked with Chris Daly last week and it was not their intent to capture Trinity. There was some discussion about changing the definition of the existing tenant.  We have agreed to that.  We agreed that an existing tenant will be anybody at Trinity Plaza with a lease on the day of the first Certificate of Occupancy or Temporary Certificate of Occupancy. There was another open issue on the variances that Craig mentioned – we'll agree. Give us the parking and the maps. There is another issue.  Somebody is suggesting that the north-south pathway between Mission and Stevenson through the private open space be open to the public. We can't agree to that and hope you won't make us agree to it. We have a great big public plaza area.  It's the way it was designed.  We expect the building to be mapped with restrictions subject to City Attorney review. We are going to waive the Ellis Act, waive restrictions.  There is no way that will be sold as condominiums. [His time ran out.] Tom Radulovich, Executive Director of Livable City We have some concerns about this project that we would like to see resolved before it's allowed to go forward. We do support the contentions in Supervisor Maxwell's letter and would ask you to consider those. I am going to use most of 3 minutes here to talk about transportation and urban design issues. As we are located in Mid-Market, I am a frequent walker and cyclist in Mid-Market and have some big concerns about this project. First of all, we do support the staff recommendation that the short-term parking be eliminated. There are several hundred parking spaces that are going in next-door that will be short-term and I think you read the article in the Chronicle on Monday.  It mentioned that there are hundreds of potential short-term parking spaces in the C-3 area now. They are being leased out in short-term garages but if the demand for short-term parking were to increase, they would go back.  The converse is also true. If you glut an area with parking spaces, they will go back to leased spaces and that will have an effect on walking and cycling. We understand some accommodations were made not to shadow 1160 Mission, but we are very concerned about how this project treats the public realm; what it does to Market Street; what it does to Mission Street; and what it does to 8 th  Street. Market Street in particular is San Francisco's main street.  Probably the most important street in terms of urban design in the city.  We feel the additional height, these kind of masses – slab-like structures pushed up against Mission are going to have bad effects in terms of wind, in terms of urban design, in terms of shadow on a street that has been devastated by a series of bad building on Market. We would very much like to see a public right of way along that side. We applaud them for bringing Mission Street all the way through.  But you can see if that public right of way was connected between Stevenson, we would get away from that frequent of a giant wall of building on the south side of Market. Jazzie Collins, South of Market Community Action Network and tenant in the South of Market area. I live two blocks away from the housing site. If you look down out 8 th  Street, you see there are four lanes of traffic going southbound on 8 th  Street. When the tenants come out of the current parking lot, they have to look north toward the public library and high in order to find a way to come out. You have pedestrian crossings there every day. To have 1,450 additional cars come through is endangering to the pedestrians that live in that neighborhood and also endangering the motorists that are pulling out against on-coming traffic. We have to keep in mind there are also three freeways that run in that neighborhood going southbound.  Yu have 80, 101 and 280. My suggestion is to put this off and continue it for another month to get the entire community's participation and also to consider safety measures that are involved. Tom Hart We have the Orpheum Theater building right across the street from this project.  It's a very active theater. It's the theater that we use to display the most shows with and it really is very dependent on a lot of things. The BART station access is right there.  It's part of the Civic Center fabric.  It also depends on close parking availability in the immediate environment. Most of our shows are at night with 8:00 starts.  And we of course do our marketing to groups and individuals not only in this city but also in the outlying areas. I know we have many repeat customers that come from congregate living homes outside the area.  They come in vans as well as automobiles. We really urge the commission to take a positive action in requiring the 250 spots. We are actually very concerned that the amount of parking available to the public is dropping from 450 down to 250. My hat's off to Mr. Sangiacomo.  Like Mr. Shaw, I don't understand how he's doing it but he's doing it and I think it is a great commitment to the city and especially to this mid-Market area. I sit on the Mid-Market PAC and work with many of the people here today trying to bring along this area to be an arts and entertainment district. Truly if we are going to do that, I think we do need adequate available parking in the area to service the customers that come not only from outside the city but also from within the city and give choices to others to either take public transit or private transportation. Ken Werner, Trinity Plaza Tenants Association I stand before you in complete confidence that this is going to be a great project. We're going to see the revitalization of the Mid-Market area. Just in one project alone, the visual design that Bernardo has created for us is just absolutely stunning. With the other new building going up at 10 th  and Mission, we are going to have two structures in the mid-Market area that are going to draw attention to creating a new neighborhood in the mid-Market area. I don't think we need Redevelopment coming and sticking their fingers in this at this point. Mid-Market is coming along just fine. We are thrilled that Mr. Sangiacomo has decided upon following a course of creating this wonderful new neighborhood in the heart of Civic Center. Angelica Cabande, South of Market Network I am here to ask you to accept Sup. Maxwell's letter today. Trinity Plaza should [not] be exempt from the inclusionary housing law. The law was fought by a different organization in San Francisco to ensure affordable housing for the people in greater San Francisco, so why should they be exempted from that? Also if Trinity isn't planning to sell the buildings then why have a condo mapping?  What is the purpose of that? I say not to condo mapping and we ask you to not move this forward until the issues that were raised earlier are actually taken into account. Community groups also need to have a greater time to actually read through the development agreement and see if this build out is going to really benefit not only the South of Market but the greater San Francisco. We already have a lot of pedestrian safety issues. We don't need any more parking and if this is really a transit friendly city, then we need to encourage visitors to use the transit.  They should be using BART. Tim Dunn, South of Market Community Coalition I am very concerned about the project as is. I think there are a number of things that have already been cited, the parking being one, of course. This is the most transit-rich location in the City.  An additional 400 cars will slow down MUNI that it is facing on Mission Street and Market Street.  It's a threat to pedestrians in the neighborhood. It's incomprehensible that this would be exempt from the inclusionary housing zoning laws. The rent-controlled units should not be substituted. Every time the rent controlled units become vacant they will go up to 100% market rate.  So it is really important that they get full inclusionary units, which are deed restricted to particular levels of area median income. Finally, I concur with Tom Radulovich.  I don't think the urban design issues have been explored closely enough. Wind on Market is very serious in terms of the pedestrian experience. Until these issues are fully addressed, I think it is critical that this is continued. Sam Dodge This is truly the product of people power. I think of my own involvement with Trinity residents has been over three years. We met every Wednesday night and I'll tell you personally being part of the prayer circle – and I'm not normally a religious person – but a lot of spirit within the building and the core of the group all met and prayed for strength for themselves and the outcome of the struggle and that is really how I feel we got to where we are today. To get to this point was no small task.  It's huge where we are now. The struggle was monumental and it was heroic but the health tolls that it takes on people, year after year; worry about your own home and your own future – it really wears on people. Checking with our own leaders, they've asked me to come and represent their views that this move forward and remind you to look at the big picture – that the forest not be lost for the trees. I look forward to your input but I hope in the end they are able to take another step in the journey and get something that the tenants can rest their hat on and move on to other parts of life beyond this struggle. I certainly hope we can do that tonight and I look forward to this project as well – living and working in the Tenderloin. I think this is going to make an improvement to the Market Street area and the preservation to the community has just been invaluable. Chris Durazo I think that one the most illuminating things out of that study process is the fact it's unfeasible to do rental housing in San Francisco. This is why we're urgently supporting not having condo mapping on this site.  Because this is such an important resource for the City, to the further of San Francisco right now. You should not give it up this soon. I think I am in agreement to discuss these issues further because this is a much bigger project than we started out with three years ago. Johanna Walozac I live half a block away from Trinity Plaza and I'd like to reiterate some points made by earlier speakers about the design of the buildings and pedestrian safety such as I walk around the neighborhood all the time, obviously, and I am also a cyclist. I am concerned about the increase in parking and feel that if there is a problem with transportation and if we feel that there is a need to increase parking spaces that we really need to reconsider that and instead look at public transit and try to make it more efficient and affordable to more people and encourage more people to use it. I am also concerned about the design of the building and the wind that would be created. Sally Ramon, Tenant of Trinity Plaza I would like to thank some of the people and organizations that helped us to get through this. Every since I was very small, I always had caped crusaders that were my heroes. Right now I'm looking for a cape large enough to fit Chris Daly.  Thank you very much. Jim Salinas, Carpenters Local 22. I think it's a great agreement, I think everybody should be excited. You get to make the decision this evening and benefit many people. So here we are again with this great opportunity to bring so many great benefits to folks, including those jobs that are going to be coming as a result of the fact that Mr. Sangiacomo has chosen or see fit to choose a great San Francisco headquarter company called Cannon. I am always delighted to be here because it means great apprenticeship opportunities. This is a great design by a great architect.  It's a great agreement, great contractor, and now you have the ability to make a great decision. April Generation I am here to discuss broader concerns around the Trinity Plaza Development. I want to commend Mr. Sangiacomo for the movement that's been made protecting the tenants around Trinity Plaza, and the tenant's ability to move back into the new development in rent controlled units. I am asking you to be thoughtful about the remaining planning issues that this project brings up and its relationship not just to the Mid-Market area but the broader South of Market and the whole of San Francisco. We have a transit first policy in the city and this is a transit rich area.  250 commercial parking spaces is not needed at this particular site.  There is plenty of transit available to this site. Although the rent controlled units are very important, we want to introduce a variety of housing opportunities for the various ranges of income in the city and affordable rental housing for the work force is an important part of that process. We want to ask you to support inclusionary housing at this site. We also want you to look at the design issues raised by Mr. Radulovich.  Really look at the relationship between Mission and Market. We hope you will be able to address these concerns in the near future.

name_raw: Dorothy Peterson, Vice President of the Shoreview Residents Association
role_title: Vice President of the Shoreview Residents Association
comment: I sent to you a letter last week. It deals with an issue that's important to all of us. There was a settlement between the City and our owners. As part of the settlement the owners are supposed to adhere to City, State, and Federal regulations. None of those have been adhered to. One the City and State regulation in particular deals with the first right or refusal. It has been triggered by the sale of our properties. It's very important because if it's not addressed, then this is the biggest land grab since reconstruction. These are not suggestions. They are regulations. All we are asking is, look into it, because it could mean that we rightfully own. There are people like Ms. Jackson, Ms. Westbrook, and several others who fought hard for us to have the right to own those properties in Hunters Point The only thing I can ask is who is watching out for the watchdog? A bond resolution was pushed through yesterday to go to the Board of Supervisors. Again, over the objections. Look into whether or not these regulations have been adhered to. It seems that the City is rushing headlong to fulfill it's part of the bargain of the settlement but no one is asking is the second party fulfilling it's part of the bargain. If this bond resolution is pushed through, it is to the detriment of the residents. Tax money would leave Bayview Hunters Point to go to a corporation. There is something grossly obscene about a billion dollars corporation on the backs of a community. Sue Hestor I will ask for something you already have a report on. There have been three large PUD's approved in the past 5 years that have a lot of attention and are anchored by grocery stores. In particular, the one on Alemany Boulevard. I request that the staff go over the terms of PUD's and whether or not it is an enforcement mechanism. If a grocery store, which was the big feature for the development goes bust, does the developer have the responsibility to put in a new grocery store or not? We've had trouble with Albertson's in the City and there at least two of them in the PUD's approved by this Commission. If we are giving extra other things for a retail facility, is there the ability to enforce those conditions? I have no idea what the answer is. I have not pulled those PUD resolutions. I think it's a question that needs to be asked. What do you do when a national chain strips the City of grocery stores? We have had grocery store problems in several neighborhoods. Secondly, whoever put the flowers and photo [of Sue Bierman] here I thank you. She was the longest Planning Commissioner we had and she was my friend as well. I know you and a lot of the staff knew her. She supported the Planning Department and the Planning Commission. I will miss her and I think the city will miss her.

section: PUBLIC COMMENT ON AGENDA ITEMS WHERE THE PUBLIC HEARING HAS BEEN CLOSED
comment: [Re: Item 7 – 85 Saint Elmo Way] I am here to oppose the project at 85 St. Elmo Way. My family and I are the backyard neighbors. I oppose this project because it's not in compliance with the Planning Code regarding height. The project proposed a separate structure in violation of one dwelling per lot. It contains 3 separate units. The project is situated on the lot only eight feet from the property lines of adjoining neighbors and it violates rear yard setback lines and open space. The encroachment into the rear yard and the space that increases the living property creates a mega mansion in a neighborhood zoned for single-family homes. If I or any other neighbor were to bring this before the Commission, it would be flatly denied. At the time of purchase of Monterey Heights' property we know that the building and land use runs with the land in addition to the City's prevailing Planning Code. A good neighbor is someone who adheres accordingly. All Monterey Heights' homeowners have the right to remodel and expand their home. They give little merit to the unenforceable conditions of approval. This project would create an unwanted compound in the midst of a residential, single-family neighborhood and is not in keeping with the character of the neighborhood. The Planning Commission is charged to protect the character of our San Francisco neighborhoods and I urge you to vote no. Mr. Jeremy Lieberman I received the plans late Friday and reviewed them and remain opposed to the project. In the last three months I've become an expert in architecture. The Planning Code states the Commission may grant a conditional use that's compatible with the neighborhood or community if that use will not be of harm to the welfare & ; that such use will not affect the General Plan. The project fails to meet many of the established policies. Many people in the neighborhood do not desire the project. There is no one in the neighborhood that really wants to see this project as planned to be built. The project will not benefit or improve the beauty of this neighborhood. Multiple structures on one project site are out of character with the single-family homes on the block. This project is not necessary for the rest of the neighborhood. It will reduce commuting by staff members who work on the premise. It will increase activity and traffic during non-business hours. Thereupon there is ample off street parking on the property. The scale is excessive. A more modest proposal could achieve 9 bedrooms with less rear setbacks. The proposal is harmful to the neighborhood. It will reduce mid-block open space and will block open space on the property. The harm will arise by the unwillingness of the applicant to grant inspection during construction and publicly admit access by fire and utility services. Laurie Bernestein I live across the street from the proposed addition and object to it. I would like to address two issues. One is a safety issue and the concessions that were made by the Council and his representatives. In terms of the gentlemen who spoke last week from the State Department, one of the current concessions was that the State Department would be given phone numbers that could be contacted in case of emergency. If there is an emergency that arises because of something that occurred at the residence but affected a neighbor as was the case several years ago when there was a fire in a home two doors down, but there was no issue on the property and nobody was allowed on the property. If the Fire Department or PG &E have to go through the State Department to receive access to the property there could be severe damage done to existing homes in the neighborhood. The other issue I have is although there have been conditions of approval that have been given to the neighbors by the representative of the Council General they are not enforceable because it's at the discretion of the Council General as to whether or not anybody, any inspection can be made. I think it would be a good faith initiative by the Council General if initial inspections were allowed. If the property were sold to a non-diplomatic enterprise would the Planning Commission mandate inspections that were not allowed previously? Peter Schweikhardt I am at 116 Saint Elmo Way, a couple doors down and across the street. After the meeting last week I reflected on the remarks. There was a remark that said something like it's not clear what the opponents want. I thought perhaps it's true. I looked at my objective as describing concerns rather than prescribing solutions. A second later it appears negative and suggest a view that I don't hold, personally. I do not oppose an increase in the amount of space that the Council General has and the People's Republic of China. I oppose the shape that that proposal has taken so far. Deborah Stein, representing People's Republic of China I want to thank you very much in this last week. The purpose of the continuance was to allow neighbors that were not part of the homeowner's negotiation to review the plan. We gave the plans to the neighbors who testified last week, the ones who gave their address. On Monday, members of the homeowner's association met to review this. I had 12 to 20 phone conversations with Susan from the Homeowner's Association and Mark Campbell who felt that they were not being represented by them. We have consensus and China added a new condition. You will see conditions number 3 adds a condition that China will give 24 contact information to the State Department to ask the State Department to provide to San Francisco's emergency officers for any emergency involving this property. In discussions with Mr. Patton representing the other homeowners, there is a question, what about mandatory DBI inspections? As we heard last week, the City cannot condition issuance of a permit. I want to stress that the People's Republic invited DBI to look at the construction and may do so in the future. There was concern of whether or not this project would increase impacts to the neighborhood. It won't. It is going to house existing employees who are there. The People's Republic will work with good neighbor issues. Leaa Zhang, Project Architect With photos, gave a further review and description of the project. John Bielan I live at 66 Saint Elmo Way with my wife We've lived there for 30 years and live directly across the street from the Chinese Council. They are good neighbors, accommodating and un-obstructive. I think their proposal is reasonable and accommodating to our needs as it can be. We don't oppose the Chinese Council's proposal. David Bisho, President of Home Association and West of Twin Peaks Central Council The west of Twin Peaks Council is against this project because it would violate the City's zoning for RH-1 properties. It would allow more than one dwelling unit per lot and more than one kitchen per lot. It would look like a compound or mid sized hotel with 10 bedrooms and four kitchens and a four-story addition. It would result in a palace look that would intimidate all the houses around it. It is out of character and is not within the Residential Design Guidelines. This would no longer be a single-family house and the coming and going of activities would affect the neighborhood. Robert McCarthy I want to point out how the West of Twin Peaks Council works. Only the neighborhood association that's affected can be allowed to make a motion. Before they were worked out which were acceptable by the homeowner's association, they requested the Twin Peak's Council to oppose the projects, which they did. In this instance they worked long and hard with Mrs. Stein to reach the compromise. The Twin Peaks Council has not had a meeting since then and has not recognized that the organization that made the request is accommodated and supports the projects. It is important for you to note that. The second thing is the question of the enforceability of the CC&R's. This Commission and the Board of Appeals when Commissioner Sugaya served on it and when I did, we were reminded by the Zoning Administrator and the City Attorney that you can't involve yourself with the legal discussions. The fact is this is a unique lot. It's almost an acre. Including this addition the building will occupy only 24% of the lot and 76% of the lot is preserved as open space.

I'm an attorney in San Francisco I wanted to start out by clearing up confusion on what the Center's intensions are. We are not trying to be bad neighbors. The problems that the Center has are twofold. One is a general concern related to the size and scope of the project – whether it is a full EIR or negative declaration. If you look at the photos and drawings, it gives you a good indication of the changes. The Russian Center is adjacent to the project. The current building stands three stories. It has parking on the ground floor and two more stories. The one being built is six stories. The full 65 feet. The current building is not a large building. The new one has to apply for a variance. The photos speak for themselves. It is 20 feet higher than my client's building and larger than anything around it. We have four specific concerns that may be related to the conditional use if we get to that this evening, which relates to my client's property and structural and other concerns of what will happen when construction is going on. On the environmental review – in some ways the two petitions are related. If this were a project that was not the full 65 feet and not larger than allowed under requirements we would not be concerned about the environmental review. The appeal mentions three areas. One is parking. I should note that my clients have been in this building for many years. The Russian Center of San Francisco organization goes back decades and they have been at this location for a long time. They are familiar with the neighborhood and how things changed. There is already a lot of traffic and congestion and events and movement in and out. The project that will be built will increase that. There will be more people in the building. From a small medical building, it will be a medical and residential facility. It's a concern from our client's standpoint because a lot of the people that use our facility can't park three blocks away. There are a significant number of elderly members of the Russian Center. The Russian Center does not have a parking garage. That is an issue. There are environmental impacts in terms of traffic congestion and smog and additional cars. I realize there are two items. On the environmental impact statement, the issue is do we need a full environmental review? Our client's position and concern is that because of the nature of the project more review is needed than described in the report. Vice-President of the Russian Center - [A name was not given] Russian Center is a non-profit organization. We have a day care center; we have children from 2-3 years old. We have dance classes for the children. The Russian Center has been there for 60 years. We have many elderly members, which is the only place they can come. If there is no access to Russian Center there is no way we can help them. We have concerts during the weekend and this is done to help the people who need companionship and need to be with people. Actually, we have a lot of American children studying and learning Russian dances and song. We have a museum of Russian culture. This is a place where people are constantly coming and going. Steve on behalf of Project Sponsor The only question before you is whether the negative declaration is sufficient or an additional EIR is required. I haven't heard anything that was not analyzed. The project site is zoned at 65 feet. We are not succeeding that limit. The building to the east is 65 feet. This neighborhood includes Kaiser and many large institutional buildings. This is a project suitable for this mixed-use neighborhood. The one exception we are seeking is for bulk. The building is U shaped so more of the units have access to light and air. It is not giving us additional square footage. The bulk exception is for the U shape of the building. I wanted to let you know that they analyzed the parking issues. They concluded the project would have 8 vehicle trips in the p.m. peek hour. That's one every 10 minutes. The staff has concerns with how much parking we have – 44 spaces. Half of it is for medical use and the other half is for Sunrise. The residents are not driving. They all have Alzheimers or other impairments. We have over night staff and nursing requirements. There will be 24 hour staffing and a need for parking. The 21 spots for the Sunrise project will take care of that.

Project Sponsor I am an officer with Sunrise Senior Living. I am here to present the project we are proposing at 2420. The property is located in a mid block, almost caddy corner from the Mount Zion Hospital complex. This is going to be a structure for the impaired. Starting with the early stages of Alzheimers. It is three stories with a lobby on the first floor and two additional stories. Sunrise is the largest provider of seniors in the world. We are established in four countries. The property profile we are trying to do is a 15,000 square feet of land a six-story building. 58 units of cognitive impairment care and underground parking. Cognitive impairment is for seniors, particularly those with Alzheimer's. It is a home environment and has trained staff members. We do activities of daily living. If you have relatives that have cognitive impairments you know the difficulties they encounter in waking up in the morning, conducting business, and going to bed. We are low traffic impactor. We don't affect schools, parks or libraries. Our residents are as quiet a neighbor as you can get. We fill an essential community need and fill up housing stock. People are giving up their homes to move into a home like sunrise. In the ten year period from 2000 to 2010 the average population will grow in the United States by 9% across the board. People 85 years and older are going to grow by 34%. The amount of people moving into this area needing assistance with cognitive impairment care is increasing by leaps and bounds. Jim, on behalf of the Russian Center We have actually only four things we would like to add on this. Four concerns we hope will be included in any final approval of the conditional use permit. Some may seem small but are of importance to the Center. One relates to the reality that during 18-21 month of constructions there will be a lot of trucks and people working on the site. The Russian Center would like insurance that their frontage and access to their two entrances on Sutter Street would not be used as a staging area for the construction people. The second point has to do with the excavation that would be a part of this. As mentioned earlier the Russian Center is old.  It has run through renovations a few years ago like a seismic retrofit. There is concern what that would do during this construction. What we request in connection to that is that the project sponsor allow, pay for, or coordinate with an engineer on behalf of the Russian Center to make sure there are no structural problems to the Russian Center. The third thing is a concern of our neighbors. The Center does have a number of events that attract a large number of people. They have a ballroom upstairs and a gym in the basement. Every February they have a Russian festival that draws thousands. They have dances and balls. Steve, on behalf of Project Sponsor The two concerns are under the jurisdiction of other agencies, the Department of Parking and Traffic. I do not see a possibility we would be blocking their entrances. We certainly could agree to that. I think DPT has that jurisdiction. And DBI has jurisdiction over excavation. It is to the benefit of the project sponsor to work with the neighbor. We have been talking to the Russian Center, but it is under the jurisdiction of another agency.

Representing T-Mobile T-Mobile will install four antennas and equipment in the basement and the project would not result in changes to the appearance of the building. The U.S. Bank building was chosen because it's considered a preference 2 location under the city's guidelines and provides the height to meet the coverage and shows the site to be visually un-obstructive. Additionally this site will provide E911 services which allows law enforcement and emergency personal to locate and respond to 911 calls made from T-Mobile phones. Under emissions guidelines under the FCC and San Francisco of Public Health emissions will be less that one percent of the public exposure limit at ground level. RF levels remain below the limit. I would like thanking staff and asking that the Planning Commission uphold the staff's recommendations. John Maymoni I've been a Mission resident for six years. I'm a block from this building. I can see it from my front window. I'm a T-Mobil customer because it's the most affordable plan. I am here today because my phone does not work well in my neighborhood and I think this will help. I think my neighbors and I deserve affordable phone service. I urge the commission to approve this on behalf of neighbors and myself.

name_raw: Harvey Hacker, Architect for the Project Sponsor
comment: I want to thank whoever arranged this little memorial to Sue Bierman. I appreciate it. This project has an interesting story socially. The sponsor is an OB/GYN nurse. She worked in San Francisco long enough so that the present audience might include people who were delivered by her as babies. She lives in a house on Cesar Chaves and bought the project as an investment in the 1980's. She is approaches retirement. She is experiencing mobility problems due to a knee injury, which is affecting her ability to work. Her mobility problems are exacerbated by the steep grade of the block. She has decided to provide for her retirement housing by moving to the flat block of Duncan Street, which includes the subject project. We designed a unit for someone with impaired mobility with elevators and a modify kitchen and bathrooms if needed in the future., The project includes the second unit, which will be the essential key that permits and ordinary working person to afford to build such a house. James Gabbard I live on 27th Street, which is behind the property in question. What appears to me is that the design of the new building is commiserate to the building to the east. That building is out of proportion to the other buildings in the neighborhood. Most are the size of the building to the west of the subject property. I really think to keep the neighborhood flavor as it is, we need a building the size of the one to the west. Silvia I live on Duncan Street and am raising my daughter as a single mother. I oppose the current plan and the staff report's failure to look at the character of Duncan Street. There is a failure of due process. The report doesn't mention that these are earthquake Victorians. The buildings are where the railroad went through. Most are modest with a living space setback from the sidewalk. Most have vegetation in the front. This two-unit building is larger than any single living space or any unit or home on the block It is probably bigger than the combined living space than the two units. None of this is addressed in the staff report. The staff report failed to address community concerns. A number of people made calls and emailed. None of this was described in the staff report. Paul Ordi I encourage you to approve the project. It's not out of scale with the neighborhood and would be a benefit to the owner and the neighborhood. Barbara, property owner I've been a nurse for 30 years and it's hard to believe I will need assistance for myself. I am trying to live as independently as possible. The house is ADA accessible. I am working any angle I can to live independently and hope you approve it. Mary I think you should approve her project so this lovely, beautiful lady can be a productive part of San Francisco, which she loves an adores. Pamela Robins I am speaking in favor of the project.

Susanna Susoeff I need to understand a little better first before I make my comments. What does the affordability requirement mean? If I an understanding you correctly, certain variances granted would have to do with me providing the second unit as affordable housing to someone else. My project is on 1130 Harris Street. I'm the owner of the property. This property has been in my family for 75 years or more. For the entire time it's been a two unit dwelling. The City did not reflect that. Many years ago I don't know if it was required but the property was used as a second unit for rental. I'm coming for parking on August 23 rd . This has been a yearlong project to get this put through for various reasons. But my main aim is to restore the property to a two-unit residence as it has been used for many years. The restriction that's been, I need a variance for is that there's an additional off-street parking and the property has an area in front of the lower unit, which is the second one that a car fits in and that's how it was used in my family for all those years. But by definition, to me, affordable housing means somebody has to pay more so someone else can pay less. Having a really strict restriction and not taking this case by case or allowing fluctuation and discretion would mean I'm the one that has to pay more so somebody can pay less. I believe that's unfair and discriminatory to me and limits my usage of this property. This is true all over San Francisco but particularly on my block. Making things more restrictive discourages people from acting in a legal manner. Many people don't want to go through the effort and expense that's incurred in doing it legally. It's expensive and may not go through so a lot of people may do it illegally. Brett Gladstone I'm not representing anyone. I don't have a variance on this. Keep in mind clients come to my law firm and they are in a situation where they live in a unit that's illegal and they don't discover it until they were doing improvements or bought it and didn't know they were illegal. They have to get a parking variance to legalize what they are in or be kicked out. There are a lot of circumstances like that. I wonder how in that instance you would make an affordability requirement to the people that are already living there. I have concern about the fact we spent a year analyzing what the inclusionary requirements should be if building 5 [units] and over and sometimes we are dealing with building only 2-4 units. If we add affordable units to 2-4 we have an inclusionary requirement of 20 or 30 percent. I'm wondering if we have a strong policy to keep families in the City. Mr. Badiner mentioned the in-laws that were moving it and couldn't afford it. If there were an affordability requirement this would be an example of how that runs counter to that policy. We need to look at it carefully. If we do it, I hope we have written criteria. As a lawyer, it's hard to advise people when we are not sure what's going to happen at a hearing and years in advance of buying the property. If I don't know the rules, God help them. I'm looking forward to a further discussion of this. Deborah Stein I actually never represented a parking variance nor do I particularly want to do so in the future. I am always interested in the rational of the policies and ask the Zoning Administrator if you could clearly articulate the nexus and the affordability housing. Sue Hestor I want to encourage Mr. Badiner to think along these lines. I've been to housing discussions and they discuss what in-law units are; at least the trust of it. I lived in an in-law for 16 years on 20 th Street. They had no parking in the entire building. They tend to be more affordable because of their natural nature. We have to keep struggling to maximize affordability. I agree with Mr. Badiner, it helps to have the criteria down because it will help him think through things. And the exception for a real family - that should do the public good and encourage that. At the same time if your mother doesn't move in and you rent it out to people and if the sky is the limit on the rental it's not such good policy. We are getting a lot of condos that sell for a million dollars. We are getting extremely few small rentals. They should be disbursed throughout the City, not all in affordable housing and South of Market. I lived in the Castro in an in-law and it was created in the 30's for the son when he moved downstairs from this parents. This is something to think about. The affordable housing community should be encouraged to participate in this discussion.

Representing family members on this project. My sister, she has been living there since she bought it. She wanted to occupy the space on the ground floor and turn it into a salon to create employment for herself. This also allows her the flexibility of taking care of her kids while running the business. The premises are not tenant occupied. We are giving up the one parking space to open the business.

on behalf of Project Sponsor The building was constructed in 1913. The merger will bring the building closer into conformance with its original construction. I agree with the Planning Department there is no dispute to the guideline. The purpose of the merger is to provide additional space to the owners. Removal of the unit would remove owner occupied housing. That unit was a rental until the tenant left. Since that time the owners used that unit as storage. It will bring the building into proportion to the density. Property Owner I own the property with my sister Stephanie who has occupied the proposed merged unit for the past year. I feel there are positive aspects to the merger. I feel this is good for the North Beach Telegraph Hill Community and my neighbors who are in support of the project to ease the density in the neighborhood and bring back families in the North Beach. This is a good thing for my tenants their building is small and it's close nit group. They want to keep it that way. I feel this is good for the city because I'm proposing to bring the building back to its original intent of four units like the units up and down the block. All the buildings were built by the same builder. The building I own was chopped up over the years.] I plan on being in the neighborhood for a long time. I would like my children to live in the area and attend schools near by. I will not rent out the unit. The merger of the unit will be good for my family and neighbors and tenants of the city. Stephanie I currently live in Seattle and I use this as office storage space. Prior to my brother's engagement we shared the space. I don't want this to be permanent. I would love to see my brother have a family here and I can transition into the city. I wanted to attest to the fact that I have been using this but I'm in support of everything he said and the family aspect of it. [No name given] I am the fiancé. I think it's important that this project is considered very thoughtfully. This is a man who has grown up worked in the city lived here his whole life. Some of that is lacking in the area. The homegrown group gets forgotten about. We want to have a family and don't want to move to the suburbs like everyone else. It think it would be nice to look down the street and see children instead of groups of people yelling down the street at each other about parking.
