But the plan is translated into zoning and community improvement planning. I urge you to have additional meetings besides the public hearings where the details can be worked out. We need to put things in that are not there now that modify some things and move fast at the same time. Hopefully in a couple of months we could have this tied up. Let's get some of these things like affordable housing and the community benefit's plan nailed down more tightly and better. Sue Hestor Looking at your scheduled, hearing number 2 is a killer hearing. One of the unfortunate thing this Commission does is call up the entire calendar. Items 1-6 the only time the public has time to comment is a one three-minutes opportunity on areas on Market Street. There are huge differences in the communities on Market Street and huge difference in the topic items. If you are going to do things right commit yourself that each item is called separately, show you don't' really cheat the public. I think you need to have serious discussions on the backside impact on Imrket Street. You need to see the scale of what is there.  That includes photos. You don't have that now unless you got different things than I did. You really need to see what is the impact where you have large buildings on Market Street and small possibly historic buildings to the rear. Those are the issues I have dealt with over my cases. There needs to be appropriate attention paid to the non-Haze Valley part of this. I don't think it is unusual to say you maybe should have a little bit of explanation on issues particular to neighborhoods that are not the core. Marilyn Amini I feel it is good you will mail to every resident that will be impacted. I'm wondering, will the mailed notice be neighborhood specific? That touches on the question as to how you are going to organize discussions. As Sue mentioned, there is a huge difference in communities and how they are impacted. If you will communicate in your notice area specifically and how those particular areas will be impacted, people will feel they are given adequate notice. Gary Weiss, President, Upper Market Association, EDPA, the CDB and Merchants of Market and Castro. I want to speak as a small business owner in the Castro. I wish I could have participated earlier on. None of the groups I am affiliated with were aware. The main point is parking. We don't feel the point of view of Eureka Valley residents were included.  We need more parking not less. The small businesses in the area are suffering from lack of parking spaces. When large projects are in the works regular information forums are a tool to educating the public. This one, despite the neighbors in the eastern end of the plan, is lacking. We are asking for a delay. This will ensure a large element of the plan area will have the ability to review the plan and input its views.

It was nice seeing those cities, all of which I think are bigger than ours. One of the things we struggle with in the city is the compactness of the city and the interface between tall buildings on one street and there rear yards of the house on the other. They are about to come before the Commission with Market/Octavia. What I didn't see and which we had more of is how to fit the contexts in when you have lots 25 feet wide or 50 feet wide and no big green space around the high rise. They are literally up against the house behind them. It would be nice to struggle through those principles and not have the Boston, Chicago tall buildings where you have the abstract discussions – which are nice – but you deal with the  real world  every Thursday. We all do. If we don't sort it out with Market/Octavia, I don't think we ever will. Unidentified Speaker I was glad to see the presentation and the training going on. Some of those things are missing in the department. What I want the department to think about in green buildings is they have to be in a green block. It has to have transit. We have been patting ourselves on the back by creating the new residential neighborhoods like Rincon Hill and say that everyone is going to walk. They are not. Rincon is a hill. You have to walk up it and we don't have MUNI on that list. Why is it MUNI has had cuts in their service; cut their lines? How can we justify reducing parking and doing green buildings and not at the same time mass transit? MUNI capacity was added to Market Street but it wasn't added to Mission Street. The [number] 14 is a pit. I tell you now; you will have problems on Market Street because people won't be able to get on in all the areas. It's over capacity.

The reason I am here is I was hoping to have Commissioner Hughes here to speak to the issues raised. I am not sure why an informational presentation. I think there is a decision that should be make relative, in light of the presentation the AIA made I think these are concerns that this Commission is taking seriously. In deed if there is redesign, hopefully it does conform and fit with the direction that this Commission seems to be taking. Sue Hestor I want to point out a context issue. This is Harrison Street between Third and Second Streets, right north of the freeway. It's not an attractive walking environment. We are missing the opportunity to look at the context when we do these projects piecemeal like this. This is like an offshoot of Rincon Hill, down two blocks. It's not going to be a pleasant place to walk. They have little street trees in front. Harrison is encroached to the freeway. Cars come down it at a slip. It's a big accident intersection at Harrison and Fourth. When are we going to decide we need to look at what is the context of this site for housing? We are approving a lot of conversions. At a certain level it is easy to do in the North of Market because it is transit [rich]. Do you know what Harrison Street feels to a pedestrian and how isolated you will feel from the north when you come down Fourth Street? It's long blocks and bleak. Are we going to pay attention to that? Put trees in front. That will not solve the entire problem. It may make it worse by darkening the street. It's not an attractive area for pedestrians.

Project Sponsor representative [did not give name]

What we are talking about is a benefit that's conferred on the Sponsor by the Planning Code only if they agree to put the BMR units on site.

By doing that they get a bump in the floor area ratio.

They picked up a little bit of storage space in the basement and a small amount of residential space.

It's to make use of the floor area, which would be dead space in the building.

 This conditional use is encourage by the Planning Code in order to encourage the Sponsor to have the BMR units located on site as opposed to paying an in lieu fee.

Jim Salinas

We have stated this position in the past, we believe the greatest benefit to the city is to have the below market rate units on site as opposed to off site.

 We are not in agreement with in lieu fees.

We believe the City doesn't gain anything by it and the City benefits greater when those below market units are on site.

section: CONSIDERATION OF ITEMS PROPOSED FOR CONTINUANCE
comment: Representing the Project Sponsor on item 10. There is no basis for continuance. The building application is separate from any matters involved in litigation between the builder and the neighbor. If the requestor of the continuance had made their request in a timely fashion they would have heard that it was not granted and would have been prepared. This permit holder has been waiting a long time. It is a minor permit application.  There is little substance. Staff is here and prepared to move forward. I don't believe we should take more staff or commission time with a matter as minor as this. I think we should hear it today and get it over with.

We live in a beautiful city. People come to enjoy the architecture and things that give the City character. I think in general this ordinance may be a good idea. As I read it, or the language I've read so far there are ambiguities. As a person that might apply for a garage permit, I am concerned. It would be nice if the language could be clarified. For example, what gives a building architectural merit? How will the homeowner approach this? The other comment I heard raised was consideration of whether the interior of the space will be altered. You do have to do modification to the front room otherwise you couldn't get the clearance to get your ramp down. I would question what relevance that has to preserving the exterior architectural part of the building. Nobody will come through your house to see the interior as long as it complies with the codes for livable space. I am concerned about the language regarding bay windows. Any alterations to bay windows [shouldn't] be prevented because I rarely see a garage put in where some alteration hasn't been required unless the building is high enough off the ground that you can drive in and it wouldn't create an obstacle. Joe Butler I was here a couple of weeks ago and in looking at the revised draft of the bulletins, some of the things that were mentioned on the September 14 meeting are not here. The issue of affordability, which was discussed by many of the speakers; tenant displacement. I'm wondering if the full commission would like to see some consideration of those items.

Project Sponsor [did not state name]

We will keep it one family with the kids in San Francisco.

This is what your recommendation is – to keep them in San Francisco.

This project is a small 500 square foot addition.

Our main concern is the blockage of sunlight to our kitchen, which is on the south side and there is a bay window that sticks out. We will have minimal light in the kitchen if the proposed project is approved. The sponsor has placed a balcony in that area. It's a clear view to our kitchen and [will cause a] severe lack of privacy and it did not meet our concern to the sunlight in the kitchen. I recommended alternative suggestions. Because the residents concern is not a garage, they can build in that area. They don't have to build a second floor. We want an adequate setback that doesn't block the light from our kitchen. Most kitchens are designed for the most sunlight to enter. We will have minimal if the proposed project is approved. George Sang, Representing the Project Sponsor I have known the family for more than 20 years. They have been living there for 15 years. All these years they have wanted to have a house like everyone else on the block. The house now is less than a thousand square feet. They want another 600 square feet. We feel that we are not asking anything that's not in the neighborhood. Yu Chi Chin When they bought the house, they had not much money. Now that the children are grow-up, she would like to make her house a safe environment to get out of her car to go to the new addition.

representing Dennis McCarthy, DR requestor I live in back to the south of the subject property. The subject property is adjacent to this property, which has been sold. The former owner signed a letter of support; these owners have not signed a letter of support. We object to the proposed three-story building because it's not compatible with the other two-story buildings. This project will affect the adjacent houses.  It is going farther and higher.  It is going 13 feet deeper; and 17 feet deeper to the buildings to the north. We proposed  a two-story building in accordance with their proposal. We proposed a 2-story building.  Downstairs, which has a room that they call an exercise room but looks like an illegal in-law or second unit has a second entrance and a direct connection to the garage that can be converted to an illegal unit by moving this door and moving that door there.  We propose that can be a bedroom and the staircase can descend straight down. We propose the bedroom they renamed a study remain a bedroom; and we propose dining room remain as the dining room and the rear bedroom become a bedroom and bathroom. They will achieve their goal of three bedrooms, four bathrooms with a two-story building. It can be achieved much cheaper than a three-story building and we feel this is a win/win proposal. Karen Mitchell I live on 26 th  Avenue behind the subject property and a little to the north. My topic is the height of the project. The height of the three-story building is not compatible with the neighboring of two-stories in the RH-1 District. The plan to put on a front deck is incompatible with any of the houses Deli Young, Project Sponsor Dennis McCarthy filed DR and he is not here. Karen, I don't believe, lives within the 150-foot radius. In October 2004 and September 2005, we had our first and second out reach meeting to discuss concern about blocked views. On December 22, 2005 we had a third out reach meeting at the request of certain neighbors that claimed their concerns were not being addressed. To address Sheila and Lucy on how the property will fit in the character of the other houses -- these flats are made out of a mix of two and three story houses. The purpose of the front setback incorporate my plans to minimize the impact on the character of the existing block. For Sheila McCarthy concern how the property will affect her privacy and amount of light -- the current subject property plan sufficiently addresses her concerns pertaining to her house. To address Rose and Margaret, they didn't have concerns on how the property will block the ocean view.  It was indicated that we were in our right to expand our property. Karen is outside the 150-foot boundary criteria. The Meeting was adjourned when no one had additional questions or concerns. Today, we are here at the hearing of Discretionary Review because a neighbor is complaining that his concerns regarding my project have not been addressed. The trend you may see is that every time we have a meeting to discuss the concern of the project they come back with more issues to delay the project. I do not think there is anything we can do to satisfy the neighbor.  In other words, they don't want us to build in any manner. I do have a letter of support from the neighbor's house that was sold. Larry I am a 35 years resident on 27 th  Avenue. Much the neighbors to my north have three-story buildings. [Showing a picture] This project is almost on the sidewalk and blocks a significant amount of my light and air. I want to note that the Wong's project does not and I see no reason why it shouldn't go forward.

name_raw: All the paperwork I have seen
comment: All the paperwork I have seen it looks like a lawful project. I don't see how one person can stop another person from their project as long as they follow the guidelines. These neighbors are good neighbors.  They have bent over backwards to conform to the laws of San Francisco and keep to the shape and look of our neighborhood. I am asking you to approve their project. Paul Nazaler I live across the street from the proposed project. I have no problems with this project. It conforms to the Planning Commission and zoning. I hope you will pass an opportunity not to discretionary review it and will approve it. Don Wong, Project designer My brother and sister-in-law asked me to do this project three years ago. Had I known this would happen, I would not drawn the plans up. I did not know it would take three years. We are not talking about building a mansion. They have two kids. I worked with Michael Smith at Planning.  We complied with everything he asked us to do.
Unless you have questions for me, we will await your pleasure

name_raw: Joel Yodowitz, on behalf of Project Sponsor
comment: We want to take over two storefronts on Union Street. Keep the exterior with a new coat of paint and original signage. This proposal will be good for San Francisco residents and the health and convenience of the City by allowing people a full service health club and gym. If would be good for local businesses because it will generate pedestrian traffic on Union Street and promote patronage of near by businesses. No parking is required by the code. We expect most people to walk or take public transit to the gym. The person requesting that this be taken off the consent calendar is a competitor of a very small palates studio. We don't compete with yoga or palates studios. Crunch has weights. It doesn't offer personalized studio type classes like the person who wants this taken off the consent calendar. The concern that Crunch would affect their business is over stated and it shouldn't be a fear. Daron Press I would be the co-owner of the studio that Joel is referring to. My wife and I own Mercury Fitness focusing on palates. It has come to our attention that Crunch is opening a block and a half away from us. There is a focus on small group classes there. There is a Crunch three blocks up the street on Polk and Union. 1500 feet away. For me, I find it hard to believe that crunch would want to open up another so close to another gym. The Union Street [association] prides itself on supporting businesses and tries to stop saturation of formula businesses retail or personal services. This is not an added benefit to the community. There are many fitness facilities in that district that offer the same classes they offer. Parking will be an issue. Our bottom line as well as other small fitness centers will be adversely affected by this place opening up two blocks away. I am asking to protect the small fitness centers by taking their application for conditional use and removing it from the calendar, which we are doing now, and oppose it. 1)

Substantial neighborhood organizations have requested that the Supervisors file of improvements of Eastern Neighborhoods be brought back to the Commission. The legislation sets forth and establishes major planning policy. It's a Better Neighborhood Planning and Implementation legislation that was not recommended by the Committee. You have been told it was not before you and Planning testified in your behalf at the only two Board committee hearings held on the matter. The legislation sets precedence in that it legitimizes its task force concept by codifying it as with the West SOMA Citizens Planning Task Force. The prototype West SOMA Task is politically appointed. Its planning department for planning plans expertise rests in the Planning Department As acknowledged before the Board of Supervisors, the Planning Department acknowledged functioning in advisory capacity to the West SOMA Citizen's Planning Task Force. Important presidencies are being established with this particular piece of legislation, which is up for its final on Tuesday. We strongly request that you bring this back. You have the right to. It's major planning policy. You shouldn't be left out of the loop. There should not be a short circuit to not have you consider these items of major importance. The Brown Act allows you to direct staff to place the item on a future agenda. That is something you could do as action, which is appropriate at the time of Public Comment. I'm pleading. President Alexander Linda, can we send a letter to the Board of Supervisors asking they send this for [our] comment? Commission Secretary Avery It will go out over your signature. None

Representing T-Mobile T-Mobile is intending to install antennas above the Sprint and Cingular antennas It will not interfere with the church. It's considered a preference one location under the City's guidelines. It provides adequate height and visually is un-obstructive. Our report concludes under the emission's guidelines of the San Francisco Public Health Department and FCC that exposure levels are below the [minimum] levels and are less than two percent of the public exposure limit. This installation will allow coverage in the surrounding residential neighborhood. It allows law enforcement and emergency personal to locate and respond to 911 calls from cell phones. A meeting was held and five people attended the meeting.  They were given a brief presentation of the project.  There was no opposition.

Project Engineer The project Sponsor has the support from neighboring business. They are willing to consider a three-year conditional approval of the lot or sooner of the site development plan for approval and implementation. I have a letter from McDonalds [the land owner] and we have a gentleman here to speak on this. Drew Nash I work in the Real Estate Division of McDonalds. We are in the process of negotiating for the re-development of the site. We are working with the franchise at that location in the system to attain an agreement to develop the existing site. We are looking at a two to five year program for re-developing the site. In 1994 it was approved for 144 low-income units for senior citizens. We are looking at a comparable mixed-use development to go in that location. [No name was given] The parking lot next door to McDonalds is fenced up and at night is broken in by the homeless. All they want to do is fix it up and give revenue for the City and parking to the neighborhood. The schools love the idea of the parking.  They can park and be safe instead of it being dark and abandoned. The Commission should approve this as interim parking for two to three years. [Name was not understood] – Liberty Management I believe one of Mr. Li's concerns is that McDonalds Corporation will take their time in terms of starting the project because the developer is coming in from Liberty Park Management. The monthly rent is something close to $3,000 a month. As indicated, it would be a good project in terms of providing a good parking place for people in the neighborhood and for teachers and parents coming to pick up kids from school. If I had my kid in that school I wouldn't want my kid to hang around people using drugs. If you walk the lot you will see needles and garbage in the lot. Even though it is fenced, people get in.

I want to address one absence here under height and bulk; siteing and massing. At all times when we are measuring how tall buildings are, how big they look and how big a bulk to you, you are looking at whether or not it's on a hill, which could make a four-story building look like a seven-story building. You have to address this section. I would like to have that added. I would say that I revised the language of Mr. Nikita's presentation in the case of the corner building he showed early on where the massing is on a corner and you see two facades. It was gracious of him to imply that a variance be considered so it would complete the block face. Then what? A wall everywhere? I don't know if we want that. Corner buildings are a special case. If you have a requirement for rear yard open space there is more coverage allowed by the code. I think it's gratuitous to say to close up an open space viewed to the street. Joe Butler I'm an architect in the city. I think it's a nice presentation, if you are not skilled in the terms or language you would use around town and look and see if you can find examples that do please and delight. I think uniformity and exception could be the 12 th pairing, and in some ways it goes to Maryann's comments in the building law and do we want the entire block wrapped. The exception with the block face can be an inviting and delightful thing. When you are in a part of Russian Hill and the buildings make the street wall in a strong way and you come to a smaller building with gardens and trees, that exception can be something pleasing and delightful.

DR Requestor All vital reports that should be required on a project of this size and scale are lacking. Instead, I discover that a concern of Art Aguilar, former employee of DBI, granted a person the most specious environmental exemption. When I sought this hearing it behooves the commission to [question] Art Aguilar because untoward activity and deal making are part and parcel of business as usual at that Bureau. The fact that the Mayor had to order an FBI raid on that Bureau the very day and hour of my submitting my DR is& All studies and reviews, which now include a soil report, were not forth coming from Michael Smith. Had he done the necessary documents and my fears of imminent death and destruction [were addressed], my neighbors and I would not be here. My imminent death and destruction scenario was spelled out in my DR application submitted to Smith. This was five days prior. Undermining the stability of the wall or grant sequoia& The wind tunnel necessary& May the commission's common sense prevail before the winds do in its absence of necessary analysis that is germane to the project that caused me consternation& Douglas Gillies and an obscure absentee partner of 461 Chenery named de la Cruz, if they exist, and the contractors of record be held financially responsible to whose homes are damaged. The Gillies are required to post a $3 million dollar bond for ten years from date of construction for the sequoia to be removed [language is not clear]; service elevator, lift garages or crane hoisted over 61 [foot] roof; new tree of same variety to be installed and crater left in yard; the new sequoia over Gilly roof; all destroyed neighboring homes to be built to code. In support of DR [name was not given] I live across the street from the proposed construction site. My concern is parking. In front of 461 there is space for two cars to park now. They are proposing a garage to go in. That will probably remove both off street parking places. They are proposing a two-lift garage in this small building. I think in theory a lift garage is a good idea. In practicality, if there are two lifts, it's a multi-unit building that will house several people. There will be at least four people and they will all have cars. This is not practical at all. I ask the commission to review this and look at that.  And study it because that is not practical to do this. If they build that type of building with those units and have that many tenants in the building, it is due diligence to the owners to provide off-street parking.

Representing the Project Sponsor We are prepared to address the issue raised in the DR request. This is a project consistent with the neighborhood character and guidelines. This is a code complying project. It will add one new housing unit and add 4 more parking spaces to the building where there are presently none. We propose a ten- foot curb cut to get to the parking spaces. One on-street space will be lost.  There will be a net of three spaces added to the neighborhood. You heard from the [DR requestor] that this project was approved in violation of the California Environment Act. This project was exempt as an addition to a single family home because of it's height. It's less than 40 feet; there was no need for a shadow concern. The main complaint is that the vertical addition and the excavation building to the rear yard will damage the tree and pose a risk to the house next door. I would like to point out as far as we know there was no evidence submitted before today. I haven't seen anything from an arborist that there will be damage to the tree. Under California Law, a property [owner] has a right to remove branches or root if it is a reasonable matter. All work will be in due regard for the safety of the neighbor and if possible, without damage to her tree. As Mr. Smith said, we agreed to hire an arborist to evaluate whether or not there will be damage to the tree. If there will be damage, we will replace it with a tree more appropriate to a dense urban environment. Legally, maintaining the tree is the DR applicant's responsibility. The tree is covered in ivy. There are brown leaves on it and it is pushing over the fence. It is a maintenance problem for the sponsor. And it is really something that we could ask the DR applicant to fix, but we agreed to replace the tree if we cause damage to it.

Executive Director of Services We are the project sponsors of 275 10 th  Street.  It is 135 units for homeless adults.  We expect to open in 2008. Our organization has been present in the SOMA since 1894, when our predecessor organization opened a center for immigrants on 2 nd  Street. We have been located on 8 th  Street, which moved there in 1941. We rebuilt that as residences in 1994 and moved to Howard in 1983, and we opened the community house as residents for homeless families. We provide permanent housing with support services for homeless adults and children. This is consistent with the city's ten-year plan to end homelessness and it is key to supportive housing. We are asking your review of the Environmental Impact Report and your approval of the report as accurate and adequate. This is a project in which we partner with the Department of Public Health for services as we do at other sites. We are partnering with the Mayor's Office of Housing. We think it is in the spirit of the SOMA neighborhoods. Bob Hermann, Architect I would like to open by assuring you that the site for this affordable housing does not have a single tree on it.  That may simplify matters. [Laughter] As I understand the purpose is to give you an accurate and broad-brush explanation of what the proposal is about. I'm not going to get into interest detail. I will be happy to answer questions if you have any. [Using slides/renderings, showed the proposed project, its design, and how it functions.] [The Commission President reminded him that the focus of this hearing was to address the environmental document.]

The letter that the Director referred to that was sent to the Board of Supervisors apparently took a while to be delivered. Because here you have 140 people in the Department and a request was made on Thursday by the Commission that is going to be acted upon one way or another by the following Tuesday. The letter gets to the Board on the afternoon on Monday and only gets there because someone in the community hand carries it to the Board of Supervisors. When do you know [think] your request would have been considered if it had been done through the normal distribution process? You need to ask yourself and consider carefully the issue that was raised earlier about how much time does the Commission have to respond to a referral from the Board of Supervisors? The whole battle here is not all about property rights or who's building something and blocking someone's view. The Coalition is coming back and speaking to you about your rights and authority to be exercised under the City Charter to have on all planning issues and matters before you. Here, you have an effort being made by the Board of Supervisors to basically, push everything under the Administrative Code. How long does it take Mr. Sider for the Department to review this? We have is the Department gets 90 days because it is referred by the Board of Supervisors according to the Planning Code. What we are trying to protect is the rights and the authority and responsibility of the Planning Commission to conduct its business so the public can proceed to help and provide the support in the public process. Ms. Espanola Jackson I want to speak on the Supervisor's meeting that occurred last Tuesday. This was without Committee reference. That is how you get things done behind your back. Because they did not want it to be hard by you or the community. It was item 31. I know because one of the residents that was there had to be pulled by Supervisor Maxwell. And it was read. And you know what it was? It has to do with eminent domain on 2 acres of land. Please, do not be passing on things that have not been heard by the community or you because she says so. You got the responsibility. It's not up to her to make the decision for you and the entire City. Tony Kelly I wanted to speak in reference to the comments of the others about what happened on Tuesday. It seems that this is a property issue. No one can do anything before talking to Planning first. It was done properly. It is for the Supervisors to consider. It was discussed at the Planning Commission. Yet there are individuals from the Coalition of San Francisco Neighborhoods that say it's not enough. My association is a member of the Coalition. It was not brought to my association or brought to anyone in the Eastern Neighborhoods. If they have a campaign of their own, it's these three individuals doing it themselves. They don't represent the Coalition or the Southern or Eastern Neighborhoods who need this legislation and more. Francisco DA Costa I belong to the San Francisco Coalition of Neighborhoods. I participated in all the planning workshops regarding the Eastern Neighborhoods. This matter came before the Coalition as an emergency, because that way it was sneaked in. It was in a bad way. All I'm saying if you want to bring certain types of amendments, or certain types of policies linked to the Administrative Code, then we need to have a public discussion. These types of policies are sneaked in on a fast track and sent to the Board of Supervisors. We, the constituents, do not have a say. It is wrong for people to say this doesn't pertain to the Eastern Neighborhood. We have the right to introduce any type of amendments and legislations through our process within the Coalition. No name Thank you for your action requesting an important plan on land use issues authored by Supervisors be sent back to you. I am sad by the Board of Supervisors action on last Tuesday, in response to your request for return of file 61206. I feel in particular that Supervisor McGoldrick's remarks were questionable. He said that the planning issue comes back for your hearing and response. That was the Eastern Neighborhood's policy and rezoning and community planning matter. Supervisor McGoldrick reported to all Supervisors present, that the Planning Director and Zoning Administrator were in support of the community legislation. And on Tuesday, in his comments, he implied that your [the Commission's] request was not appropriate. Judy Berkowitz I would like to tell you that the Coalition for San Francisco Neighborhoods unanimously passed two resolutions at our meeting on Tuesday. The second one I think that you have not been briefed on was that we urged the veto of the ordinance to the Mayor and that the Board refer it to the Planning Commission for your comment and review. D. GENERAL

It's important that this Commission maintained vigilance where the PDR issue is concerned. There are businesses that want to come to the City, but feel the city is business unfriendly. This Commission has the ability to change that perception and make sure we are earning a livelihood. Ms. Espanola Jackson The question I want to ask is whether or not you, the Commissioners, weighed in on the proposed earthquake plans that has been put together? Did you all discuss it with that committee about what would happen if there were an earthquake? I have a concern because they have here that staging areas would be set up for emergency supplies and equipment at AT&T Park, Candlestick Park, and Pier 48. It frightens me. People do not know that area. Candlestick Park - the whole area was built on landfill that used to be the bay. Francisco Da Costa What I came to talk about was I know the Director of Planning is going to leave us and hopefully we get a good Director. I am also concerned about the Zoning Administrator, and I am also concerned about the role of our Chief Planner. I hope that when the new Director comes, that we have a better vision. What I have been saying is, we need a sound housing element. The other thing we need is the transportation document by the Planning Department not the Transportation Authority. Calvin Welch I want to speak to the reference made by the Economic Development Committee and this Commission regarding the Housing Element target, the affordability target. If we force compliance with the Housing Element in the Eastern Neighborhood planning process we will be increasing the inclusionary zone requirement. For some reason this Department continues to only measure new construction in meeting the affordability goals even though the Housing Element of 2004 recognized acquisition and rehab especially in producing affordable units in San Francisco. The Housing Element ignored acquisition and rehab as a factor. This factor is cited as a reason. It is impossible to meet the affordability goals without them. Tony Kelly Speaking more about hysteria surrounding the Maxwell resolution, which is not a controversial resolution. Why it causes this reaction by the Planning Commission? It is following the planning of the City. It has been said before that the resolution is attempting an end run around planning. Everything in the resolution about housing, about arts and opens space is actually included in the City's General Plan, which has had public and Commission review. Your job as commissioners is not to adjudicate planning issues, it is to implement the City's General Plan.
[Introduced his organization and gave out newsletters.] None

I want to focus my time on changes I think need to be made that deal with your operations. In the golden years, 10 years ago, the Planning Commission did "Intent to Approve" resolutions rather than amend on the fly. That allowed them to have the exact language they approved and the exact plans. When that's the case, it's easy to make an appeal because you know what the resolution and the project are. At the same time, the State law requirement allowed appeals to the Board of Supervisors. The Planning Commission changed their practice and said, we are macho and we will amend on the fly. What has happened is that resolutions are not available sometimes for weeks. I have had them not available for six weeks after the action. Therefore, when you appeal a project like I have done, you don't' have an approval resolution. You don't have the approval resolution on the environmental document. The time lines are tight for an appeal. An appeal has to state your grounds for appeal. If you don't know how the project is modified, it might affect the environmental appeal and you are up a creek without a paddle. What I am suggesting that this Commission do is either recommend changing the deadline for appeals to when the final resolution on the environmental and project approval is complete. That is when the clock starts running, or you should change your practice. Robert Pender I don't think the public has enough opportunity or knowledge of when you cut down on the opportunity for the general public. I think we need more openness. I would like to add my voice to making the procedures more open and more accessible to us ordinary citizens, who will live with the results. Steve Williams CEQA is our main tool for protecting historical resources in the City. Without that and the procedure to use that in an effective way, we are really lost. Almost always the Department will issue a Categorical Exemption for those projects. Without a procedure to use to appeal the Department's decisions as well as the developer's project, we are lost. I think that this a bad legislation for much of the reasons you just heard. Is it intentionally to make it difficult for neighbors and people in the public to bring the appeals or understand they need to bring these appeals? This legislation sets up short deadlines, 10, 30 and 90 days in a situation where we have no deadlines until the project is under way or the permits are issued. John Bardis The whole criteria by which legislation is done - as we have seen by looking at the end run being done with the Administrative Code - with the plan process and so forth is a similar axiom that's referred to where there are three criteria for making a real estate decision which is location, location, and location. In City Hall there are three criteria for legislation: process, process, process. You have here another kind of process issue where people who are covered in trying to introduce modifications that in effect take away the rights of people to emphasize not for their personal information but for your own edification.

My husband and I are the requestors. We live next door and have lived there for 22 years and were happy until the time we had the backyard flooded because of heavy rain. It's never a pleasant experience to wade in cold water in winter to drain buckets of water. In June, when we found the owners plan on extending 20 feet in the rear, we were very upset. If our yard were as long as theirs, we would have no problem with that length. Unfortunately our yard is short. The project would leave not enough space for good air to circulate. In order to allow our neighbors to expand and to have less negative impact on us the best solution would be to modify the project plan. We suggest two modifications: 1) setback the south wall 6-1/2 feet on both levels. This will allow them to keep their existing door downstairs and the door upstairs; 2) keep the length to 14 feet. This length matches the adjacent property's extension and is in tune with the neighborhood. With this extension the project owner would have a huge master bedroom of 14 x 18 and 1⁄2 feet. If the project is not setback on the ground floor, we would feel devastated from our second floor window. We would look at a wall and a dirty roof. Jeffrey Chin The sponsor is willing to listen to the recommendations of the staff. We were willing to reduce it, give it a 3 foot setback on the south side and setback 5 feet as staff requires and install windows on the second floor six feet from the floor in accordance with staff's request. The project sponsor needs more space. The belief is that the addition is not taking up all of the space he could take. The issue they have with the flooding on the side that's a structural issue and has nothing to do with the planning and the plans being proposed. The construction will be done so the rain comes out of the rear of the house. Mike Chan My brother, my sister, and my parents have lived in this house since the 90's. It is a 2-bedroom house. We were cramped. Now that I am married and have a baby with us, we are even more cramped for space. We can't afford to buy anything in the City.

Our family came to San Francisco in the 1880;s and they fell in love with this country and wanted to stay. They struggled for many years and during World War II they lost everything they had to build it back again. It was with great sacrifices and work and dedication that they are able to build themselves to the level they are and be able to purchase a home in San Francisco. They were not allowed to rent or buy homes in certain areas of the City back then. I don't think it was City law. It was exclusionary. A social injustice. They chose that home because it's a peaceful place. We will loose our light and view and privacy on that side of the house if their project is able to build up on the third level. I wish we could some how figure a way out where we could both be happy. I suggested they build in the front of their house, so they can get the same new area in their home, as if they built the penthouse there and it will not interfere with my view, privacy, light and space. No name Former speaker is my sister and we both live in the house. I would like to say the decision to come forward was not an easy one for her or me. It was really difficult for us. We are not confrontational people and we struggled with this. We didn't want to cause waves or step on anyone's toes. We really did try to consider whether we could live with this addition so close to us. The proposed extension is tall - almost 13 feet vertical elevation of the existing structure. It would block a good portion of the direct light entering our bedroom and block entirely our view of Lincoln Park Golf Course. In addition, we would be loosing the privacy we enjoy in our home and backyard with the neighbors boarding our property. In San Francisco the open space and privacy is relished and it's a treasure. Jonathan, Architect for the project Gave a brief description of the project. Michael Saksteder, Project Sponsor We like our neighborhood and neighbors and tried hard to be sensitive to everybody's needs, while still getting what we thought we could get out of what we think is a modest project. We were sensitive to our neighbor's needs in the planning and design of the project and in the approval process of the project. We oriented the project so it was angled such that it didn't block the views of our neighbor. We did not build it as large as it could have been because we didn't want to disrupt or impact the neighborhood. In the approval process we tried to make sure we got the entire neighborhood input we could. It's at a point now where it's significantly delaying our project to be asking for input on the project when we provided opportunity for that input some significant time ago. I also think that the privacy concern that's been raised is not an issue. We are trying to be good neighbors and we have tried to do the project right. Bryan Eckert I live at 259 32 nd Avenue across from the subject property. I am in full support of the proposed project. I think it's an enhancement to the neighborhood.

Hope Net is a good cannabis facility. They have served our City and their neighborhood well. Much before the existence of Hope Net, the energy that Steve and Kathy Smith have brought to the medical cannabis community says great things about these two individuals and this facility. They have put together a wonderful staff that understands the needs of the patients. This should be approved. It is in the best interest of our community and the best interest of the City. Michelle Aldrich I am speaking for Hope Net. It is one of the model dispensaries for the whole City. Steve and Kathy are great people. A lot of the patients live in Section 8 housing, and they can't medicate at home. These people feel safe at Hope Net. The whole neighborhood feels safer because Hope Net is there I hope you will vote for it. Richard Muller I met Steve and Kathy a year and a half ago. Since then, I have gone to their facility. Before we had access to go to Hope Net we met a group, the Patients Health Defense Union. A lot of us were poor, the prices of normal clubs were above what we could afford for our medicine. Rose Kenyon I am a medical cannabis patient. I've been in this area for 40 plus years and have been prescribed many different types of medications for the health issues that I have. I find that medical marijuana is best for me. I feel that since we have voted to have medical marijuana in the City, it's almost a travesty and a slap in the face that we have to deal with issues that are outside of being able to medicate at any time. These dispensaries are being eliminated. They are well established and reputable and not fly-by-night establishments. They do give compassion. And in our language that is no cost medication or little cost. I recommend that you take the proposal of your staff. John Caldera I am a United States Navy Veteran and a California card-carrying member and I have lived with HIV since November of 1995. Medical cannabis has helped keep me alive. I am here to speak on behalf of Hope Net, which is a phenomenal dispensary. They have done a lot for the community. I ask you to allow them to continue the services to so many patients in the community. Terrie Frye I'd like to say that I am grateful to Kathy and Steve Smith for the priorities of the Hope Net dispensary and for their donations to me. I have been able to quit taking medicine for depression, which didn't work anyway. I am not taking them anymore and I am not depressed. The only thing that would depress me now is if you didn't permit them to stay open. Rev. Randi Webster Hope Net is a model facility through compassion and community awareness and their striving to be better in helping patients. They care for their patients and open their doors to everyone. Please, do not take discretionary review. They are doing a fine job. Cathy Smith I am the owner and operator of Hope Net We are here to hopefully obtain the community's consent to operate. It's our goal to continue our compassion program to the terminally ill and we want to help as many as we can. We would like to thank the businesses and the community for their support and we would like to thank you people, the Planning Commission. We really have been a community minded organization. We would like to continue to be an organization that can service the community and we want you to let us keep operating and helping these nice people in San Francisco. Johnny Nolen When I became involved with the medical cannabis community, I realized I was helping the direct needs of the patients by obligating myself to a political movement to protect the rights of the patients. I met caregivers and listened to different people on how we can be integrated into San Francisco. I was impressed by their services and professionalism and community awareness. Hope Net helps San Francisco's largest compassion program by supplying medicine to severely ill patients. This is an important precedence to set with no insurance covered medical cannabis. Shona - Executive Director of a patient advocacy organization. I am nervous out of excitement that our City can be a model for the nation. We believe that Hope Net co-op should be a statement and standard for all to follow in this process, because of their unbelievable compassion program. We want permitted low impact costs for people with fixed income. They offer their space to the Women's Health Collective and other community groups. I believe the permitting of this compassionate co-op in San Francisco becoming the model for the nation. Leslie Thomas I am a patient that uses medical marijuana. I have gone to Hope Net on 9 th Street in order to obtain my medicine since they first opened. I feel comfortable going to Hope Net because they have made a conscious effort to make the neighborhood a clean and safe environment. Supervisor Maxwell I came today because I feel that it is very important and because this needs more clarification. As we talk about San Francisco being in a housing crisis, it is important that we understand what that really and truly means to all of us. As the Board of Supervisors, we have a responsibility to act on that crisis and create a clear direction on what we think can and should happen. As I look around and see the population of African Americans living the city - unlike any other city in this country - it concerns me. Something needs to be done. There needs to be a voice from the Board of Supervisors. That is what this legislation was about and this resolution is about. It was never about turning this Department upside down. It was never about making things so ridiculously hard for you to do. It was to say that there is a crisis and that the Board of Supervisors needs to have a policy dealing with that crisis. We have adopted plans for Rincon Hill in which there would never be a single unit of affordable housing built within the plan area. To balance this fact, we need land specifically set aside for affordable housing. The logical place to do this is in the Eastern Neighborhoods. That is where the vast majority of affordable housing is currently built and where neighborhoods welcome additional productive [PDR]. Let us make that city policy. There is an additional policy direction put forward in this resolution and it is also about land. We cannot undermine our viable blue collar industries to land speculations and we must set aside land for neighborhood improvements to happen concurrently with the new developments. These are sound planning and economic development principles. I believe they are worth including as the City's policy for the Northern/Eastern Neighborhoods. I want to make sure that plans brought forward to the Board of Supervisors are developed with clear policy guidance from the Board. That is what we are trying to do with this resolution. There are a couple of issues that I want to particularly talk about that I think were misunderstood. Regarding the production target of 64 percent affordable housing. What I am proposing is that the area plans brought forward by Planning staff will facilitate and lay-out a frame work such that 64 percent of our housing production within the Eastern Neighborhoods will be affordable for the housing production established in the Housing Element. First and foremost in that effort is the set aside of land for affordable housing. That will complement what we already get from inclusionary housing and what we do around acquisition and rehabilitation of existing buildings. Let me tell you what I am not saying. I am not saying that the inclusionary percentage should be raised to 64 percent and I am not saying that we need to meet the entire city's affordable housing production here or that we need to make up for past deficits of affordable housing. The other misunderstanding that I have heard is that the resolution makes all industrial lands off limits to new developments. That is not my intention. My intent in this resolution is to make the protection of existing businesses within the appropriate zones and sites a priority for the Department as it is drafted in the plan. Let us talk about land speculation and displacement of viable industrial businesses. I realize that we may loose some lands in the Eastern Neighborhoods but let us have a real discussion about land values and impacts to our city. Let us make sure that we appropriately address the displacement of people and businesses through the market-rate housing and office speculations. I want to end by saying that what we do here, and I know that you do know this, is extremely important to the City. The decisions we make will have profound repercussions for years and years to come. I think that is why it is important we have this discussion and that the Board of Supervisors has some say and directions. We need to do all of these in order to keep our city what it really truly is. In order to keep the balance of our City. Its real treasures are the people that live in the city and we have to do something about that. This should be a city about building middle class not importing them. We have to look at our industrial properties, land, and speculations. That is what this resolution is about. I hope that you will come up with other ways to consider this as you go through it. Rosario Ramirez You need to analyze impacts to low/middle income families before approving any legislation that will set the Eastern Neighborhoods policies. Families in those neighborhoods have lived there for generations. Other families have moved in the Eastern Neighborhoods because rents have increased in upper zoning neighborhoods. name_raw: Judith Hoyam, Board member of Friends of 1800
comment: We are dedicated to protect the City's Historic Resources. This garage addition would remove 2 parking spaces near shopping centers. The curb cut would appropriate for private use space that belongs to the City and general public and would remove a mature tree. In the 1900 nothing was constructed on Hartford Street and in 1902 it was all full. Every house was setback for landscaping. It is the simple characteristic of this block. None of the houses were constructed with garages. It was created that way to provide open space. We are asking the Commission to require that an independent historic evaluation by a qualified consultant be part of the Environmental Report. Mark Paez, Chair of Friends of 1800 and Co-Chair of Duboce Triangle Neighborhood Association This Planning Department really needs some policy guidance from this Commission to elevate this process and make more qualitative analysis for these types of proposals. This project in particular needs historic resource evaluation, environmental review, and careful policy consideration. We believe it is not ready for approval. Numerous garage additions to constructions in the Castro and Eureka Valley are being approved by the department without adequate historic evaluation and environmental review and in conflict with the criteria for the garage guidelines. The project is also contrary to the Transit First Policy of the General Plan and also the intentions of the Market-Octavia Plan by promoting the no longer required off-street parking. Take DR and require additional analysis. Charles Chase, Executive Director of San Francisco Heritage This project does not conform to the Planning Department procedure for garage additions and we question the validity of staff comments on the [Secretary of] Interior Standards application in this case. There has not been adequate environmental review and it violates the Transit First policy of the General Plan in the Planning Department. Insertion of garages has a potential negative impact on San Francisco's historic resources. It should be fully reviewed to determine the extent of the historic fabric loss, the applicability of the Interior Standards, and how the project meets the current policies and those proposed in the Market-Octavia Plan. Susan I want to echo the Friends of 1800's concern of the historic character of the neighborhood and the impact there. I wonder how the garage is going in without considering the mature tree. Finally, I have a concern about parking and taking these public parking spaces to convert it to private space. It would take away three spaces with the curb cut. Marcus Connen, Owner The house needs a lot of work. The entrance way and back porch are rotted and need to be replaced. It needs new bathroom and kitchen. The building is on a non-cement foundation and needs to be reinforced. The cost of this project is about $400,000 to renovate the building to the point that these units could be rented or to sell it. Currently it is my primary residence. It is virtually impossible to rent or sell a house in the Castro without parking. The parking is going to be underground and it is that way on many houses on the block. Gordon Atkinson, Architect The Planning Department has confirmed that this project conforms to the guidelines and regulations. The mandate of the Commission is to review projects only when there are extraordinary circumstances. We are asking permission to bring the building into compliance with DCP parking requirements for new residents, and to restore the historic ornamentation. There are no sidewalk improvements or removal of trees. We are proposing to build new concrete benches along the side walk as an amenity. There is nothing extraordinary or exceptional about this project. This property is not a landmark designation nor is it in a historic district.

name_raw: Brian Kuester, on behalf of Project Sponsor for item 8a
role_title: on behalf of Project Sponsor for item 8a
comment: When the project sponsor purchased the business, the ATM had been in place three years by then. They had no idea that there was no permit for it. As soon as they were notified by the department that a permit was required, they filed immediately. The charge for the use of the ATM is $1.50 where most other places charge $2.50 If anybody has a problem, the owners handle it right away. Danny Parker, General Council for Swipe USA LLC - Project Sponsor Representative for item 8c We have an alliance with Designer Brand.  Swipe' has been managing ATM's for seven years. They follow banking guidelines. One of the concerns is graffiti at this location and I want to assure you that Designer Brands owner works carefully with  Swipe' to ensure that any graffiti is removed clean within 24 hours.  Swipe' is a very responsible business and engages with the Police Department's Patrol Division. We have neighborhood support. I urge you to apply fundamental fairness to both ATM's and look at the contributions to the community. Jeff Christen I just want to point out that this belongs to the Cannabis Club and they will use the funds from the cannabis to fill the ATM machine. I do not know how legal that is. Imagine having an ATM and everything else at this one location Gary Bell [8c] I am here in support of the ATM. The very first goal of the Commerce Industry section of the General Plan is to maintain healthy and diverse economy. There are no banks anywhere within easy walking distances. In addition to contributing to the local economy, there is no adverse impact on city services from this machine. The machine has been in this location for over a year. Hasah Khader, Designer Brands Owner I have been doing business on Haight Street for the last 15 years. There were no ATM machines before and now we have more. There are no complaints and it is helping to bring more people to spend more money in our community. Many residents and merchants support the idea of having both ATM's on our street. Laurence Odhner I am the former owner of this place and during the interim term I noticed that other merchants added ATM's and none have been turned down, to the best of my knowledge. To turn down Mr. Khader's request, which is as valid as the others, it would be highly discriminatory. Marwan Ouziz, Technical Manager for Swipe Management Company Approve the conditional use. Swipe has been a respectful member of the San Francisco Business community and has extended the amount of service to our customers. Scott Hart, San Francisco Patrol Special Police  Swipe' has hired our services to patrol the ATM's at night and make sure that there are no problems. If there are any problems, they call Marwan and he contacts us to go out. Rodney The impression is that the ATM being next to the medical marijuana dispensary will bring a negative type of traffic. There could be a problem with marijuana and money. We are going backwards in the City. Look at the fact that there is more marijuana in the Haight. Putting money next to the dispensary is not a good idea. Michael Aldrich I am here in support of having the ATM's at both locations. I want to raise a couple of points; Mohna has worked very hard to have the medical dispensary working properly and this ATM brings accessibility to people in a wheel chair. This ATM charges only $1.5 which is much less than most ATM's. Juli Carter There were no ATM's before in the area. Walgreens put in the first and now there are a few. There is a need for an ATM on Sundays. These are the only ones available on Sundays when people come to the neighborhood and need to buy stuff or dine in the area. Rev. Randi Webster I'm speaking in favor of both ATM's because of accessibility for patients of the Medical Dispensary and because the community needs this service.

The proposal includes reconfiguring the sidewalk by making it continuous and accessible. This has gone to the Department of Public Works and it has been approved. Linda Goldman Pedestrian safety on our block is very important to us. Sululagi Palegk I think what they are proposing would be great if there were more space on that street. The street is so narrow that even for fire fighters it is very difficult to get down the hill. We would like our area to be cut it from the plan area. We do not really relate to Hayes Valley for the Market/Octavia plan. All the elements work together and it is important to keep the integrity of it than piece it out. Developments in the pipeline are waiting for this plan to move forward. I urge you to approve the plan without the completion of the historic survey. The community has truly come together to have a plan that is fully community based. We need to go forward and have this plan adopted. People choose to live in certain areas and we need to honor those choices. All areas in the city do not need to be the same. We need to give people the choice of living in an area that is pedestrian oriented. Jason Henderson The summary this evening is really compromising. We are willing to move this process forward. What needs to happen is a better management of off-street parking spaces. Steve Vettel The original idea for this plan was to have community consensus of what development should be in the area. This is basically to replace four existing antennas for channels 2, 4, 5 and 7 in the tower. They would be of the same length but slightly curved. It would eliminate interference issues. This is because of federal mandates. For many years this sector had been in constant use. Nextel, law enforcement, and first responders depended on the eight hundred mega hertz. As the use by law enforcement became greater then expected, there was inevitable interference. The remedy was straightforward. The result was that Sprint-Nextel would remain with the eight hundred mega hertz. They allocated nine hundred mega hertz to accommodate first responders. This is a national play and is not just about Sutro Tower. Sprint is not on the tower. One antenna is going to serve existing customers - KSFS and KDTV - to reach across twin peaks in their program to broadcast in Spanish. It is more important because the competitive broadcast station, Telemundo, decided to withdraw from the news business. San Francisco's Spanish population relies only on KSFS and KDTV for news. KGO has applied to receive only broadcast antennas that are five and 12 feet in diameter. Those antennas are for reception only. Gene Zastrow, General Manager of Sutro Tower I am going to focus on some of the project details that Bob [Robert McArthur] has described. The project is to replace four small BAS [Broadcast Auxiliary Service] antennas. They are used for electronic newsgathering. The fifth antenna would be for the same purpose for KDTV and KSFS. The Sutro Tower is the most appropriate location for these antennas. It is the only location that could receive the signal. There is no other location that could serve for the purpose. They would operate on the same spectrum as the existing one. They are virtually invisible from any public location. For thirty-five years, Sutro Tower has provided a facility to local stations to provide cultural and educational entertainment and informational services to the public. This project would enhance our ability to keep the public informed on an emergency nature. Kristin Jacobsen, Sprint-Nextel This project is being undertaken in order to comply directly with the Federal Communications Commission [FCC] order. It is a necessary and critical component of this order. It is designed to eliminate harmful interference to public safety communicators, particularly first responders. Our proposed project in San Francisco is part of a nation wide undertaking. Sutro Towers is one of twenty locations throughout the Bay Area that would need to do these changes. The replacements have already been discussed. They do not produce any radio frequency. On October 24, the Board of Supervisors voted unanimously to uphold the Categorical Exemption determination. I just want to mention that I am here because Nextel has partnered with public safety organizations and broadcasters around the country. We ask and seek your assistance to comply with the Federal Communications Commission order. Walter - Forrest Knowles We are not here to oppose this project. We are here because this is a mandatory discretionary review hearing The Forrest Knowles is an over 400 home neighborhood adjacent to Twin Peaks Neighborhood and Middle Town. Sutro Towers was constructed in our RH-1 neighborhood. It was approved in 1960 and constructed in the early 1970's. It is authorized by a conditional use. The Planning Code prohibits transmission towers in a RH-1 zoning district unless they are there by necessity. In 1988 Sutro Tower decided to expand. They were faced with a denial of that conditional use. The Planning Commission at that point determined that all future Sutro Tower issues would require a mandatory discretionary review. We ask staff again and again the same question: is this permit application that makes a showing necessity? Are there any alternatives to the addition to more stuff to Sutro Tower? Could some of that stuff be placed anywhere else? Doris Linnenbach, Member of the Twin Peaks Association For forty years I have been attending meetings regarding Sutro Towers. For years, our residents have endured horrible noises and signs of earthquake notations. A few weeks ago, in the Examiner Newspaper, there was an article about garage doors that could lock up because of antenna interference. Many people in our neighborhood are having problems with garage doors because of Sutro Tower. One of our neighbors who is 90 years old has not been able to find a company that could offer service in case of an emergency because of interference from the Sutro Tower.

NONE At this time members of the public may address the Commission on items of interest to the public that are within the subject matter jurisdiction of the Commission except agenda items. With respect to agenda items your opportunity to address the Commission will be afforded when the item is reached in the meeting with one exception. When the agenda item has already been reviewed in a public hearing at which members of the public were allowed to testify and the Commission has closed the public hearing your opportunity to address the Commission must be exercised during the Public Comment portion of the Calendar. Each member of the public may address the Commission for up to three minutes. The Brown Act forbids a commission from taking action or discussing any item not appearing on the posted agenda including those items raised at public comment. In response to public comment the commission is limited to: (1) responding to statements made or questions posed by members of the public or (2) requesting staff to report back on a matter at a subsequent meeting or directing staff to place the item on a future agenda. (Government Code Section 54954.2(a)) None

name_raw: Matt Franklin, Director of Major's Office of Housing
role_title: Director of Major's Office of Housing
comment: Area medium income in San Francisco is the major engine that drives a lot of affordable housing programs. It is set by United States' Housing and Redevelopment and is 60% for rental and 100% for owners. San Francisco has a severe economic disparity. There is a challenge for rental housing. Ownership is dramatically higher. Most of families in the City pay more than fifty percent of their income toward housing. Public Housing: Agencies and Departments dealing with Housing: Major's Office of Housing San Francisco Redevelopment San Francisco Housing Authority Human Services Department of Public Health Four percent of the total public housing in San Francisco is administered by the Housing Authority. 40 percent of public housing serves singles and senior citizens. Our challenge for public housing is funding. Affordable Housing: The Major's Office of Housing and the San Francisco Redevelopment Agency are the capital funding [source]. We would typically put up 30 to 50 percent of development cost. We leverage other sources such as Tax Credit Programs. We target people with 25 to 50 of median-income for 55-year terms. Almost 50 percent of affordable housing we build are family size. Our 10-year plan is targeting permanent housing rather than shelter and transitional. We have Homeownerships Programs that includes help with down payments, owner occupied rehabilitation and lead program. Doug Shoemaker, Deputy Director, Mayor's Office of Housing Inclusionary Housing: The policy for Inclusionary is for projects with four or more units and includes three options: 15 percent if provided on site. 20percent if provided off site. 20 percent if providing an in-lieu fee. The Major's Office of Housing administers what comes through the Section 315 policy. Frequently, small projects choose the on site unit option while bigger projects choose off site. The Inclusionary Program has three new improvements: E-mail sign up for interested parties [will receive e-mail with information when list of projects is updated] Weekly updates to counseling agencies. Lottery requirement for resale to keep objective criteria. Pending Legislation, forwarded to Board of Supervisors, would clear: Marketing outreach to public with different languages. Fee update every year to represent cost issues. Minimum occupancy guidelines. Fixed formula for resale. The five most recent major plans and projects in the city includes at least 30 percent of affordable housing. [Bayview, Mission Bay, Transbay, Hunters point, Treasure Island] We would like to see in the Eastern Neighborhood private, non-profit and for profit get together and create more affordable housing. Bernie Chodin Thanked the Director for the presentation. Housing has been addressed for low and high income but not for middle income. We need a Housing Element that deals with sustainable resources to meet our needs. He advocated to not sell land, but development rights to use ground rents. Suggested the organization of public/private partnerships for development corporations. Calvin Welsch There are about 180,000 units under rent control in San Francisco. It is important to understand different programs of housing and their policies [rent control, affordable, market rate, below market rate and public] There is very little that this Commission could do about public housing, but so much for below market rate and affordable housing. Affordable housing production is about policy and advocacy. Octavia Boulevard Plan seems to ignore the question of designated sites for affordable housing. I had assurance by Staff that it would not happen in the Eastern Neighborhood Plan and hope it would be much more transparent. It is very important to map different types of housing built over the last decade. The Eastern Neighborhood Plan is an incredible and important resource to build affordable housing. Mark Solomon We need to prioritize the plans that are coming out of the Planning Department. It is important to see what the city needs first and then plan developments based on those needs. None of the plans -- Eastern and Market-Octavia Neighborhoods -- reflect acknowledgement of changes in the market. Most of my coworkers, friends, and my student's families no longer can stay here. You need to build housing for those of us who work in the City and want to live here.
